> stan-mode is based off of emacs cc-mode, which has a very customizable indentation engine, which you can read about  here. It's based off of the syntatic class of the first element in the line, which in your example would be arglist-intro (you can find this using C-c C-s). messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] simple inference problem given prior distributions and sum of variables observed
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] simple inference problem given prior distributions and sum of variables observed
messages.body_plain:
Your model's only identified by the prior, but that's no big deal
in this case.  There's also only a single degree of freedom, because
given a, b = 4 - a.  From your note, you're assuming the density

  p(a) propto normal(a | 1, 1) * normal(1 - a | 2, 1.5)

In Stan, you can do that directly and define b along the way or not:

  parameters {
    real a;
  }
  transformed parameters {
    real b;
    b <- 4 - a;
  }
  model {
    a ~ normal(1, 1);
    b ~ normal(2, 1.5);
  }

You could've also skipped the transformed parameters block and
written the second line of the model as:

  (4 - a) ~ normal(2, 1.5);

Either way, given your intent, you can ignore the Jacobian warning.

This behaves well and produces a posterior sample with mean
and quantiles:

      mean se_mean   sd  2.5%   25%   50%   75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
a     1.30    0.02 0.83 -0.30  0.73  1.27  1.84  2.93  1470    1
b     2.70    0.02 0.83  1.07  2.16  2.73  3.27  4.30  1470    1
lp__ -0.65    0.02 0.71 -2.59 -0.82 -0.38 -0.20 -0.15  1980    1

That doesn't match your report from Infer.NET, but I have no idea
what Infer.NET does to fit.

- Bob

> On Jan 2, 2016, at 11:38 AM, Nikolay Evdokimov <kolyaev...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hello. I am new to Stan and I try to solve simple inference problem.
>
> I would like to solve a simple one before applying Stan to making inference in more complex models.
>
>
>
> About the problem. The task is to estimate posterior destibution for variables given some observed values.
>
>
>
> Given:
>
> a ~ normal(mu=1, std =1);
>
> b ~ normal(mu=2, std = 1.5);
>
> In our single observation we get information that a+b = sumValue.  Let’s fix it at 4.
>
> What is pdf for a variable now? I mean pdf(a | a+b==sumValue).
>
>
>
> I have solved this problem with Matlab and Infer.Net library, but I can’t reproduce it with Stan.
>
> I have read the manual, and especially  part 20. on Problematic Posteriors,  on  and some threads ( https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/rKxrs2gsPr4.) on Forum. But I still can’t understand if Stan is suitable for this inference task.
>
>
>
>
> The problem can be easily solved analytically:
>
>
>
>
> pdfOf(a | a+b== sumValue)By(x) = pdfA(x).*pdfB(2-sumValue-x) / k, where k = Integral(pdfA(x).*pdfB(sumValue-x)).
>
>
>
>
> See matlab code for this:
>
> x = [-2:0.01:8];
>
> pdfA = @(x)normpdf(x, 1, 1);
>
> pdfB = @(x)normpdf(x, 2, 1.5);
>
> sumValue = 4;
>
>
>
> pdfA_condNoAdj = @(x)pdfA(x).*pdfB(sumValue-x);
>
> pdfA_condTotal =  integral(pdfA_condNoAdj ,-10,10);
>
> pdfA_cond = @(x)pdfA_condNoAdj(x)/pdfA_condTotal;
>
>
>
> figure(1);clf
>
> hold on;
>
> plot(x, pdfA(x));
>
> plot(x, pdfB(x));
>
> plot(x, pdfA_cond(x));
>
> hold off;
>
> grid on;
>
> legend('pdfA','pdfB','pdfA cond');
>
>
>
> So we see that posterior distribution for A is easily calculated.
>
>
>
> Now let’s try to that in infer.net <http://infer.net>
>
>         static void Main(string[] args)
>
>         {
>
>             Variable<double> a = Variable.GaussianFromMeanAndVariance(1, 1).Named("a");
>
>             Variable<double> b = Variable.GaussianFromMeanAndVariance(2, 1.5).Named("b");
>
>             Variable<double> c;
>
>
>
>             c = a + b;
>
>             c.ObservedValue = 4;
>
>
>
>             InferenceEngine engine = new InferenceEngine();
>
>             engine.Algorithm = new ExpectationPropagation();
>
>             Console.WriteLine("Dist over x=" + engine.Infer(a));
>
>             Console.ReadKey();
>
>         }
>
> The engine makes inference that is close to Matlab’s version, but not identical. Posterior PdfA  is normal with mu=1.4, std = 0.6.
>
>
>
> How can I get posterior  distribution for a in Stan?
>
> I try to do something like following:
>
> data {   real cInput; // s.e. of effect estimates   }
>
> parameters {   real a;    real b; }
>
> model {
>
>     a ~ normal(0,1);
>
>     b ~ normal(0,1);
>
>     cInput<-a + b;
>
> }
>
> And I would NOT like use model where C = a+b + noise, because it would change the problem.
>
>
>
>
>
> Can Stan solve the problem above the way Matlab and Infer.Net did?
>
> How can I infer posterior probability density function?
>
> Is there some way to assign observed value to linear combination (or any function) of parameters?
>
>
>
> Regards,
>
> Nikolay
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Thanks a lot. That worked and helped. I tried the same for recovering random walk with noisy observations and that worked.

data {
  vector[10] yObserved ; // s.e. of effect estimates
}

parameters {
  vector[10] dx;
}

transformed parameters
{
   vector[10] yTrue;
   vector[10] yObservationErrors;
   yTrue <-  cumulative_sum(dx);
   yObservationErrors <- yObserved  -yTrue;
}

messages.subject: Modelling a classical nonlinear state space model benchmark - problems inferring latent states
messages.subject_clean: Modelling a classical nonlinear state space model benchmark - problems inferring latent states
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan developers and users

can you please help me model in Stan this classical nonlinear state space model benchmark, used for example in the experiments of these NIPS papers http://arxiv.org/pdf/1306.2861.pdf http://arxiv.org/pdf/1506.03338v3.pdf

So far, I get poor results in Stan for it, divergent RHAT and wrong parameter fits and poor likelihood.The attached file stan_nonlin_param.py has the python/pystan code to create the data, and then infer the latent states x and the parameters a,b,c,sigma.

I tried to split the problem in smaller chunks and understand better what fails in my approach. The attached file stan_nonlin.py has the parameters set to the correct values and only needs to infer the posteriors of the latent states x. Stan also fails to do this, which is otherwise quite easy for a vanilla particle filter/sequential importance sampling method. Can you please help me improve the model:

1) In general, is my coding of a state space model too direct and naive? I am basically just encoding the joint distribution consisting of state transition and observation probabilities. Should I instead really code a full particle filter with particles and ancestors in STAN? The papers cited do Particle Gibbs Sampling, but it seems this would be too cumbersome to encode in STAN, so I hoped that some ellegant small model can do the job instead

2) does the nonlinear state space transition and the nonlinear transformation in the observation probability cause any specific problems for STAN? The y~ x^2 part makes the latent states distribution bimodal, is this an issue for STAN?
Also the term weighted by b=25 is problematic, the nonlinear state evolution term. State x inference works a bit better with b=0 (so a linear state evolution), but still seems worse than a particle filter forward sampling.

3) how should I change my Stan settings? Any special step sizes for the NUTS, other priors on the parameters? Will ADVI work better for the task - it is currently not available in pystan but I can try with cmdstan?

have a successful new year and thanks a lot for your help
Nikolay

Hi, initial  points could be an issue.  If you have x[1] ~ normal(4,0.05), then you could be getting problems with default initial values.  Probably best to supply reasonable inits.  Or reparameterize so that all parameters are on a unit scale.

If convergence is slow I don’t recommend ADVI as a solution.  ADVI is more appropriate when your model is expensive to run because of big data or whatever.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Skew normals likelihood bug?
messages.body_plain:
It looks approximately correct.  For this model:

  parameters {
    real theta;
  }
  model {
    theta ~ skew_normal(1, 10, -1000);
  }

I get

======================================
> fit <- stan("skew.stan", control=list(stepsize=0.001, adapt_delta=0.9999), fit=fit)

SAMPLING FOR MODEL 'skew' NOW (CHAIN 1).
...
Chain 4, Iteration: 2000 / 2000 [100%]  (Sampling)
#  Elapsed Time: 0.506487 seconds (Warm-up)
#                0.113476 seconds (Sampling)
#                0.619963 seconds (Total)

Warning messages:
1: There were 1409 divergent transitions after warmup. Increasing adapt_delta may help.
2: Examine the pairs() plot to diagnose sampling problems

> print(fit)
Inference for Stan model: skew.
4 chains, each with iter=2000; warmup=1000; thin=1;
post-warmup draws per chain=1000, total post-warmup draws=4000.

       mean se_mean   sd   2.5%    25%   50%   75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
theta -6.73    0.34 5.88 -20.67 -10.19 -5.52 -2.13  0.78   308 1.01
lp__   0.22    0.04 0.67  -1.65   0.07  0.48  0.64  0.69   363 1.01

Samples were drawn using NUTS(diag_e) at Mon Jan  4 12:21:00 2016.
For each parameter, n_eff is a crude measure of effective sample size,
and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at
convergence, Rhat=1).
==================================

The actual mean is -7.0, so we're within the MCMC std error, but I'm worried
because of the divergent translations and low n_eff.  Going up to 20K iterations,
I get this:

       mean se_mean   sd   2.5%    25%   50%   75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
theta -6.93    0.10 5.97 -21.28 -10.35 -5.74 -2.22  0.70  3517    1
lp__   0.20    0.01 0.70  -1.79   0.05  0.46  0.64  0.69  3746    1

So I think what's happening is that it's finding it hard to get out into
the negative tail of this distribution.

But you probably want to reparameterize to get rid of the divergent
transitions (these are cases where there is an arithmetic underflow or
overflow in the basic math).  We're probably not doing a good job on
the log(1 + erf) term, which should really have some tricks played on
it algebraically.

In fact, looking at the implementation that's in there now, it's
pretty bad in terms of efficiency (lots of repeated subterms), but
it should be about as good as we can do for arithmetic stability
until we write a composed log-erfc (the code uses the erf/erfc identities
correctly).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi again,

I'm trying to understand how my model does / doesn't converge. One suggestions was to specify initial values, and as a way to see if there is something fundamental broken, I wanted to specify the "true" values as the initial values and see if it still fails to converge.

(In doing so, I realized the documentation for RStan is sparse on this, and the documentation for Stan doesn't fill in many of the holes.) It seems I can specify the initial values for only some of the variables, though the documentation doesn't say anything about this. What happens with the others? Are they random, or 0?

Thanks,
David

Dear list,

I usually use Stan through rstan and rstan often via Sage's version of R. Since  Sage often updates in ways needing recompilation of R and installed packages, I have to reinstall rstan more often tan more "normal" users of this package.

A recent reinstallation failed :

ERROR: loading failed
* removing ‘/usr/local/sage-7.0/local/lib/R/library/rstan’

I noticed that the "StanHeaders" packages was also installed, at version 2.9.0. So I worked around the problem by desinstalling StanHeaders, reinstalling the 2.0.0 version and reinstalling rstan (successfully).

Plus, of course, the implicit "when will rstan-2.9.0 be released ?"...

HTH,

--
Emmanuel Charpentier

messages.subject: rstan 2.9.0 released or not released depending on your perspective
messages.subject_clean: rstan 2.9.0 released or not released depending on your perspective
messages.body_plain:
A lot of people have been running into problems with rstan installations yesterday and today.
Version 2.9 of the Stan Math Library, the other Stan Library, and CmdStan were released before the NIPS conference in early December. However, rstan could not be uploaded to CRAN at that time because CRAN prefers "a month or two" between uploads and rstan 2.8.2 was uploaded on November 26.
The StanHeaders R package (which essentially includes the Stan Math Library and the other Stan Library) was uploaded to CRAN January 3 but that is really only relevant to package developers (and had no effect on OpenMx)
The rstan package was uploaded to CRAN today, but we have no control on when CRAN will approve it (typically less than a day), when binary versions will be available for Mac and Windows (typically a day or two after approval) or when those binary versions will appear on the CRAN mirror you download from (typically a day or two after the binaries are built).

For most users, rstan is effectively released when a binary is available on their CRAN mirror, in which case 2.9.0 is not released yet. For some users, rstan is effectively released when the source is available, in which case it is perpetually released because the source is always available on GitHub. I suppose you could say rstan is effectively released when the source is tagged on GitHub, which I don't do until CRAN approves it, in which case 2.9.0 is not released yet.

If you are attempting to use Stan today, I would suggest not trying to update an existing installation. Failing that, you can install StanHeaders and rstan 2.8.2 via

devtools::install_url("https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/StanHeaders/StanHeaders_2.8.0.tar.gz")
install.packages("rstan", dependencies = TRUE)
If you do not want to use rstan 2.8.2 today and are on Windows, you can execute

install.packages("http://win-builder.r-project.org/46ZTjEGxl4O9/rstan_2.9.0.zip",
                 repos = NULL, dependencies = TRUE)
to install an unofficial but identical to the rstan 2.9.0 binary that would be official if CRAN approves what I uploaded today.
If you do not want to use rstan 2.8.2 today but are not on Windows, you can execute

devtools::install_github("stan-dev/rstan", ref = "develop", subdir = "rstan/rstan")
to install the develop version of rstan, which would be identical to rstan 2.9.0 if CRAN approves what I uploaded today and I can then tag it as v2.9.0.

If you are reading this message more than a few seconds after it was first posted, then some of the above may no longer be operative depending on when you read it.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to manually provide the gradient of log probability?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] How to manually provide the gradient of log probability?
messages.body_plain:
For all the gory details on the C++ and derivatives, see:

  http://arxiv.org/abs/1509.07164

The in-between solution for external libraries without gradients
is to template out the scalar type.  But if you have gradients,
then you want the above.  Sorry it's so long --- you only need
the first bit on how to write simple functions.

For the interfacing with Stan itself, see:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Contributing-New-Functions-to-Stan

It explains where things have to go in the symbol table to be
picked up by the Stan parser.

One of our to-do items for next year is making Stan extensible at
run time, which should be possible given that it's header only.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Dramatically slower runtimes after upgrading to rstan 2.8.2
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Dramatically slower runtimes after upgrading to rstan 2.8.2
messages.body_plain:
In case anyone's interested, I finally figured this out. Turns out the problem was that I neglected to call

Sys.setenv(MAKEFLAGS = "-j4")

before installing RStan. In my defense, I was just following the letter of the instructions on the RStan Getting Started page, which says "For source builds only (which is atypical on Windows and OS X), set the number of processes to use for the build to the number of cores on your machine you want to devote to the build." My install of R is not from source and I'm not building RStan from source, yet evidently this still makes a difference. Lesson learned. Thanks again for everyone's suggestions, and hopefully this thread might save someone else from the same boneheaded and frustrating mistake.

Now back to fitting models!

> In case anyone's interested, I finally figured this out. Turns out the problem was that I neglected to call
>
> Sys.setenv(MAKEFLAGS = "-j4")

I'm glad things are working well for you again, but that can't be the solution to the problem you were facing. The -j4 only affects the installation time (by using 4 cores to install it). It doesn't have any effect on the runtime, although you can execute the chains in parallel using as many cores as you want (either by specifying the cores argument when you call stan() or sampling() or by setting options(mc.cores = ?) in advance). So, something else must have caused / solved the slow runtimes, and I hope that it stays solved when you upgrade to 2.9.0 sometime this week.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Possible to use parameter values from optimization as initial values for sampling within rstan?
messages.body_plain:
Optimization and sampling _answer different questions_.  Optimization
gives a _single_ MAP estimate of the parameters which might be okay
on average in some  cases, but does not yield reasonable uncertainty
quantifications.  Sampling, on the other hand, explores _all_ parameters
that are consistent with the data.  In all but a low-dimensional models,
the neighborhoods in parameters space that are most consistent with
the data are very far away from the mode where optimization ends.

There are lots of pathologies that could be affecting your model.  You
could have regions of parameter space that are consistent with the
data but very hard to fit (especially likely if you have hierarchical
structure).  You could also have non-identifiabilities, in which case
the neighborhoods of consistent parameter values are very complex
and hard to explore.  In any case, starting at the optimum does
absolutely nothing to help.

Below is some code I used to use, but it never ended up saving me any time so I’ve since gone back to using random inits. YMMV.
rng_seed = 1111
model_file = 'foo.stan'

stan_model = stan(model_file, data = data, chains = 0)

lp_fun <- function(y) {lp = log_prob(stan_model, y); return(ifelse(is.na <http://is.na>(lp),-Inf,lp))}
gr_lp_fun <- function(y) grad_log_prob(stan_model, y)

n_each_par = sapply(stan_model@par_dims,function(x)ifelse(length(x)==0,1,prod(x)))
n_each_par = n_each_par[-length(n_each_par)]
n_pars = sum(n_each_par)

initf = function(){
    lp__ = -Inf
    while(is.infinite(lp__)){
        init = runif(n_pars,-1,1)
        lp__ = lp_fun(init)
    }
    constrain_pars(stan_model,init)
}

message("Finding finite inits.")
optim_init = unconstrain_pars(stan_model,initf())

message('Optimizing.')
set.seed(rng_seed)

ptm = proc.time()
o = optim(optim_init,lp_fun,gr=gr_lp_fun,method='BFGS',
    control=list(fnscale=-1,maxit=100000,reltol=.Machine$double.eps), hessian=TRUE)
message(sprintf('Optimizing took %s minutes.',round((proc.time() - ptm)[3]/60),1))

initf_optim = function()constrain_pars(stan_model,o$par)

# then use init=initf_optim in the stan call

messages.body_plain:
It would help to know what you're doing, because it
depends on what the "complex stuff" is.

The point is that every expression that gets evaluated
and assigned to a temporary or used in an operation with
a parameter adds to the autodiff cost.

To be more concrete, with

  matrix foo(real y, real mu) {
     return normal_log(y, mu, 1);
  }

and

  matrix foo(real y, real mu, real sigma) {
    return normal_log(y, mu, sigma);
  }

calling foo(y, mu) vs. foo(y, mu, 1) will have the same cost.
So passing data in doesn't intrinsically have any cost (at least not
one you're going to be able to measure).

- Bob

[after a longer holiday-hiatus]

Bob,
thanks for the pointers (and sorry for not remembering, checking the manual better).

I also looked at the hurdle model, and analog to what you
were showing in the manual for the poisson model there is a
faster version to calculate the cdf for the negative binomial distribution.
I'll post this when I am sure I got it right.

I had troubles implementing this because, i believe, the example
for the hurdle model on page 115 has a small but consequential error:
When implementing the truncation, I think the code increments the log posterior by
 -log(poissonCDF(0,lambda))      instead of the correct
 -log(1-poissonCDF(0,lambda)).

Alternatively, log(1-exp(-lambda)) is already the CCDF, and not the CDF as
it sais on page 115.

Or am I misunderstanding something/not reading carefully enough?

Guido

> >   else

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Thanks Bob, this answers my question, i.e. specifically I intend to make the initial PK concentration of each patient in my population a parameter. That is, during inference this will be set to 0 for time t=0 for all patients, but for simulation purposes I find it more convenient to have a function which can start simulating a patient from different initials.

Best,
Sebastian

On Wednesday, January 6, 2016 at 8:18:03 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> It would help to know what you're doing, because it
> depends on what the "complex stuff" is.
>
> The point is that every expression that gets evaluated
> and assigned to a temporary or used in an operation with
> a parameter adds to the autodiff cost.
>
> To be more concrete, with
>
>   matrix foo(real y, real mu) {
>      return normal_log(y, mu, 1);
>   }
>
> and
>
>   matrix foo(real y, real mu, real sigma) {
>     return normal_log(y, mu, sigma);
>   }
>
> calling foo(y, mu) vs. foo(y, mu, 1) will have the same cost.
> So passing data in doesn't intrinsically have any cost (at least not
> one you're going to be able to measure).
>
> - Bob
>
>
> > On Jan 6, 2016, at 3:27 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi!
> >
> > Nowadays I tend to write pretty general user defined functions for my models and I wonder what the numeric cost is if I add more arguments to the function which I only call with data arguments. An example:
> >
> > # simple function
> > matrix foo(real a, real b) {
> >   # do complex stuff here
> >   return(result);
> > }
> >
> > Now suppose I call foo in my model block with a and b being parameters in the model. The autodiff will calculate gradients wrt to a and b. However, what if I extend that function to
> >
> > # expanded function
> > matrix foo2(real a, real b, real c) {
> >   # do more general complex stuff here
> >   return(result);
> > }
> >
> >
> > But I call again in my model block the function foo2 with a and b being parameters while variable c was declared in the transformed data block (for example). The question is: Does this increase the cost for autodiff during sampling?
> >
> > I am asking as it can be convenient to make functions more complex than possilby needed during the inference step, i.e. during simulation it may be more convenient to have a more general function.
> >
> > Many thanks!
> >
> > Best,
> > Sebastian

> On Jan 7, 2016, at 10:04 AM, Yao Xiong <xy.xi...@gmail.com> wrote:

>  31:          prob[n, j, 1] <- normal_cdf((gamma[1]-a[j]*theta[n]-delta[j]), 0, sigma[j]);

>  32:          prob[n, j, C] <- 1 - sum(prob[n, j, 1:4]);

>  33:          Y[n, j] ~ categorical(prob[n, j]);
>                                                 ^

The error messages says you used:

> int ~ categorical(real[])

That is,  Y[n, j] is an int and prob[n, j] is an *array* of reals.

You can then see that the available argument signatures are:

>   int ~ categorical(vector)
>   int[] ~ categorical(vector)

So the mismatch is that you've provided a real[] argument (array
of reals) and the multivariate distributions all require *vector* parameters.

There's an entire chapter of the manual near the front devoted
to arrays vs. vectors and their usage in Stan.  Hint:  It's more like
MATLAB than R or BUGS.

Rather than to_vector, which does copying, you want to read the
chapter of the Stan manual on arrays, so you'll understand why I'm
about to suggest that you declare prob as

  vector[C] prob[N, J];

an N x J array of C-vectors, rather than as an N x J x C array.

But that's still a holdover from BUGS style.  Stan has local variables,
so you should just declare

  vector[C] prob;

and define that in the loop.  But your code there isn't wrong so
much as suboptimally coded (it would have been wrong in BUGS):

 for (n in 1:N) {
>      for (j in 1:J) {
>       for (c in 2:(C-1)) {
>       prob[n, j, c] <- normal_cdf((gamma[c]-a[j]*theta[n]-delta[j]), 0, sigma[j]) - normal_cdf((gamma[c-1]-a[j]*theta[n]-delta[j]), 0, sigma[j]); }
>       prob[n, j, 1] <- normal_cdf((gamma[1]-a[j]*theta[n]-delta[j]), 0, sigma[j]);
>       prob[n, j, C] <- 1 - sum(prob[n, j, 1:4]);
>       Y[n, j] ~ categorical(prob[n, j, 1:C]);   // here is the bug
>      }
>   }
> }

You want to define prob[1] and prob[C] outside of the loop for C.

But if you're just trying to code up an ordinal logit, we have that
built in.

- Bob

No!  It means it's a C-vector.  But that's all you need.  It's
a local variable and can get redefined in each loop iteration.
Much more efficient than allocating a huge array and filling it
and then just throwing it away.

all that munging of the CDFs for you.   It looks like you're using
probit, but logit is much much faster to compute and gives almost
identical (albeit differently scaled) results.

- Bob

messages.subject: Spatially correlated probit regression
messages.subject_clean: Spatially correlated probit regression
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am using Stan to model and simulate precipitation occurrence using probit regression.  The latent Gaussian process (GP) is a regression on some covariates -- the theoretical variance of the latent GP is by definition 1.  As the latent GP is unobserved, there are no observed residuals.  What I have done so far is obtain posterior distributions of the beta coefficients that make up the latent GP for a network of 13 locations, with the beta coefficients being spatially correlated via partial sill and range parameters.

However, I would also like to infer the spatial correlation of the GP "residuals".  For example, at a single site, simulation can proceed by calculating the mean function of the latent GP, and perturbing with a mean-zero, variance unity random sample.  I would like to extend this to multisite.  What I am thinking is if I can obtain the noise from the bernoulli function, I can infer the spatial correlation of this noise, and use the correlation matrix to produce realizations from a mean-zero multivariate normal distribution.  The diagonal of the correlation matrix would be 1, thus preserving the variance unity of probit regression.

Long story short: is there a way to get at the noise of the bernoulli function?

Thanks so much.

Andrew Verdin

messages.body_plain:
I don't understand what you mean by the "noise of the Bernoulli
function".  If you mean y ~ bernoulli(theta) or bernoulli_log(y, theta),
they're both functions, so there's no noise arising from the functions
themselves.

If you think about residuals, though, what you're getting is that
Pr[y = 1] = theta, so the "noise" is all packed into theta.  If
theta = 0.55 and y = 1, then the residual in some sense is (1 - .55),
or you can think in terms of log loss, which is -log(.55) (where
-log(1) = 0, or no noise).  You just have to be careful to flip everything
for y = 0 cases.

- Bob

> On Jan 8, 2016, at 3:19 PM, David Manheim <davidm...@gmail.com> wrote:

Run multiple chains and evaluate R-hat and use our effective
sample size calculations.

But yes, it almost certainly implies that the model's not
converging because the variable lp has nowhere near the same
posterior mean in two chains.

> 2) How should I prevent this? I'd prefer not to specify the initialization, but that may prevent it from converging to strange places. Alternatively, I can lengthen warmup, or alter parameters?

Reparameterization can often help.

> 3) Can I exclude the chain? (No, I'm sure.) Can I consider the median instead of the mean value of the posterior? (Implicitly excluding it, since I have many other chains?)

Not safely.  You can look at posterior medians (in theory,
the posterior median is the estimate minimizing expected
absolute error whereas the posterior mean minimizes expected
squared error [i.e., Euclidean distance]).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan Reference Manual - an easy question on a mixture model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Stan Reference Manual - an easy question on a mixture model
messages.body_plain:
Mixtures can be hard to fit, but that one has enough data
and is well separated enough.

The problem you're likely running into is running with the default four
chains.  With mixtures, there's an index-swapping problem.  See
the chapter on problematic posteriors.

If you fit with one chain, the fit looks OK:

            mean se_mean   sd    2.5%     25%     50%     75%   97.5% n_eff Rhat
theta[1]    0.27    0.00 0.04    0.20    0.24    0.27    0.30    0.34   656    1
theta[2]    0.50    0.00 0.03    0.43    0.48    0.50    0.52    0.56  1000    1
theta[3]    0.23    0.00 0.04    0.17    0.21    0.23    0.26    0.31   629    1
mu[1]       8.70    0.01 0.17    8.37    8.59    8.70    8.81    9.02   528    1
mu[2]       0.00    0.00 0.10   -0.21   -0.07    0.00    0.06    0.19   526    1
mu[3]       5.90    0.01 0.19    5.51    5.77    5.91    6.04    6.28   616    1
lp__     -477.71    0.08 1.50 -481.62 -478.55 -477.38 -476.57 -475.76   393    1

mu[1] just squeaked into the 97.5% interval, but everything else was in its
50% interval.

- Bob

P.S.  You want to define log_theta as a temp and reuse rather than computing
log(theta) N times.

...
model {
  real log_ps[K];
  vector[K] log_theta;
  log_theta <- log(theta);
  mu ~ normal(0, 50);

  for (n in 1:N) {
    for (k in 1:K)

      log_ps[k] <- log_theta[k] + normal_log(y[n], mu[k], 1);
    increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log_ps));

  }
}

messages.subject: Re: rstan 2.9.0 released unconditionally
messages.subject_clean: rstan 2.9.0 released unconditionally
messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, January 5, 2016 at 1:55:17 PM UTC-5, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> For most users, rstan is effectively released when a binary is available on their CRAN mirror, in which case 2.9.0 is not released yet.

I think 2.9.0 binaries are available on most mirrors now. The main features of Stan 2.9 were announced in another thread shortly before NIPS. The main new features of rstan 2.9.0 are:
Approximate posterior inference via variational inference (see the vb function). We still don't recommend this for final inference, but it can be good for quickly seeing if a model is plausible when you have so much data that evaluating the log-posterior function is slow.
There is a save_warmup flag for stan() and sampling()

Each of these new features has a bug
vb() will return the wrong results (although the .csv file in tempdir() is correct) when one parameter name is a prefix of another parameter name (e.g. beta and beta_x). To avoid this without renaming your variables, you would have to install rstan from GitHub via devtools::install_github("stan-dev/rstan", ref = "develop", subdir = "rstan/rstan")
The documentation for save_warmup is backwards: It actually defaults to TRUE (which is consistent with the <= 2.8.2 behavior) but you can set it to FALSE to possibly avoid some memory errors that people occasionally experience, although any post-estimation function with an inc_warmup argument will fail if inc_warmup = TRUE and stan(*, save_warmup = FALSE).

And there is another bug where expose_stan_functions() will fail to compiled the exposed Stan functions if any of the user-defined functions uses the new slicing syntax, but you can get a fixed version of expose_stan_functions() without installing rstan from GitHub just by executing source("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stan-dev/rstan/develop/rstan/rstan/R/expose_stan_functions.R")

Finally, rstan 2.9.0 requires ggplot2 2.0 and should avoid the debug bug from 2.8.2.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
What sort of works for Gibbs won't work for Stan.  You can't
sample from a non-identified posterior.   Some people (like
Andrew in some of his books) have tried to use Gibbs to sample
from an improper prior and then try to normalize, like zero-centering
the predictors.

You can weakly identify the model by using a prior that controls
the coefficients going into the predictors, but it tends to be
better behaved with the K-1 parameterization.

You don't ever want to be doing the normalization after the fact.
If you sample from a prior with mean of zero, you don't need to then
further subtract the mean to get it exact.  Same principle as
above --- you can't fix an improper posterior, but it's not even
improper in this case.

Zero-centering is usually just the default for regression.  That
often presupposes that the predictors are themselves standardized.

- Bob

Is that not the case? Or did you mean that because you originally suggested I should switch to a non-centered parameterization then I would thus need to go to K - 1 for identifiability? Sorry for the confusion here, I just want to make sure I understand.

> One last question - when I was trying a centered parameterization, why is it that having the prior be ~ normal(0, ...) is enough and I don't need to subtract the mean? messages.body_plain:
What Bob said.  Sampling from an improper posterrior and post-processing can work in Gibbs but it won’t work for autotuned HMC as we have in Stan.

> On Jan 10, 2016, at 2:54 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> What sort of works for Gibbs won't work for Stan.  You can't
> sample from a non-identified posterior.   Some people (like
> Andrew in some of his books) have tried to use Gibbs to sample
> from an improper prior and then try to normalize, like zero-centering
> the predictors.
>
> You can weakly identify the model by using a prior that controls
> the coefficients going into the predictors, but it tends to be
> better behaved with the K-1 parameterization.
>
> You don't ever want to be doing the normalization after the fact.
> If you sample from a prior with mean of zero, you don't need to then
> further subtract the mean to get it exact.  Same principle as
> above --- you can't fix an improper posterior, but it's not even
> improper in this case.
>
> Zero-centering is usually just the default for regression.  That
> often presupposes that the predictors are themselves standardized.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
>> On Jan 10, 2016, at 1:42 AM, ricka...@gmail.com wrote:
>>
>> Thanks a ton, that clears up quite a bit for me.
>>
>> What I meant about the K vs. K - 1 identifiability: I knew about the issue with K predictors being invariant upon adding a constant, but I thought that was resolved by zero-centering the predictors. Is that not the case? Or did you mean that because you originally suggested I should switch to a non-centered parameterization then I would thus need to go to K - 1 for identifiability? Sorry for the confusion here, I just want to make sure I understand.
>>
>> One last question - when I was trying a centered parameterization, why is it that having the prior be ~ normal(0, ...) is enough and I don't need to subtract the mean? I've seen examples from Kruschke where he does this: i.e. https://github.com/boboppie/kruschke-doing_bayesian_data_analysis/blob/master/2e/Jags-Ymet-Xnom1fac-MnormalHom.R). Did I misunderstand something or was it unnecessary on his part to subtract the mean?
>>
>> -Rick

messages.body_plain:
Stan does use a symplectic integrator for the Hamiltonian simulation.
We're using a 5th-order Runge-Kutta from Boost for Stan's language and
we're about to add a stiff solver from CVODE (can't recall the algorithm
it uses).

If you're working in RStan, I believe the pairs plot will point
out where things go wrong.  You can also inspect the divergences
directly --- they'll be 1 or 0, depending on whether there was
or wasn't an arithmetic issue.  There's some fiddling to get them
out of the fit object.  You can also look at the traceplots,
where a chain getting stuck for a long time will show up as a straight
line.

- Bob

> On Jan 9, 2016, at 6:46 AM, Dominic Steinitz <dom...@steinitz.org> wrote:
>
> Thanks very much for your response.
>
> My R code implemented Euler's method to solve the ODE (actually a version with "white noise" but the noise is very small in my example). I solved the same equation in Stan and got reasonably similar results. I assume Stan uses RK4? Although maybe it should use a symplectic integrator ;-)
>
> The initial value is the initial value for the simulation.
>
> I can't explain it but the inference is now working both for simulations generated by Stan and for simulations generated by my R code. It's possibly because I am not very used to imperative languages and assume when I calculate something then all the dependencies get re-calculated. Of course I thought I had selected the whole region (in emacs) and recalculated but maybe I was missing something.
>
> Yes I noticed n_eff=2 wasn't good but thanks for pointing it out.
>
> For future reference, how would one inspect how a chain is getting stuck?
>
> For info, I was using Stan to confirm that my Sequential Monte Carlo inference was giving sensible answers; it seems that it does.
>
> Thanks once more to everyone who responded. I hope to write up the example so it might be of some use to other Stan users.
>
> Dominic.
>
> On 08/01/2016 20:51, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> Why doesn't the simulation code involve an ODE simulator?  Or
>> does it implicitly somehow?  You might want to try verifying
>> that the simulation is making sense somehow.
>>
>> Also, it looks like a different ODE, so it's a rather different
>> simulation.
>>
>> I also wasn't sure what you mean for initial value --- is that
>> where you start simulating or an initialization given to Stan?
>>
>> Also, what David Manheim said is important --- if you are
>> only getting n_eff=2, your chains aren't converging.  So you
>> might want to inspect how they're getting stuck.

>>> On Jan 7, 2016, at 2:24 PM, idontgetoutmuch <idontge...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>
>>>
>>> I've modified the example in Stan Manual Figure 19.3 to have one unknown parameter, theta, but so that the observations are a noisy non-linear function of the state. The equations describe a pendulum with only noisy observations of the horizontal displacement available. I simulate data with a value for theta with the value 9.81 but the inferred value below is nowhere near this. I assume I have made a mistake in the model somehow. Perhaps someone can help me out?
>>>
>>>               mean se_mean       sd      2.5%       25%       50%       75%
>>> theta[1]     -2.27    2.80     3.97     -8.84     -3.44     -0.97      0.20
>>> lp__     -25397.21 9324.91 13194.01 -33838.87 -33044.87 -32592.90 -24948.26
>>>             97.5% n_eff     Rhat
>>> theta[1]     1.70     2   560.20
>>> lp__     -2567.77     2 20217.25
>>>  Here's the Stan
>>>
>>> functions {
>>>   real[] pendulum(real t,
>>>                   real[] y,
>>>                   real[] theta,
>>>                   real[] x_r,
>>>                   int[] x_i) {
>>>     real dydt[2];
>>>     dydt[1] <- y[2];
>>>     dydt[2] <- - theta[1] * sin(y[1]);
>>>     return dydt;
>>>   }
>>> }
>>> data {
>>>   int<lower=1> T;
>>>   real z[T];
>>>   vector<lower=0>[1] sigma;
>>>   real y0[2];
>>>   real t0;
>>>   real ts[T];
>>> }
>>> transformed data {
>>>   real x_r[0];
>>>   int x_i[0]; }
>>> parameters {
>>>   real theta[1];
>>> }
>>> model {
>>>   real y_hat[T,2];
>>>   real z_hat[T];
>>>   theta ~ normal(0,1);
>>>   y_hat <- integrate_ode(pendulum, y0, t0, ts, theta, x_r, x_i);
>>>   for (t in 1:T) {
>>>     z_hat[t] <- sin(y_hat[t,1]);
>>>     z[t] ~ normal(z_hat[t], sigma);
>>>   }
>>> }
>>>
>>>
>>> and here's how I am simulating the data
>>>
>>> library(rstan)
>>> library(mvtnorm)
>>>
>>> qc1 = 0.01
>>> deltaT = 0.01
>>> nSamples = 500
>>> m0 = c(1.6, 0)
>>> g = 9.81
>>>
>>> bigQ = matrix(c(qc1 * deltaT^3 / 3, qc1 * deltaT^2 / 2,
>>>                 qc1 * deltaT^2 / 2,       qc1 * deltaT
>>>                 ),
>>>               nrow = 2,
>>>               ncol = 2,
>>>               byrow = TRUE
>>>               )
>>>
>>> bigR = matrix(c(0.1),
>>>               nrow = 1,
>>>               ncol = 1,
>>>               byrow = TRUE)
>>>
>>> etas <- rmvnorm(n=nSamples,mean=c(0.0,0.0),sigma=bigQ)
>>> epsilons <- rmvnorm(n=nSamples,mean=c(0.0),sigma=bigR)
>>>
>>> x <- matrix()
>>> length(x) <- 2 * (nSamples + 1)
>>> dim(x) <- c(nSamples + 1, 2)
>>>
>>> y <- vector()
>>> length(y) <- 1 * nSamples
>>> dim(y) <- c(nSamples)
>>>
>>> x[1,1] = m0[1]
>>> x[1,2] = m0[2]
>>>
>>> for (i in 1:nSamples) {
>>>     x[i+1,1] <- x[i,1] + x[i,2] * deltaT
>>>     x[i+1,2] <- x[i,2] - g * (sin(x[i,1])) * deltaT
>>>     x[i+1,] <- x[i+1,] + etas[i,]
>>>     y[i] <- sin(x[i+1,1]) + epsilons[i,1]
>>>     }
>>>
>>> samples <- stan(file = 'PendulumInfer.stan',
>>>                 data = list (T  = nSamples,
>>>                              z = y,
>>>                              sigma = array(bigR[1,1],dim=1),
>>>                              y0 = m0,
>>>                              t0 = 0.0,
>>>                              ts = seq(0.01,nSamples/100,0.01)
>>>                              ),
>>>                 chains = 4,
>>>                 iter =1000
>>>                 )

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Spatially correlated probit regression
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Spatially correlated probit regression
messages.body_plain:
I think the best way to approach this problem is a nonparametric copula, such as:

1. Calculate the "residuals" for N days and M locations,
2. Transform using empirical CDF approximation (in R, the ecdf function),
3. Transform again using inv_Phi (such as inv_Phi(ecdf(residuals))),
and
4. Use the multi_normal(...) function to account for this spatial correlation.

Is there a built-in function similar to ecdf?

Best,
Andrew Verdin

> > function".  If you mean y ~ bernoulli(theta) or bernoulli_log(y, theta),
> > they're both functions, so there's no noise arising from the functions
> > themselves.
> >
> > If you think about residuals, though, what you're getting is that
> > Pr[y = 1] = theta, so the "noise" is all packed into theta.  If
> > theta = 0.55 and y = 1, then the residual in some sense is (1 - .55),
> > or you can think in terms of log loss, which is -log(.55) (where
> > -log(1) = 0, or no noise).  You just have to be careful to flip everything
> > for y = 0 cases.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > > On Jan 8, 2016, at 3:22 PM, Andrew Verdin <andrew...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > > Hi all,
> > >
> > > I am using Stan to model and simulate precipitation occurrence using probit regression.  The latent Gaussian process (GP) is a regression on some covariates -- the theoretical variance of the latent GP is by definition 1.  As the latent GP is unobserved, there are no observed residuals.  What I have done so far is obtain posterior distributions of the beta coefficients that make up the latent GP for a network of 13 locations, with the beta coefficients being spatially correlated via partial sill and range parameters.
> > >
> > > However, I would also like to infer the spatial correlation of the GP "residuals".  For example, at a single site, simulation can proceed by calculating the mean function of the latent GP, and perturbing with a mean-zero, variance unity random sample.  I would like to extend this to multisite.  What I am thinking is if I can obtain the noise from the bernoulli function, I can infer the spatial correlation of this noise, and use the correlation matrix to produce realizations from a mean-zero multivariate normal distribution.  The diagonal of the correlation matrix would be 1, thus preserving the variance unity of probit regression.
> > >
> > > Long story short: is there a way to get at the noise of the bernoulli function?

No, there's not a built-in function like ecdf:

  The e.c.d.f. (empirical cumulative distribution function) Fn
  is a step function with jumps i/n at observation values,
  where i is the number of tied observations at that value.

Stan doesn't play nicely with step functions --- everything
should be at least differentiable.

It only gives you as much speedup as there is

then reuse them.

And I think the likelihood can be simplified by using
vector addition on a slightly rearranged log_theta and
log_phi.

>       real gamma[K];
>       for (k in 1:K) gamma[k] <- (log(theta[doc[n],k]) + log(phi[k,w[n]]));
>       increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(gamma) * w_count[n]);  // likelihood
>     }

model {
  vector[K] log_phi[W];
  vector[K] log_theta[M];
  ... define these locals once ...

  for (n in 1:N)

    increment_log_prob(w_count[n] * log_sum_exp(log_theta[m] + log_phi[w[n]]));

I don't see how to do much better than that.

Hi both,

Thanks very much for your messages. I've tried a log transformation, but the errors are replaced with log(0) initialization errors. I'm attaching the full model. You'll see that it's a Q-learning model, so the threshold term (a) is a function of an intercept and the difference in learned values (q[2] - q[1]), which is weighted by a coefficient. This value difference is naturally bounded between -1 and 1.

Thanks again for any advice!

Best,
Tor

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Try declaring V as a cov_matrix.

The Stan model block defines the calculation of the log joint probability distribution. It does not draw a V, set Sigma, then draw vecY; there is no rejection sampling happening.

I would highly suggest using the lkj priors in the manual.

Daniel

On Jan 11, 2016, at 4:49 AM, Timothée Flutre <timf...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hello,
>

> Y ~ MN(M, U, V)
> Y is NxT; M is NxT; U is NxN; V is TxT where N is the number of samples and T the number of traits

> goal: estimate V (for the sake of simplicity, I'm using an inverse Wishart as prior, even though the STAN manual gives better alternatives)
> trick: vec(Y) ~ MVN(vec(M), V kx U) where "kx" is the Kronecker product
>

>
>

>   int<lower=0> N;
>   int<lower=0> T;
>   vector[N*T] vecY;
>   vector[N*T] vecM;
>   matrix[N,N] U;
>   matrix[T,T] S;
> }
> parameters {
>   matrix[T,T] V;
> }
> model {
>   matrix[T*N,T*N] Sigma;
>   V ~ inv_wishart(T+1, S);
>   for(ti in 1:T)
>     for(tj in 1:T)
>       for(ni in 1:N)
>         for(nj in 1:N)
>           Sigma[N*(ti-1)+ni, N*(tj-1)+nj] <- V[ti,tj] * U[ni,nj];

Thanks to Daniel and Bob, who both jumped into the pharmacokinetics = differential equation trap. Probably I was not clear enough that we use nonmem for diff-equations, but my question was related to seemingly simple curve-fitting problem.

Dieter

messages.body_plain:
Tamas,

Thank you for your insight. My real quest is to find a general method for sampling a distribution subject to truncation on a general N-dimensional polytope. My recent focus is to implement this efficiently in Stan. While I've found some clever transformations that are efficient for particular sub problems, the only general approach I've found is too slow for most applications. In lieu of a Stan implementation, I have a general implementation based on Gibbs' sampling that is reasonably fast for polytopes with a small number of vertices, but becomes too slow as the number of vertices increases. I only posted to this list in the hope that maybe there is a clever general formulation for computing the Jacobian for linear change of variables where there is a null space in the new coordinates.

Michael

messages.body_plain:
This discussion's great!

As Michael says, in general you need the Jacobian of the z |-> x
transform because you are placing the density on the transformed x.

As Tamas says, if you can find a clever reparameterization, you're
better off doing that.

Maybe Michael Betancourt can answer the general question about
the Jacobians.

One thing we could conceivably do in the future is allow
user-defined transforms where we compute the Jacobian
automatically --- it won't be super-efficient compared to
doing it by hand, because we'll have to compute a Jacobian
using higher-order autodiff (not too bad --- N with a relatively
high constant) and then take its log determinant (not so
good --- N^3 with the same high constant).  And we'd probably have
to require the user to write the function as a pure vector function
with data parameters:

   vector my_transform(vector theta, vector x, int[] x_int);

where theta is the vector of parameters to transform and
x and x_int are data.  Ideally we should allow this data stuff to
be optional everywhere.  I just updated our longer-term to-do list
to include this item:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Longer-Term-To-Do-List

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Tamas,

Here is the basic idea. Let's say you want to sample x from a multinormal, but want to constrain the samples to lie in a polytope whose vertices, v_i, are the columns of a matrix V. Then the allowed region for x is defined by x = V*nu, where the vector nu is a simplex. Then the naive Stan code for this problem is

parameters {
  simplex[n_vertices] nu;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[n_dim] x;
  x <- V*nu;
}
model {
  x ~ normal(mu, sigma);
}

The Stan compiler will inform you that the Jacobian for the transformation from x to nu must be input manually, but for interesting cases the dimension of nu is much larger than the dimension of x, so standard methods can't be used for computing this Jacobian. Since the transformation is linear, the actual values of the derivatives are irrelevant. What is important is the number of nu values that satisfy x=V*nu for a given value of x. I term this multiplicity of nu values the volume of the nu null space for any given x. The Jacobian is then J=1/vol(x). I coded this formula and get the correct sampling (modulo some divide-by-zero issues near the polytope boundary). The main problem is that the computation of this volume is very slow.

So while my formulation is correct, I'm wondering if there is a faster way to implement a solution for the general case. I recognize that there are good solutions for particular polytopes, but I am seeking a global formulation. I've seen reflection boundary conditions being used in the literature for Hamiltonian formulations of problems of this sort, but I'm not sure if that is the best approach for Stan either.

Michael

messages.body_plain:
If n_vertices >> n_dim then you'll have a hugely non-identified posterior which will
be hard to sample unless the Jacobians are sufficient to identify the problem.  As
Tamas notes some analytic work will go a long way -- if nu is a simplex then V * nu
usually spans a lower dimensional simplex (depending on the null space of V, there
are some weird edge cases).  If you can parameterize that lower-dimensional simplex
directly then sampling will fly.

I coded this formula and get the correct sampling (modulo some divide-by-zero issues near the polytope boundary). The main problem is that the computation of this volume is very slow.

> > > >> > constraint can be described by x = V*z. In other words, x is constrained
> > > >> to
> > > >> > be an interpolation between the vertices. Here is my Stan code:
> > > >> >
> > > >> > data {
> > > >> >   int nDim;
> > > >> >   int nVerts;
> > > >> >   real mu;
> > > >> >   real sigma;
> > > >> >   matrix[nDim,nVerts] V;
> > > >> > }
> > > >> > parameters {
> > > >> >   simplex[nVerts] z;
> > > >> > }
> > > >> > transformed parameters {
> > > >> >   vector[nDim] x;
> > > >> >   x <- V*z;
> > > >> > }
> > > >> > model {
> > > >> >   // mu ~ normal(x, sigma);
> > > >> >   x ~ normal(mu, sigma);
> > > >> > }
> > > >> >
> > > >> > I provide two versions of the model equation, but both fail for any
> > > >> polygon
> > > >> > beyond three vertices. When there are three vertices, there is a unique
> > > >> > linear mapping between x and z, so Stan works well. But for more than
> > > >> three
> > > >> > vertices, V has a null space, meaning that there are a multiplicity of z
> > > >> > solutions corresponding to any x. Since z is a simplex, the volume of
> > > >> this
> > > >> > null space is finite, and varies with the value of x. If I use the volume
> > > >> > of this null space as the reciprocal of the Jacobian and enter this
> > > >> > manually using increment_log_prob(), then the sampling is correct.
> > > >> >
> > > >> > I'm wondering if there is a better way to sample this problem that avoids
> > > >> > the expensive manual Jacobian calculation. Any suggestions?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] speeding up zero inflation model through vectorization?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] speeding up zero inflation model through vectorization?
messages.body_plain:
I am following up with 2 points:

1) My belief that the reference manual describes

and incorrect optimized hurdle model is strengthened

2) Code for a faster zero inflated negative binomial model.

### 1) The reference manual describes an ###

###      incorrect optimized hurdle model ###

Following up on my last message:

I checked and, as described in the manual,

poissonCDF(0 | lambda) = log(1-exp(-lambda)).

However, to calculate p(y[n] | lambda) for the hurdle model,

one has to divide (or subtract on the log scale) by the

complementary poisson CDF. poissonCCDF.

Instead, the code on page 115 of the

reference manual uses the poissonCDF.

So it should not be

increment_log_prob(-log1m_exp(-lambda))

but

increment_log_prob(-log1m_exp(log1m_exp(-lambda))).

[Alternatively, I am making a fool out of myself ...]

### 2) Code for a faster zero inflated ###

###      negative binomial model. ###

Replacing the model section from page 114 in the

stan reference the following makes gradient evaluation

ca. 20% faster.

This code is for a hierarchical model involving multiple

groups, using following variables:

y: vector of length N with observed counts.

phi: vector with over dispersion parameters for groups

etas: vector of length N containing log(mu) for the negative binomial distribution

thetas: logit of p(y == 0)

sx: design matrix

sx0: design matrix for zero inflation

g_start: index of the first entry for a group in y, sx, or sx0

g_nzstart: index of the first nonzero entry for a group in y, sx, or sx0

g_end: index of the last entry for a group in y, sx, or sx0

betas: matrix with regression weights to obtain log(mu), by group

alphas: regressions weight for zero inflation part (same for all groups)

### begin model ###

...

thetas <- to_vector(sx0 * to_matrix(alpha));

for (gr in 1:M) {

    log_phi <- log(phi[gr]);

     etas[g_start[gr]:g_end[gr]] <- sx[g_start[gr]:g_end[gr],1:K] * beta[gr,1:K]';

     // y > 0  cases

     increment_log_prob(bernoulli_logit_log(0,thetas[g_nzstart[gr]:g_end[gr]])

                                   + neg_binomial_2_log_log(y[g_nzstart[gr]:g_end[gr]],

                                                                         etas[g_nzstart[gr]:g_end[gr]],

                                                                         phi[gr]));

     // y == 0 cases

     for (k in g_start[gr]:(g_nzstart[gr]-1)) {

       increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(bernoulli_logit_log(1,thetas[k]),

                                                         bernoulli_logit_log(0,thetas[k])

                                                         + neg_binomial_2_log_log(0,etas[k],phi[gr])));

     }

   }

### end model ####

Following additional modifications did make the model

 slightly faster (around 5%), but appeared to be less stable

(i.e. produced NaNs or infinite values where the above model did not):

bernoulli_logit_log(1,thetas[k]) can be obtained from log_inv_logit(thetas[k])

bernoulli_logit_log(0,thetas[k]) can be obtained from log1m__inv_logit(thetas[k])

neg_binomial_2_log_log(0,etas[k],phi[gr]) can be obtained from

(log1m_exp(etas[k] - log_sum_exp(etas[k],log_phi)))*phi[gr])).

Best, Guido

PS: getting the count of zero values to then use the binomial
distribution does not work in my case, because every participants
has a different theta value.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Wiener drift diffusion model -- initialization errors
messages.body_plain:
I guess the problem is that given how you have set up your model
it easily happens that

threshold_int[s] <  threshold_learning[s] * abs(q[2]-q[1])

I think you could either use priors to make sure that
threshold_int is relatively large.
Instead I would do what Joachim suggested;

threshold_int <- exp(threshold_int[s] + threshold_learning[s] * abs(q[2]-q[1]))

one other thing that can happen is that t_er gets larger
than your smallest RT, which will also lead log_prob values of -Inf.
One way to deal with this is to constrain t_er to be maximally the fastest RT.

Guido

>
> Bob,

>
>
> I also looked at the hurdle model, and analog to what you
> were showing in the manual for the poisson model there is a
> faster version to calculate the cdf for the negative binomial distribution.
> I'll post this when I am sure I got it right.
>
> I had troubles implementing this because, i believe, the example
> for the hurdle model on page 115 has a small but consequential error:
> When implementing the truncation, I think the code increments the log posterior by
>  -log(poissonCDF(0,lambda))      instead of the correct
>  -log(1-poissonCDF(0,lambda)).
>
> Alternatively, log(1-exp(-lambda)) is already the CCDF, and not the CDF as
> it sais on page 115.
>
> Or am I misunderstanding something/not reading carefully enough?

> Guido

> >   else
> >     increment_log_prob(bernoulli_log(0,theta)
> >                                  + poisson_log(y[n],lambda));
> > }

> > I was thinking of improving the speed of the model by
> > - splitting the array y in two parts,
> >   one where y = 0 and the other where y != 0
> > - putting the results of

> > - and finally pass the vectors log_prob_y
> >   and log_prob_y0 to increment_log_prob
> >

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] speeding up zero inflation model through vectorization?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] speeding up zero inflation model through vectorization?
messages.body_plain:
> On Jan 12, 2016, at 2:45 AM, Guido Biele <guido...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I am following up with 2 points:
>
>
> 1) My belief that the reference manual describes
>
> and incorrect optimized hurdle model is strengthened
>
> 2) Code for a faster zero inflated negative binomial model.
>
>
> ### 1) The reference manual describes an ###
>
> ###      incorrect optimized hurdle model ###
>
>
> Following up on my last message:
>
> I checked and, as described in the manual,
>
> poissonCDF(0 | lambda) = log(1-exp(-lambda)).
>
> However, to calculate p(y[n] | lambda) for the hurdle model,
>
> one has to divide (or subtract on the log scale) by the
>
> complementary poisson CDF. poissonCCDF.
>
> Instead, the code on page 115 of the
>
> reference manual uses the poissonCDF.
>
>
> So it should not be
>
> increment_log_prob(-log1m_exp(-lambda))
>
> but
>
> increment_log_prob(-log1m_exp(log1m_exp(-lambda))).
>
> [Alternatively, I am making a fool out of myself ...]
>
>
> ### 2) Code for a faster zero inflated ###
>
> ###      negative binomial model. ###
>
>
> Replacing the model section from page 114 in the
>
> stan reference the following makes gradient evaluation
>
> ca. 20% faster.
>
>
> This code is for a hierarchical model involving multiple
>
> groups, using following variables:
>
> y: vector of length N with observed counts.
>
> phi: vector with over dispersion parameters for groups
>
> etas: vector of length N containing log(mu) for the negative binomial distribution
>
> thetas: logit of p(y == 0)
>
> sx: design matrix
>
> sx0: design matrix for zero inflation
>
> g_start: index of the first entry for a group in y, sx, or sx0
>
> g_nzstart: index of the first nonzero entry for a group in y, sx, or sx0
>
> g_end: index of the last entry for a group in y, sx, or sx0
>
> betas: matrix with regression weights to obtain log(mu), by group
>
> alphas: regressions weight for zero inflation part (same for all groups)
>
>
>
> ### begin model ###
>
> ...
>
> thetas <- to_vector(sx0 * to_matrix(alpha));
>
>
> for (gr in 1:M) {
>
>     log_phi <- log(phi[gr]);
>
>      etas[g_start[gr]:g_end[gr]] <- sx[g_start[gr]:g_end[gr],1:K] * beta[gr,1:K]';
>
>
>      // y > 0  cases
>
>      increment_log_prob(bernoulli_logit_log(0,thetas[g_nzstart[gr]:g_end[gr]])
>
>                                    + neg_binomial_2_log_log(y[g_nzstart[gr]:g_end[gr]],
>
>                                                                          etas[g_nzstart[gr]:g_end[gr]],
>
>                                                                          phi[gr]));
>
>      // y == 0 cases
>
>      for (k in g_start[gr]:(g_nzstart[gr]-1)) {
>
>        increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(bernoulli_logit_log(1,thetas[k]),
>
>                                                          bernoulli_logit_log(0,thetas[k])
>
>                                                          + neg_binomial_2_log_log(0,etas[k],phi[gr])));
>
>      }
>
>    }
>
>
> ### end model ####
>
>
>
> Following additional modifications did make the model
>
>  slightly faster (around 5%), but appeared to be less stable
>
> (i.e. produced NaNs or infinite values where the above model did not):
>
>
>
> bernoulli_logit_log(1,thetas[k]) can be obtained from log_inv_logit(thetas[k])

Even better, it can be vectorized as bernoulli_logit_log(1, theta) if you do
it for all of the k values.  It's useful to spend the time to put themtogether
that way if you want.

I don't want to get too carried away optimizing the code, but would you mind
sending a complete working model?  I can check it into our example-models
repo and credit you with it after I validate that it works.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Absolute values are tricky on parameters because they wind up
providing multimodal answers at alpha and -alpha by definition.

If there's an actual constraint, it's better to put it in
the model rather than try to compensate with something like absolute
value. (I hope I understood the problem.)

- Bob

>
> not sure if the following is useful, because it appears you defined
> q[1] and q[2] as values for the wrong (low value) and correct
> (high value) options.
>
> still, stochastic payoffs will likely make that sometimes q[1] > q[2];
>
> therefore, if boundary separation shall depend on the difficulty of
> the choice, the absolute of the value difference should work.
> a <- threshold_int[s] + ( threshold_learning[s] * abs(q[2]-q[1]) );
>
> guido
>
>

> Hi both,
>
> Thanks very much for your messages. I've tried a log transformation, but the errors are replaced with log(0) initialization errors. I'm attaching the full model. You'll see that it's a Q-learning model, so the threshold term (a) is a function of an intercept and the difference in learned values (q[2] - q[1]), which is weighted by a coefficient. This value difference is naturally bounded between -1 and 1.
>
> Thanks again for any advice!
>
> Best,
> Tor

messages.body_plain:
> So, how can I change the inits for ADVI in Cmdstan? I've already had to set the init argument for Cmdstan in order for the program to run so if we're talking about the same inits, I'm not sure I can change it.
That's correct, the init argument for CmdStan is the init for ADVI (or whatever inference algorithm you choose). What I'm suggesting is to try other sets of initialized parameters.

> Where can I turn off optimization or sampling and still try the model using ADVI?
After compiling the model, at run time you select the inference algorithm: MCMC, variational inference, or optimization. Only one of these is `on' at a time so there's nothing to `turn off', per say.

Dustin

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Memory and speed for an LDA model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Memory and speed for an LDA model
messages.body_plain:
> On Jan 11, 2016, at 4:56 AM, Stefano <mangiol...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
>
> On Monday, January 11, 2016 at 7:09:18 PM UTC+11, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I think that should work.  Did you try it?
>
> Yes it seems to work
>
>
> It only gives you as much speedup as there is
> duplication of words.
>
> In some applications such as biostatistics, the number of words (RNA sequences) count can be in the order of 10^4

Other than for playing around with models, I'd think a custom
LDA fitter would make more sense.  It's not like you can do
real Bayesian inference with LDA anyway --- the posterior is
combinatorially intractable.

But the speedup from aggregation will depend on how many times
"words" are duplicated in "documents".  If each word occurs once,
it may even be slower.

- Bob

>
> And you should only compute log(theta) and log(phi)
> once --- you can define them as local variables once and
> then reuse them.
>
> And I think the likelihood can be simplified by using
> vector addition on a slightly rearranged log_theta and
> log_phi.
>
> >     for (n in 1:N) {
> >       real gamma[K];
> >       for (k in 1:K) gamma[k] <- (log(theta[doc[n],k]) + log(phi[k,w[n]]));
> >       increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(gamma) * w_count[n]);  // likelihood
> >     }
>
>
> model {
>   vector[K] log_phi[W];
>   vector[K] log_theta[M];
>   ... define these locals once ...
>
>   for (n in 1:N)
>     increment_log_prob(w_count[n] * log_sum_exp(log_theta[m] + log_phi[w[n]]));
>
> Thanks a lot, I will apply these modifications
>
> I don't see how to do much better than that.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> > On Jan 10, 2016, at 10:37 PM, Stefano <mangiol...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> >
> >
> > On Friday, August 29, 2014 at 3:12:54 AM UTC+10, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >
> > On Aug 28, 2014, at 12:51 PM, Bentley Coffey <bentley...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > > Bob and Matt,
> > >
> > > Do you still recommend against using Stan to estimate a LDA model. The reference manual (version 2.2.0) contains on page 139 the following Stan code for performing LDA:
> > >
> > > data {
> > > int<lower=2> K; // num topics
> > > int<lower=2> V; // num words
> > > int<lower=1> M; // num docs
> > > int<lower=1> N; // total word instances
> > > int<lower=1,upper=V> w[N]; // word n
> > > int<lower=1,upper=M> doc[N]; // doc ID for word n
> > > vector<lower=0>[K] alpha; // topic prior
> > > vector<lower=0>[V] beta; // word prior
> > > }
> > > parameters {
> > > simplex[K] theta[M]; // topic dist for doc m
> > > simplex[V] phi[K]; // word dist for topic k
> > > }
> > > model {
> > > for (m in 1:M)
> > > theta[m] ~ dirichlet(alpha); // prior
> > > for (k in 1:K)
> > > phi[k] ~ dirichlet(beta); // prior
> > > for (n in 1:N) {
> > > real gamma[K];
> > > for (k in 1:K)
> > > gamma[k] <- log(theta[doc[n],k]) + log(phi[k,w[n]]);
> > > increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(gamma)); // likelihood
> > > }
> > > }
> > >
> > > It seems to me that this code is missing a crucial piece of the likelihood, which appears as the last term in your linked source write-up of the collapsed likelihood:
> >
> >
> > There wasn't anything after the ":" ?  What's missing?  It
> > looks like it matches what we have in the doc.
> >
> > > And also on the bottom of page 138 of the Stan reference manual... Also noteworthy is that this could be re-written to be more efficient by using sufficient statistics (count of each vocabulary word in each document, obviating the next for stacking a ragged array).
> >
> > For cases where the word usage is dense and the counts not mostly ones,
> > this would indeed be much more efficient.  I'm used to dealing with
> > natural language data with LDA which doesn't have this property.
> >
> > Nevertheless, calculating sufficient statistics on a per-doc level
> > in a sparse way could still be worthwhile as an efficiency boost.
> >
> >
> > Hello,
> >
> > Would this be a way to implement such sufficient statistics?
> >
> >   data {
> >     int<lower=2> K;               // num topics
> >     int<lower=2> W;               // num words
> >     int<lower=1> M;               // num docs
> >     int<lower=1> N;               // total word instances //UNIQUE FOR EVERY DOCUMENT/WORD
> >     int<lower=0> tot_w_count;     //upper value for word counts
> >     vector<lower=0, upper=tot_w_count>[N] w_count;   // word count per document (e.g., cat in document 1 is present 5 times)
> >     int<lower=1,upper=W> w[N];    // word n //UNIQUE FOR EVERY DOCUMENT/WORD
> >     int<lower=1,upper=M> doc[N];  // doc ID for word n
> >     vector<lower=0>[K] alpha;     // topic prior
> >     vector<lower=0>[K] beta;     // word prior
> >
> >   }
> >   parameters {
> >     simplex[K] theta[M];   // topic dist for doc m
> >     simplex[W] phi[K];            // word dist for topic k
> >   }
> >   model {
> >     for (m in 1:M) theta[m] ~ dirichlet(alpha);  // prior
> >     for (k in 1:K) phi[k] ~ dirichlet(beta);  // prior
> >
> >     for (n in 1:N) {
> >       real gamma[K];
> >       for (k in 1:K) gamma[k] <- (log(theta[doc[n],k]) + log(phi[k,w[n]]));
> >
> >       increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(gamma) * w_count[n]);  // likelihood
> >     }
> >   }
> >
> > Thanks.
> >
> > > I'm aware of the multimodality issues but was planning to overcome that labeling-like identification concern with prior knowledge (I happen to know the 50 different topic names, so I know that some of the words in the vocabulary should be more probable for particular topics,eg the words "oil" and "gas" should be more likely in the topic "oil and gas"). Should I really abandon Stan as my platform of choice for this kind of application?
> >
> > Stan's good for exploring variant model structures and running one-off
> > model fits.  If you need something running at scale in a production environment,
> > you probably want to use some kind of optimization tailored for your problem,
> > such as a variational approach.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >
> > >
> > > Bentley
> > >
> > > On Monday, October 8, 2012 4:51:58 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > We don't really recommend Stan for models like LDA.
> > > The problem is that the multi-modality of the posterior
> > > makes Bayesian inference intractable, not just for Stan,
> > > but for any known technique.
> > >
> > > That being the case, you might as well go for an optimizer.
> > > Like the very scalable online one Matt (the inventor of
> > > our sampler, NUTS) wrote for Vowpal Wabbit:
> > >
> > >    http://hunch.net/~vw/
> > >
> > > and described in this paper:
> > >
> > >    http://www.cs.princeton.edu/~blei/papers/HoffmanBleiBach2010b.pdf
> > >
> > > The reason Stan's consuming so much memory is that we're
> > > building up the log probability expression tree in memory to
> > > use to compute auto-diff.
> > >
> > > I believe PyMC uses Metropolis, which may run and provide
> > > samples, but isn't going to give you very efficient sampling,
> > > even around a single mode.
> > >
> > > Finally, the Stan model isn't well formed because
> > > we don't do integer sampling.  So the "topic ~ categorical(...)"
> > > isn't going to do what you think -- what it will do is
> > > add log categorical(topic|theta[i]) to the log probabilty
> > > where topic is uninitialized.
> > >
> > > What you need to do is marginalize out the discrete
> > > variables because Stan doesn't sample them.  Here's
> > > a note on how to do that for basic LDA:
> > >
> > > http://lingpipe-blog.com/2011/04/14/summing-out-topic-assignments-ld/
> > >
> > > This can also be a useful move if you're applying some
> > > kind of optimization.
> > >
> > >  > model {
> > >  > int start;
> > >  > int topic;
> > >  > for (n in 1:K) {
> > >  > psi[n] ~ dirichlet(beta[n]);
> > >  > }
> > >  > for (n in 1:D) {
> > >  > theta[n] ~ dirichlet(alpha);
> > >  > }
> > >  > start <- 1;
> > >  > for (i in 1:D) {
> > >  >   for (j in start:doc_ind[i] - 1) {
> > >  >     topic ~ categorical(theta[i]);
> > >  >     words[j] ~ categorical(psi[topic + 1]);
> > >  >   }
> > >  >   start <- doc_ind[i];
> > >  > }
> > >  > }
> > >
> > > Also, I don't follow the use of start here.  Why not
> > > write this loop as in the Blei et al. LDA paper?  That is,
> > > as:
> > >
> > > for (d in 1:D) {
> > >    theta[d] ~ dirichlet(alpha);
> > >    for (j in 1:N[d]) {
> > >      topic[j] ~ categorical(theta[d]);
> > >      words[j] ~ categorical(psi[topic[j]]);
> > >    }
> > > }
> > >
> > > The indexing in Stan is from 1, by the way, so I doubt
> > > you wanted the +1 inside of psi.
> > >
> > > You'd also need an index, as in topic[j], if we
> > > supported discrete sampling.  At least the above is how
> > > I'd write it in BUGS/JAGS (modulo their matrix slicing
> > > syntax which I can never remember).
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > > On 10/8/12 3:52 PM, Julian Brooke wrote:
> > > > Hello folks,
> > > >
> > > > I'm trying to test some adaptions of the latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) model, adaptions where collapsed Gibbs
> > > > sampling isn't going to work right out of the box; I thought I'd try using a general purpose sampler, and STAN looked
> > > > like it might be the best option in terms of speed. To begin, I coded up a version of standard LDA in stan (see below)
> > > > and it seems to be working in very small data sets. However, if I push the number of text/size of the vocabulary to
> > > > anything approaching what I'd need for a real world application, STAN quickly uses up all the memory on my server (92
> > > > Gigs!) and crashes, before the sampling processes even begins. I can scale it down a bit to the point where it has
> > > > enough memory to start sampling, but I started a 50 text corpus a few days ago and its still running. This is much worse
> > > > than the other general-purpose sampler I've tried (pymc). Anyway, I thought I'd check to see if maybe the problem was in
> > > > my code, otherwise I have to reluctantly conclude that STAN (and general-purpose sampling in general) is not what I
> > > > need, and I might as well go back to trying to hack existing LDA implementations for my purposes, which is not ideal:(.
> > > > If anyone has any advice, specific or general, it would be much appreciated.
> > > >
> > > > (Note: I don't sample the hyperparameters, instead I pass them in. Beta is a matrix of vectors so that I can use it to
> > > > seed topics with specific words; Also, the entire corpus is a single vector, with switches between documents stored in a
> > > > separate matrix (doc_ind); oh, and I have to add 1 to topic because categorical gives a range starting with zero whereas
> > > > arrays start with 1, this mismatch seems like a bad design choice BTW)
> > > >
> > > > data {
> > > >   int<lower=1> K; //topics
> > > >   int<lower=1> V; //vocabulary
> > > >   int<lower=1> D; //number of documents
> > > >   int<lower=1> T; // total number of words
> > > >   vector[K] alpha;
> > > >   vector[V] beta[K];
> > > >   int words[T];
> > > >   int doc_ind[D];
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > parameters {
> > > > simplex[V] psi[K];
> > > > simplex[K] theta[D];
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > model {
> > > > int start;
> > > > int topic;
> > > > for (n in 1:K) {
> > > > psi[n] ~ dirichlet(beta[n]);
> > > > }
> > > > for (n in 1:D) {
> > > > theta[n] ~ dirichlet(alpha);
> > > > }
> > > > start <- 1;
> > > > for (i in 1:D) {
> > > > for (j in start:doc_ind[i] - 1) {
> > > > topic ~ categorical(theta[i]);
> > > > words[j] ~ categorical(psi[topic + 1]);
> > > > }
> > > > start <- doc_ind[i];
> > > > }
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > --
> > > >
> > > >
