messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Polytomous Item Response Theory
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Polytomous Item Response Theory
messages.body_plain:
For (1), you'll have to be careful that th emodel remains identifiable
if you allow the scale of the CDFs to vary.  This may be related to (2).
Usually longer chains won't help.  For the second (2), can you ask a separate
question with something like RStan or whatever interface you're using in
the title?

- Bob

> On Jan 7, 2016, at 2:33 PM, Yao Xiong <xy.xi...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks, Bob, you are so helpful!
> (1)
> I agree that ordered_logistic should be more efficient.
> But if I want to estimate the heterogenous sigma[j], like shown inside normal_cdf( ) below, it looks like ordered_logistic won't do that.
>
>     for (c in 2:(C-1)) {
>       prob[c] <- normal_cdf((gamma[c]-a[j]*theta[n]-delta[j]), 0, sigma[j]) - normal_cdf((gamma[c-1]-a[j]*theta[n]-delta[j]), 0, sigma[j]); }
>       prob[1] <- normal_cdf((gamma[1]-a[j]*theta[n]-delta[j]), 0, sigma[j]);
>       prob[C] <- 1 - normal_cdf((gamma[C-1]-a[j]*theta[n]-delta[j]), 0, sigma[j]);
>
> (2)
> The threshold parameter gamma doesn't have stable estimation, still with high autocorrelation and low effective sample size. I currently run 3 chains with each chain around 700 saved samples, without thinning. Maybe I should try a longer chain?
>
> (2)
> It looks like there used to be a file "stan.R" that supported parallel computing. But I can't find it now. Is the current rstan version automatically running in parallel?
> But when I run the chain, the progress bar still shows one chain progress at a time.
>
> Thanks very much!
>
> On Thursday, January 7, 2016 at 12:19:18 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > On Jan 7, 2016, at 12:14 PM, Yao Xiong <xy.xi...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Thanks so much, Bob.
> > I actually did changed the parameter to vector[C] prob[N, J], and the chain did run.
> > But I am aware that the code is not optimal, still working on how to make it better.
> > You are right that there isn't parallel function in BUGS as normal_cdf( ) in Stan. But in JAGS, there is pnorm( ).
> > As you suggested, if I define vector[C] prob, does that mean prob is a NxJ matrix?
>
> No!  It means it's a C-vector.  But that's all you need.  It's
> a local variable and can get redefined in each loop iteration.
> Much more efficient than allocating a huge array and filling it
> and then just throwing it away.
>
> > I do need different values for each n and j combination for prob.
> > The reason I didn't use the ordered_logistic( ) is because I wanted to add the parameter sigma[j], so there are heterogenous variances for different j.
>
> All you need is the linear predictor and cutpoints and it'll do
> all that munging of the CDFs for you.   It looks like you're using
> probit, but logit is much much faster to compute and gives almost
> identical (albeit differently scaled) results.
>
> - Bob
>
> >
> > On Thursday, January 7, 2016 at 11:21:45 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > See below.
> >
> > > On Jan 7, 2016, at 10:04 AM, Yao Xiong <xy.xi...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > >
> > > No matches for:
> > >
> > >
> > >   int ~ categorical(real[])
> > >
> > >
> > > Available argument signatures for categorical:
> > >
> > >
> > >   int ~ categorical(vector)
> > >   int[] ~ categorical(vector)
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > ERROR at line 33
> > >
> > >
> > >  31:          prob[n, j, 1] <- normal_cdf((gamma[1]-a[j]*theta[n]-delta[j]), 0, sigma[j]);
> > >  32:          prob[n, j, C] <- 1 - sum(prob[n, j, 1:4]);
> > >  33:          Y[n, j] ~ categorical(prob[n, j]);
> > >                                                 ^
> >
> > The error messages says you used:
> >
> > > int ~ categorical(real[])
> >
> > That is,  Y[n, j] is an int and prob[n, j] is an *array* of reals.
> >
> > You can then see that the available argument signatures are:
> >
> > >   int ~ categorical(vector)
> > >   int[] ~ categorical(vector)
> >
> > So the mismatch is that you've provided a real[] argument (array
> > of reals) and the multivariate distributions all require *vector* parameters.
> >
> > There's an entire chapter of the manual near the front devoted
> > to arrays vs. vectors and their usage in Stan.  Hint:  It's more like
> > MATLAB than R or BUGS.
> >
> > Rather than to_vector, which does copying, you want to read the
> > chapter of the Stan manual on arrays, so you'll understand why I'm
> > about to suggest that you declare prob as
> >
> >   vector[C] prob[N, J];
> >
> > an N x J array of C-vectors, rather than as an N x J x C array.
> >
> > But that's still a holdover from BUGS style.  Stan has local variables,
> > so you should just declare
> >
> >   vector[C] prob;
> >
> > and define that in the loop.  But your code there isn't wrong so
> > much as suboptimally coded (it would have been wrong in BUGS):
> >
> >  for (n in 1:N) {
> > >      for (j in 1:J) {
> > >       for (c in 2:(C-1)) {
> > >       prob[n, j, c] <- normal_cdf((gamma[c]-a[j]*theta[n]-delta[j]), 0, sigma[j]) - normal_cdf((gamma[c-1]-a[j]*theta[n]-delta[j]), 0, sigma[j]); }
> > >       prob[n, j, 1] <- normal_cdf((gamma[1]-a[j]*theta[n]-delta[j]), 0, sigma[j]);
> > >       prob[n, j, C] <- 1 - sum(prob[n, j, 1:4]);
> > >       Y[n, j] ~ categorical(prob[n, j, 1:C]);   // here is the bug
> > >      }
> > >   }
> > > }
> >
> > You want to define prob[1] and prob[C] outside of the loop for C.
> >
> > But if you're just trying to code up an ordinal logit, we have that
> > built in.
> >
> > - Bob
> >

messages.body_plain:

messages.body_plain:
Hi, I'm attempting to perform ADVI on a mixture model in specified in the attached file, dpmix_2.stan.  The model imposes the mixture distribution on observation-indexed random effects, rather than directly on the (multivariate) data.  The mixture probabilities are specified such that limiting mixture distribution is a Dirichlet process (which penalizes the number of clusters selected).  The number of dimensions is relatively small, so cluster-indexed covariance matrices are included to allow the data to learn dependence among the dimensions.  The dimensions index time, so an autocorrelated covariance structure (CAR) is used.  Each multivariate observation is drawn from a Gaussian with the mean defined as the sum of a fixed effects term and an observation-indexed random effects term.

The attached file, syndata_vb_run.R uses draw_syndata_mix.R to generate synthetic data, then compiles the dpmix_2.stan to stanmodel object and performs ADVI estimation.

I receive the following error message when running vb():

Rejecting initial value:
  Error evaluating the log probability at the initial value.

I'm also informed that:
   validate transformed params: Lbeta is not lower triangular; Lbeta[1,2]=1.62024e-315

the object Lbeta is the cholesky of a separable covariance matrix composed from the kronecker product of two lower dimensional covariance matrices.  everything is declared as restricted; e.g., cov_matrix, cholesky_factor_cov.

I'd appreciate your insight on the following questions:
1. Does this error message indicate that I should supply initial parameter values and, if so, how does one do that under vb() in rstan 2.9.0 (which i installed from github, yesterday)?
-- it seems vb() inputs a stanmodel object, but no input field for initial values

2. I'm using 3 x 3 and 12 x 12 covariance and precision matrices, separately, and built into a 36 x 36 separable covariance structure using the kronecker product.  Is this not a good idea for ADVI?  Said differently, is this model just too complicated for ADVI (at this time)?  I had hoped that my twist on the mixture model included in the paper was relatively minor.

3. Are there other considerations I should be aware of when assessing whether my model is estimable under ADVI?

Thank you for your help and expertise,

Terrance.

​
 syndata_vb_run.R <https://drive.google.com/file/d/0B0DIDcaf6yMwbVJ1SktxSlRpaHM/view?usp=drive_web>
​​
 draw_syndata_mix.R <https://drive.google.com/file/d/0B0DIDcaf6yMwa0Q1QVFyQjhJSkE/view?usp=drive_web>
​​
 dpmix_2.stan <https://drive.google.com/file/d/0B0DIDcaf6yMwMHVpeGVSd1lYVTQ/view?usp=drive_web>
​

--
Thank you, Terrance Savitsky

messages.subject_clean: specifying initial values for vb in rstan
messages.body_plain:
It is not currently possible to specify initial values for ADVI via rstan because the mechanism we use for sampling is not directly applicable since ADVI needs initial values for the normal variational approximation. You can however specify init_r to some value (it is 2 by default) to limit the range of the initial values in the variational approximation. I don't think the fact that you do Kronecker products or other operations make the evaluation of the log-posterior function too complicated, but it is a valid empirical question as to whether the parameters are approximately normal in the unconstrained space.

Ben

messages.subject: A question about the Change Point Model example in the manual
messages.subject_clean: A question about the Change Point Model example in the manual
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am a little confused after reading the subsection "Posterior Distribution of the Discrete Change Point" in page 126 of the Stan Manual. As described therein, one should normalize the values in the array "lp" to get the probability p(s | e, l, D). This, I get. However, I do not understand why the subsequent equation is true. The summation in this equation is an approximation of E(p(s, D | e, l)), right? [[Here E stands for expectation, which is taken over the posterior p(e, l | D).]]

I don't see why this equals to p(s | D). Isn't the quantity p(s | D) actually equal to E(p(s | e, l, D))? [[Again, the expectation is taken over the posterior p(e, l | D).]] It seems to me that these two expectations are not the same, since p(s, D | e, l) = p(s | e, l, D) * p(D | e, l) whose second term is non-constant within the said expectations.

By not correcting for the term p(D | e, l), doesn't the summation "skip" the per-iteration normalization discussed earlier in the paragraph? Where am I going wrong? Or, is there an error in this subsection of the Stan Manual?

Thanks,

Mehmet Ozan Kabak

PS. I am new to Stan, but I love it already. Big thanks to the team for making it available to the world.

> > > > }
> > > > model {
> > > > for (m in 1:M)
> > > > theta[m] ~ dirichlet(alpha); // prior
> > > > for (k in 1:K)
> > > > phi[k] ~ dirichlet(beta); // prior
> > > > for (n in 1:N) {
> > > > real gamma[K];
> > > > for (k in 1:K)
> > > > gamma[k] <- log(theta[doc[n],k]) + log(phi[k,w[n]]);
> > > > increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(gamma)); // likelihood
> > > > }
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > It seems to me that this code is missing a crucial piece of the likelihood, which appears as the last term in your linked source write-up of the collapsed likelihood:
> > >
> > >
> > > There wasn't anything after the ":" ?  What's missing?  It
> > > looks like it matches what we have in the doc.
> > >
> > > > And also on the bottom of page 138 of the Stan reference manual... Also noteworthy is that this could be re-written to be more efficient by using sufficient statistics (count of each vocabulary word in each document, obviating the next for stacking a ragged array).
> > >
> > > For cases where the word usage is dense and the counts not mostly ones,
> > > this would indeed be much more efficient.  I'm used to dealing with
> > > natural language data with LDA which doesn't have this property.
> > >
> > > Nevertheless, calculating sufficient statistics on a per-doc level
> > > in a sparse way could still be worthwhile as an efficiency boost.
> > >
> > >
> > > Hello,
> > >
> > > Would this be a way to implement such sufficient statistics?
> > >
> > >   data {
> > >     int<lower=2> K;               // num topics
> > >     int<lower=2> W;               // num words
> > >     int<lower=1> M;               // num docs
> > >     int<lower=1> N;               // total word instances //UNIQUE FOR EVERY DOCUMENT/WORD
> > >     int<lower=0> tot_w_count;     //upper value for word counts
> > >     vector<lower=0, upper=tot_w_count>[N] w_count;   // word count per document (e.g., cat in document 1 is present 5 times)
> > >     int<lower=1,upper=W> w[N];    // word n //UNIQUE FOR EVERY DOCUMENT/WORD
> > >     int<lower=1,upper=M> doc[N];  // doc ID for word n
> > >     vector<lower=0>[K] alpha;     // topic prior
> > >     vector<lower=0>[K] beta;     // word prior
> > >
> > >   }
> > >   parameters {
> > >     simplex[K] theta[M];   // topic dist for doc m
> > >     simplex[W] phi[K];            // word dist for topic k
> > >   }
> > >   model {
> > >     for (m in 1:M) theta[m] ~ dirichlet(alpha);  // prior
> > >     for (k in 1:K) phi[k] ~ dirichlet(beta);  // prior
> > >
> > >     for (n in 1:N) {
> > >       real gamma[K];
> > >       for (k in 1:K) gamma[k] <- (log(theta[doc[n],k]) + log(phi[k,w[n]]));
> > >
> > >       increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(gamma) * w_count[n]);  // likelihood
> > >     }
> > >   }
> > >
> > > Thanks.
> > >
> > > > I'm aware of the multimodality issues but was planning to overcome that labeling-like identification concern with prior knowledge (I happen to know the 50 different topic names, so I know that some of the words in the vocabulary should be more probable for particular topics,eg the words "oil" and "gas" should be more likely in the topic "oil and gas"). Should I really abandon Stan as my platform of choice for this kind of application?
> > >
> > > Stan's good for exploring variant model structures and running one-off
> > > model fits.  If you need something running at scale in a production environment,
> > > you probably want to use some kind of optimization tailored for your problem,
> > > such as a variational approach.
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > >
> > > >
> > > > Bentley
> > > >
> > > > On Monday, October 8, 2012 4:51:58 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > > We don't really recommend Stan for models like LDA.
> > > > The problem is that the multi-modality of the posterior
> > > > makes Bayesian inference intractable, not just for Stan,
> > > > but for any known technique.
> > > >
> > > > That being the case, you might as well go for an optimizer.
> > > > Like the very scalable online one Matt (the inventor of
> > > > our sampler, NUTS) wrote for Vowpal Wabbit:
> > > >
> > > >    http://hunch.net/~vw/
> > > >
> > > > and described in this paper:
> > > >
> > > >    http://www.cs.princeton.edu/~blei/papers/HoffmanBleiBach2010b.pdf
> > > >
> > > > The reason Stan's consuming so much memory is that we're
> > > > building up the log probability expression tree in memory to
> > > > use to compute auto-diff.
> > > >
> > > > I believe PyMC uses Metropolis, which may run and provide
> > > > samples, but isn't going to give you very efficient sampling,
> > > > even around a single mode.
> > > >
> > > > Finally, the Stan model isn't well formed because
> > > > we don't do integer sampling.  So the "topic ~ categorical(...)"
> > > > isn't going to do what you think -- what it will do is
> > > > add log categorical(topic|theta[i]) to the log probabilty
> > > > where topic is uninitialized.
> > > >
> > > > What you need to do is marginalize out the discrete
> > > > variables because Stan doesn't sample them.  Here's
> > > > a note on how to do that for basic LDA:
> > > >
> > > > http://lingpipe-blog.com/2011/04/14/summing-out-topic-assignments-ld/
> > > >
> > > > This can also be a useful move if you're applying some
> > > > kind of optimization.
> > > >
> > > >  > model {
> > > >  > int start;
> > > >  > int topic;
> > > >  > for (n in 1:K) {
> > > >  > psi[n] ~ dirichlet(beta[n]);
> > > >  > }
> > > >  > for (n in 1:D) {
> > > >  > theta[n] ~ dirichlet(alpha);
> > > >  > }
> > > >  > start <- 1;
> > > >  > for (i in 1:D) {
> > > >  >   for (j in start:doc_ind[i] - 1) {
> > > >  >     topic ~ categorical(theta[i]);
> > > >  >     words[j] ~ categorical(psi[topic + 1]);
> > > >  >   }
> > > >  >   start <- doc_ind[i];
> > > >  > }
> > > >  > }
> > > >
> > > > Also, I don't follow the use of start here.  Why not
> > > > write this loop as in the Blei et al. LDA paper?  That is,
> > > > as:
> > > >
> > > > for (d in 1:D) {
> > > >    theta[d] ~ dirichlet(alpha);
> > > >    for (j in 1:N[d]) {
> > > >      topic[j] ~ categorical(theta[d]);
> > > >      words[j] ~ categorical(psi[topic[j]]);
> > > >    }
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > The indexing in Stan is from 1, by the way, so I doubt
> > > > you wanted the +1 inside of psi.
> > > >
> > > > You'd also need an index, as in topic[j], if we
> > > > supported discrete sampling.  At least the above is how
> > > > I'd write it in BUGS/JAGS (modulo their matrix slicing
> > > > syntax which I can never remember).
> > > >
> > > > - Bob
> > > >
> > > > On 10/8/12 3:52 PM, Julian Brooke wrote:
> > > > > Hello folks,
> > > > >
> > > > > I'm trying to test some adaptions of the latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) model, adaptions where collapsed Gibbs
> > > > > sampling isn't going to work right out of the box; I thought I'd try using a general purpose sampler, and STAN looked
> > > > > like it might be the best option in terms of speed. To begin, I coded up a version of standard LDA in stan (see below)
> > > > > and it seems to be working in very small data sets. However, if I push the number of text/size of the vocabulary to

> > > > >

> > > > > }
> > > > >
> > > > > model {

> > > > > int topic;

> > > > > }

> > > > > }

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Memory and speed for an LDA model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Memory and speed for an LDA model
messages.body_plain:
> On Jan 12, 2016, at 8:58 PM, stefano <mangiol...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Other than for playing around with models, I'd think a custom
> LDA fitter would make more sense.  It's not like you can do
> real Bayesian inference with LDA anyway --- the posterior is
> combinatorially intractable.

...

> So, are you saying that Stan, BUGS, JAGS are not suitable for any LDA implementation? What could be an example of a custom
> LDA fitter?

What I'm saying is that you can't do Bayesian inference
for LDA.  Nobody can do Bayesian inference for LDA --- there
are too many modes in the posterior.

The best an MCMC algorithm can do for LDA is explore around a single
mode.  So if you start multiple chains, they'll never converge to
the same answer with realistic data (at least any kind of natural
language data I've ever seen).  Now there's some stability in
the major clusters found, as analyzed by Griffiths and Steyvers
for their Gibbs sampler (which marginalizes out the continuous
parameters).

So what I'm saying is that you might as well use something like
variational inference and be content with a single mode.  Or
just a point estimate.  You'll find a super-scalable stochastic
variational inference implemented by Matt Hoffman (who also invented
the NUTS algorithm we use in Stan's MCMC) in Vowpal Wabbit.
Here's the writeup:

http://jmlr.csail.mit.edu/papers/v14/hoffman13a.html

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I'm confused about where you're talking about.

If I'm looking at the right equation, there are no
expectations involved --- it's just computing the
likelihood function by marginalizing out the cutpoint.
And it's just using the usual law of total probability
to do it:

  p(D | e, l)  = SUM_s p(s, D | e, l)    [ law of total probability ]

               = SUM_s p(s) p(D | e, l)  [ definition of joint probability ]

and then the prior p(s) and the likelihood p(D | e, l) break
down into their own terms.

So I don't know what you mean by correcting for the term p(D | e, l).
We don't ever need to compute p(s | D).

- Bob

> On Jan 12, 2016, at 8:11 PM, Mehmet Ozan Kabak <wand...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hello,
>
> I am a little confused after reading the subsection "Posterior Distribution of the Discrete Change Point" in page 126 of the Stan Manual. As described therein, one should normalize the values in the array "lp" to get the probability p(s | e, l, D). This, I get. However, I do not understand why the subsequent equation is true. The summation in this equation is an approximation of E(p(s, D | e, l)), right? [[Here E stands for expectation, which is taken over the posterior p(e, l | D).]]
>
> I don't see why this equals to p(s | D). Isn't the quantity p(s | D) actually equal to E(p(s | e, l, D))? [[Again, the expectation is taken over the posterior p(e, l | D).]] It seems to me that these two expectations are not the same, since p(s, D | e, l) = p(s | e, l, D) * p(D | e, l) whose second term is non-constant within the said expectations.
>
> By not correcting for the term p(D | e, l), doesn't the summation "skip" the per-iteration normalization discussed earlier in the paragraph? Where am I going wrong? Or, is there an error in this subsection of the Stan Manual?
>
> Thanks,
>
> Mehmet Ozan Kabak

messages.subject: rstanarm package released on CRAN
messages.subject_clean: rstanarm package released on CRAN
messages.body_plain:
The rstanarm R package, which has been mentioned several times on stan-users, is now available in binary form on CRAN mirrors (unless you are using an old version of R and / or an old version of OSX). It is an R package that comes with a few precompiled Stan models --- which are called by R wrapper functions that have the same syntax as popular model-fitting functions in R such as glm() --- and some supporting R functions for working with posterior predictive distributions. The files in its demo/ subdirectory, which can be called via the demo() function, show how you can fit essentially all of the models in Gelman and Hill's textbook

http://stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/arm/

and rstanarm already offers more (although not strictly a superset of the) functionality in the arm R package.

The rstanarm package can be installed in the usual way with

install.packages("rstanarm")

which does not technically require the computer to have a C++ compiler if you on Windows / Mac (unless you want to build it from source, which might provide a slight boost to the execution speed). The vignettes explain in detail how to use each of the model fitting functions in rstanarm. However, the vignettes on the CRAN website

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstanarm/index.html

do not currently show the generated images, so call browseVignettes("rstanarm"). The help("rstarnarm-package") and help("priors") pages are also essential for understanding what rstanarm does and how it works. Briefly, there are several model-fitting functions:
stan_lm() and stan_aov(), which just calls stan_lm(), use the same likelihood as lm() and aov() respectively but add regularizing priors on the coefficients
stan_polr() uses the same likelihood as MASS::polr() and adds regularizing priors on the coefficients and, indirectly, on the cutpoints. The stan_polr() function can also handle binary outcomes and can do scobit likelihoods.
stan_glm() and stan_glm.nb() use the same likelihood(s) as glm() and MASS::glm.nb() and respectively provide a few options for priors
stan_lmer(), stan_glmer(), stan_glmer.nb() and stan_gamm4() use the same likelihoods as lme4::lmer(), lme4::glmer(), lme4::glmer.nb(), and gamm4::gamm4() respectively and basically call stan_glm() but add regularizing priors on the covariance matrices that comprise the blocks of the block-diagonal covariance matrix of the group-specific parameters. The stan_[g]lmer() functions accept all the same formulas as lme4::[g]lmer() --- and indeed use lme4's formula parser --- and stan_gamm4() accepts all the same formulas as gamm::gamm4(), which can / should include smooth additive terms such as splines
If the objective is merely to obtain and interpret results and one of the model-fitting functions in rstanarm is adequate for your needs, then you should almost always use it. The Stan programs in the rstanarm package are better tested, have incorporated a lot of tricks and reparameterizations to be numerically stable, and have more options than what most Stan users would implement on their own. Also, all the model-fitting functions in rstanarm are integrated with posterior_predict(), pp_check(), and loo(), which are somewhat tedious to implement on your own. Conversely, if you want to learn how to write Stan programs, there is no substitute for practice, but the Stan programs in rstanarm are not particularly well-suited for a beginner to learn from because of all their tricks / reparameterizations / options.

Feel free to file bugs and feature requests at

https://github.com/stan-dev/rstanarm/issues

If you would like to make a pull request to add a model-fitting function to rstanarm, there is a pretty well-established path in the code for how to do that but it is spread out over a bunch of different files. It is probably easier to contribute to rstanarm, but some developers may be interested in distributing their own CRAN packages that come with precompiled Stan programs that are focused on something besides applied regression modeling in the social sciences. The Makefile and cleanup scripts in the rstanarm package show how this can be accomplished (which took weeks to figure out), but it is easiest to get started by calling rstan::rstan_package_skeleton(), which sets up the package structure and copies some stuff from the rstanarm GitHub repository.

On behalf of Jonah who wrote half the code in rstanarm and the rest of the Stan Development Team who wrote the math library and estimation algorithms used by rstanarm, we hope rstanarm is useful to you.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Bob:

q1 and q2 are not parameters.
they are reward expectations learned in an experiment
where  subjects learn from feedback how valuable two
choice alternatives are.

in this context, abs(q[1]-q[2]) serves as an indicator of
decision difficulty, i.e. choices are more difficult when
abs(q[1]-q[2]) is small.

It is a common assumption that people take more time
to make choices when they are difficult (commonly
referred to as speed accuracy trade-off). When modelling
choices with the the wiener distribution (which should be
renamed to wiener first passage tome distribution ...) this
can be achieved by making the boundary separation
parameter of the wiener fpt distribution dependent on
ab(q[2]-q[1])

Guido

PS:
Tor:
A student of mine has implemented combined RL-DDM models
(in jags) and he found that making boundary separation dependent
on the absolute difference of Q values did not make the model fit
noticeably better.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Are the ODE integrators exposed in function_signature.h?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Are the ODE integrators exposed in function_signature.h?
messages.body_plain:
No, they're built into the statement grammar directly.  The reason
for that is that our regular functions allow any combination of
data (double) and autodiff (stan::math::var) types to be mixed
as arguments.  The ODE integrators require some of those to be data
and additionally require the name of a function to be passed in;
we don't have higher-order functions in the language (yet, anyway).

I believe our develop branch now has two such functions, one for
the Runge-Kutta solver from Boost and one for the CVODE solver
from Sundials.  At least I'm seeing sundials in my builds!

There's a fair number of places that need to change with it built
into the language like this, but it's not too bad.  If you get stuck
with something, let us know.

And it's great to hear you could get your function implemented.

- Bob

messages.subject: A newbie question: system of equations with cross-parameter constraints
messages.subject_clean: A newbie question: system of equations with cross-parameter constraints
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan users,

I've been considering the following problem:
We observe two vectors of data (for a single period), x and y. We wish to estimate a transintion (or bridge) matrix B, such that:
 1. y=B*x
 2. each element of B is constrained to <0,1> interval
 3. the column sums of B all equal one
Typically there would be some prior knowledge of B, but as a first step I would like to start with an uninformative prior.
(This example is an abstraction of a data recovery problem).

A natural formulation of the model is in the form of the system of equations (say, for a 3x2 B matrix):
y[1] = B[1,1]*x[1] + B[1,2]*x[2]
y[2] = B[2,1]*x[1] + B[2,2]*x[2]
y[3] = B[3,1]*x[1] + B[3,2]*x[2]
(plus priors and constraints for B elements)

I am not sure how this translates to Stan notation, and whether it requires formulation of a custom likelihood function.
I would appreciate hints regarding the coding of this model (I'm new to both Stan and Bayesian modeling - I'm actually trying to identify the possibilities of the use of Bayesian estimation in my field).

Best regards
Jakub

What the error message says.  You can only define (i.e., assign)
variables in the block in which they were declared.

You can't declare Mu as data (telling Stan to read it in) and
then define it (telling Stan to forget what you read).

You want to define Mu as either a transformed parameter or
as a local variable in the model block, the difference being
that the former will save it.

- Bob

the manual lists all the rules.

  gradient value

get from Stan even if it doesn't converge and the one that R's
optimize() finds?  You could compare those results.

not mu[1], ..., mu[N-1].   Stan can't use what you don't
define.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Bob,
Thank you for your message.

The relationship is exact, but nevertheless B is unknown and not determined - there are more unknowns (in B) than observables (y, x) here, and hence different Bs will satisfy the relationship y=B*x.

The problem I'm trying to solve is that y and x are vectors of some economic data for industries, reported (for a single year) under two different industrial classifications. The condition sum(x)=sum(y) is guaranteed by the statistcal office that supplies the data, and in that sense I don't deal with measurement error here. The case is that the data supplier does not report the links between classifications (represented by the B matrix; the elements of this matrix actually tell what proportion of, say, output of an industry j according to one classification goes to industry i according to the other classification), which I would like to uncover and show the related uncertainty in terms of probability distribution of B (as the 1st step I assume no prior information on B, but in fact some scarce information is available - including it would be perhaps the second step).

Jakub

I see two possible solutions:

1. Reparametrize the problem in a subspace C such that
y=B(C)*x. Basically you will get back your transformed prior, so this is
not so useful, and may be tedious to implement too.

2. Model the correction that the data supplier performed, with latent
variables, measurement errors, and some normalization. Use examples in
the manual as a starting point. Even in this case, I am not sure what
your model strongly identifies.

Best,

Tamas

Hi!

I am trying to simulate a repeated event counting model. So I have J subjects (fixed) and for each subject a censoring time C_j. The issue I run into when simulating this is that the number of events per subject is a random number such that I need a dynamically sized data structure for this (I have to record the time-points when an event occurs).

Any idea on this?

The brute force solution would be to pre-allocate a data-structure with a fixed maximal number of events, but this feels bad...

Best,

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] dynamically sized data structures?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] dynamically sized data structures?
messages.body_plain:
If the simulation is a pure simulation in generated quantities,
then there's no problem --- use a local variable.  There's no
way to output variable-sized structures --- it would break all of
our posterior reporting.

I'm also afraid there is no good way to convert real values
to integers.  That's by design, because it loses derivative
information.

You could preallocate and use a while loop to hack around
this restriction.  I'm waiting for someone to write the master
hack function that uses binary search and while loops to make
it at least O(log n) instead of O(n), but I'm not going to be
the one to do it :-)

- Bob

> The vb() generally works *great* on this model, which has some complexity.  There is, however, some estimation bias (elicited by estimating the model on synthetic) data for the tau[k] parameters, which are CAR precision parameters, and I suspect I may not have a sufficient number of time points to well-estimate them (rather than the issue being the ADVI approximation).  So i'd like to check this by sampling() under NUTS for this model.  Yet, sampling() doesn't move past the first warm-up iteration.  I receive no messages (other than it is at iteration 1/2000 of chain 1).  All to say, the model script is listed, below, and I appreciate any insights you'd offer about how I might change it to get the NUTS sampler to move.  Thanks.

Presumably that'd be because it's trying to evaluate many leapfrog
steps.  If you can give it a good starting point and if the variables
are all scaled similarly, it'll really help to get things moving.
You can also set refresh=1 to see where it's really getting stuck.

- Bob

>
> /*
>   y[i] ~ N_{T}(B'x[i] + u[i], sigma_y),  where sigma_y are known
>   B    ~ 0 + N_{PxT}(Lambda,Q^{-1})
>   Q    = (D - rb*Omega) - a proper CAR construction without precision param for identifiability
>   rb   ~ U(0,1)
>   Lambda = diag(lam_tau) * corr_Lambda * diag(lam_tau), of dimension P x P
>   lam_tau ~ cauchy(0,5)
>   corr_Lambda ~ lkj(4)
>   u[i] ~ prod_{k=1}^{K} theta[k] * N_{T}(0,mu[k],invSigma[k]^{-1}),
>   invSigma[k]  = tau[k] * (D - rho[k]*Omega)
>   mu[k,j] ~ N(0,5)
>   tau[k]  ~ Gamma(1,1)
>   rho[k]  ~ U(0,1)
>   theta   ~ Dirichlet(alpha/K), which limits to a DP mixture
>
> */
>
> functions{
>     // sum a matrix, by rows
>     vector row_sums(matrix X)
>     {
>       vector[rows(X)] s ;
>       s <- X * rep_vector(1, cols(X)) ;
>       return s;
>     }
>
>     // V \kron U
>     matrix kron(matrix U, matrix V, int P, int T)
>     {
>       // U is P x P and V is T x T
>       // result VU = V \kron U
>       // so P is fast and T is slow
>       matrix[P*T,P*T] VU;
>       for(ti in 1:T)
>         for(tj in 1:T)
>           for(ni in 1:P)
>             for(nj in 1:P)
>               VU[P*(ti-1)+ni, P*(tj-1)+nj] <- V[ti,tj] * U[ni,nj];
>       return VU;
>     }
>
>     // Convert an NT x 1 vector to an N x T matrix, by column
>     matrix vec_to_mat(vector v, int N, int T)
>     {
>       // Fill, by column, so N is fast and T is slow
>       matrix[N,T] V;
>       for( j in 1:T ) /* fill by column */
>       {
>         for( i in 1:N )
>         {
>           V[i,j] <- v[(N*(j-1)+i)];
>         }
>       }
>       return V;
>     }
>
> } /* end user functions{} block */
>

> It is not currently possible to specify initial values for ADVI via rstan because the mechanism we use for sampling is not directly applicable since ADVI needs initial values for the normal variational approximation. You can however specify init_r to some value (it is 2 by default) to limit the range of the initial values in the variational approximation. Thanks for the tips, Bob.  I'm re-jiggering initial values and prior formulations as a model that estimates well under mean field vb() may not under NUTS.  I was wondering whether you would offer any insights on whether any of my prior formulations are particularly bad.  Yes, I know about the scaling issues, which defeated my previous attempts to estimate models in Stan with many levels of hierarchy.

Armadillo is a C++ linear algebra library made available for use in R programming with Rcpp via the package RcppArmadillo.  It relies on the user's rblas, unlike RcppEigen used by Stan, but has easy-to-use syntax.  My point was that Armadillo also allows for restrictive declarations, which it enforces, to either employ a speedier decomposition algorithm or to aid in numerical stability.  So, for example, if one declares a matrix as lower triangular, it automatically zeros out the upper triangular elements.  Stan, differently, checks and may produce an error if any of the upper triangular elements of a declared cholesky covariance matrix are non-zero within some precision, which sometimes happens for me due to numerical precision issues.

Hello!

I have tried to run the Rats (from BUGS) example, but the parameter estimates for the alphas are very different under NUTS and ADVI.

For instance:

rats_model <- stan_model(file = "rats.stan")
rats <- sampling(rats_model, data = data, chains = chains,
                 init = init, iter = iter)
print(rats)

Gives:
Inference for Stan model: rats.
2 chains, each with iter=1000; warmup=500; thin=1;
post-warmup draws per chain=500, total post-warmup draws=1000.

                 mean se_mean    sd    2.5%     25%     50%     75%   97.5% n_eff Rhat

alpha[3]       252.58    0.09  2.86  246.74  250.62  252.70  254.46  258.19  1000    1

But:
rats_model <- stan_model(file = "rats.stan")
rats_advi <- vb(rats_model, data = data)

Gives:
--
Inference for Stan model: rats.
1 chains, each with iter=1000; warmup=0; thin=1;
post-warmup draws per chain=1000, total post-warmup draws=1000.

                  mean      sd     2.5%      25%      50%      75%    97.5%
alpha[1]         11.24   17.75   -24.17    -0.48    11.05    22.64    45.84
alpha[2]          8.78   15.95   -21.72    -2.18     8.36    19.63    40.85
alpha[3]         11.94   16.10   -19.12     0.76    12.32    22.52    43.54
--

I note that the sismasq_alpha parameter is unreasonably large:
--
sigmasq_alpha 61314.73 7601.37 48000.31 55781.03 60716.20 66063.05 77905.34
--

The ADVI algorithm claims that it has converged:
------
Begin eta adaptation.
Iteration:   1 / 250 [  0%]  (Adaptation)

Iteration: 100 / 250 [ 40%]  (Adaptation)

Any idea what's going on here? This is a pretty simple model, so I wouldn't have expected such a disparity.

Thanks in advance!

messages.subject_clean: try ADVI with multiple inits; we hope that ADVI autotuning will improve at some point
messages.body_plain:
One thing you can try is different starting points.  We’ve had lots of discussions in the stan meeting about ADVI failing in lots and lots of these simple examples, and it’s never clear whether the problem is with the variational solution or with the algorithm not converging.  Our guess is that in these settings the result is highly sensitive to initial values and turning parameters.  We have hopes that ADVI’s tuning can be improved so it will give reasonable answers more reliably.  For now, I think it’s best to be safe and run from multiple inits.

Hi, All,

I am pretty new to Stan language although I used to have some experience in WinBUGs, but I am still learning the Stan language in R, with RStan.

Here is my detailed problem:

I am trying to examine guessing as a student characteristic in Rasch model. Rather than assuming guessing is an item parameter and is a constant across all student, I assume, more realistic, that guessing varies based on students' latent ability --- the higher the ability, the less chance for guessing. Then whether student answer one particular item correctly, is the weighted combination of guessing and their ability:

Bernoulli (gurssing_j*1/k + (1-guessing_j)*(exp(theta_j - item.diff_i)/(1+exp(theta_j - item.diff_i)))

where i is the number of items, and j is the number of students.

I generated the data in the way that I proposed [In the attached R file, line 23 - 75 is the function that I generated the data], and want to analysis the data. I think this model cannot be analyzed in traditional IRT models, because now guessing is now at the student side. Then I am trying to analysis the data with Rstan using the Bayesian approach.

So I write my model in Stan language, and try to compile it. At a start point, I started with simplest prior distribution for all parameters, and the model:

for(i in 1:n_student)
  {
    for (j in 1:n_item)
      {
        y[i,j] ~ bernoulli(guessing[i]*.2+(1-guessing[i])*inv_logit(theta[i] - item_diff[j]));
      }
  }
}

First, we strongly recommend taking the model code out of
the R program and making it standalone so that you can get some
use out of line numbers.  I'd also strongly advise indenting
and using standard bracketing.

Also, fewer comments.  I always say that comments go stale,
and here's a prime example:

item_diff ~ uniform(0 ,1); # a normal prior for the difficulty

Anyway, there are several problems with this model, the main
one of which is that you need to constrain parameters.  If
you really require item_diff in (0,1) uniform, then you need
lower- and upper-bound constraints on item_diff's declaration.
Also, the "guessing" parameter is unconstrained, so you'll get
negative values unless you constrain it or put it through an
(inverse) link function yourself (inv_logit) or constrain it
to fall in (0,1).

- Bob

code_mm<-'data {
int<lower=0> n_student; # n_student: the number of students
int<lower=0> n_item; # n_item: the number of items
int<lower=0,upper=1> y[n_student, n_item]; # the matrix of responses
}

parameters {
vector[n_student] theta; // ability theta for student
vector[n_item] item_diff; // difficulty for item
vector[n_student] guessing;  // guessing factor for item
}

model {
// assigning prior distribution for paramaters;
// item_diff is the item difficulty on a uniform(0,1)
item_diff ~ uniform(0 ,1); # a normal prior for the difficulty
// theta is the latent ability with mean 0 and variance 3
theta ~ normal(0,1.732); # a normal prior for the student ability
// guessing follows a prior of uniform(0,1)
// guessing ~ beta(5,23);
guessing ~ uniform(0,1);

// Likelihood:

for(i in 1:n_student)
  {
    for (j in 1:n_item)
      {
        y[i,j] ~ bernoulli(guessing[i]*.2+(1-guessing[i])*inv_logit(theta[i] - item_diff[j]));
      }
  }
}

> On Jan 14, 2016, at 5:32 PM, terrance savitsky <tds...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks for the tips, Bob.  I'm re-jiggering initial values and prior formulations as a model that estimates well under mean field vb() may not under NUTS.  I was wondering whether you would offer any insights on whether any of my prior formulations are particularly bad.  Yes, I know about the scaling issues, which defeated my previous attempts to estimate models in Stan with many levels of hierarchy.

I'm not the right person to ask about this.  Maybe if
there's a more specific question than checking a very
complex looking program it might be easier for someone
else to answer.

Empirically, you want to check that the posteriors make
sense and aren't too sensitive to the priors (unless you
made the priors informative for a reason).

> Armadillo is a C++ linear algebra library made available for use in R programming with Rcpp via the package RcppArmadillo.  It relies on the user's rblas, unlike RcppEigen used by Stan, but has easy-to-use syntax.  My point was that Armadillo also allows for restrictive declarations, which it enforces, to either employ a speedier decomposition algorithm or to aid in numerical stability.  So, for example, if one declares a matrix as lower triangular, it automatically zeros out the upper triangular elements.  Stan, differently, checks and may produce an error if any of the upper triangular elements of a declared cholesky covariance matrix are non-zero within some precision, which sometimes happens for me due to numerical precision issues.

Eigen has that capability, too.  And we have some
specialized operatiosn built in, but they all validate
their arguments rather than just providing views of them.

If you take a symmetric view of a matrix in Eigen, it ignores
above diagonal and duplicates below diagonal.   We thought
telling users to pass in a lower-triangular matrix for
symmetric multiplication might be confusing, but we're looking
into things like this now going forward.

If there's something you think's going wrong in error
checking, let us know specifically what function for what
inputs and we can look into it.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Bob,

I constrained parameters both item_diff and guessing with lower=0, upper=1. And the model is actually run, I am wondering what other problems you see from the proposed model from your point?

Thanks, your suggestion is really helpful!

Sincerely,

Jiaqi

On Friday, January 15, 2016 at 1:39:24 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> First, we strongly recommend taking the model code out of
> the R program and making it standalone so that you can get some
> use out of line numbers.  I'd also strongly advise indenting
> and using standard bracketing.
>
> Also, fewer comments.  I always say that comments go stale,
> and here's a prime example:
>
> item_diff ~ uniform(0 ,1); # a normal prior for the difficulty
>
> Anyway, there are several problems with this model, the main
> one of which is that you need to constrain parameters.  If
> you really require item_diff in (0,1) uniform, then you need
> lower- and upper-bound constraints on item_diff's declaration.
> Also, the "guessing" parameter is unconstrained, so you'll get
> negative values unless you constrain it or put it through an
> (inverse) link function yourself (inv_logit) or constrain it
> to fall in (0,1).
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
> code_mm<-'data {
> int<lower=0> n_student; # n_student: the number of students
> int<lower=0> n_item; # n_item: the number of items
> int<lower=0,upper=1> y[n_student, n_item]; # the matrix of responses
> }
>
> parameters {
> vector[n_student] theta; // ability theta for student
> vector[n_item] item_diff; // difficulty for item
> vector[n_student] guessing;  // guessing factor for item
> }
>
>
> model {
> // assigning prior distribution for paramaters;
> // item_diff is the item difficulty on a uniform(0,1)
> item_diff ~ uniform(0 ,1); # a normal prior for the difficulty
> // theta is the latent ability with mean 0 and variance 3
> theta ~ normal(0,1.732); # a normal prior for the student ability
> // guessing follows a prior of uniform(0,1)
> // guessing ~ beta(5,23);
> guessing ~ uniform(0,1);
>
> // Likelihood:
>
> for(i in 1:n_student)
>   {
>     for (j in 1:n_item)
>       {
>         y[i,j] ~ bernoulli(guessing[i]*.2+(1-guessing[i])*inv_logit(theta[i] - item_diff[j]));
>       }
>   }
> }
> '
>
>
>
> > On Jan 15, 2016, at 1:25 PM, Jiaqi Zhang <219zh...@tongji.edu.cn> wrote:
> >
> >
> > Hi, All,
> >
> > I am pretty new to Stan language although I used to have some experience in WinBUGs, but I am still learning the Stan language in R, with RStan.
> >
> > Here is my detailed problem:
> >
> > I am trying to examine guessing as a student characteristic in Rasch model. Rather than assuming guessing is an item parameter and is a constant across all student, I assume, more realistic, that guessing varies based on students' latent ability --- the higher the ability, the less chance for guessing. Then whether student answer one particular item correctly, is the weighted combination of guessing and their ability:
> >
> > Bernoulli (gurssing_j*1/k + (1-guessing_j)*(exp(theta_j - item.diff_i)/(1+exp(theta_j - item.diff_i)))
> >
> > where i is the number of items, and j is the number of students.
> >
> > I generated the data in the way that I proposed [In the attached R file, line 23 - 75 is the function that I generated the data], and want to analysis the data. I think this model cannot be analyzed in traditional IRT models, because now guessing is now at the student side. Then I am trying to analysis the data with Rstan using the Bayesian approach.
> >
> > So I write my model in Stan language, and try to compile it. At a start point, I started with simplest prior distribution for all parameters, and the model:
> >
> > for(i in 1:n_student)
> >   {
> >     for (j in 1:n_item)
> >       {
> >         y[i,j] ~ bernoulli(guessing[i]*.2+(1-guessing[i])*inv_logit(theta[i] - item_diff[j]));
> >       }
> >   }
> > }

> Oops, just saw this—it was under a different thread than the previous message. Yes this makes sense, I interpret this as the adaptation of eta being bad. That is, one can either force the relative tolerance for convergence to be very small as you put, or one can force the step-size eta to be very small. In any case this is a tell-tale sign that black box variational inference (and stochastic optimization in general) needs a better convergence diagnostic.

Looking at it, I wonder if I shouldn't constrain sigma even more.

We recommend only constraining sigma > 0 and adding
a weakly informative prior for it (that doesn't impose
a hard constraint like uniform or bound sigma away from
0 strongly like the gamma priors).  The problem with
just adding an arbitrary constraint is that it has
a very strong effect on the prior uncertainty.

- Bob

> On Jan 15, 2016, at 2:31 PM, Jiaqi Zhang <219zh...@tongji.edu.cn> wrote:
>
> Thanks, Bob,
>
> I constrained parameters both item_diff and guessing with lower=0, upper=1. And the model is actually run, I am wondering what other problems you see from the proposed model from your point?

> On Friday, January 15, 2016 at 1:39:24 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> First, we strongly recommend taking the model code out of
> the R program and making it standalone so that you can get some
> use out of line numbers.  I'd also strongly advise indenting
> and using standard bracketing.
>
> Also, fewer comments.  I always say that comments go stale,
> and here's a prime example:
>
> item_diff ~ uniform(0 ,1); # a normal prior for the difficulty
>
> Anyway, there are several problems with this model, the main
> one of which is that you need to constrain parameters.  If
> you really require item_diff in (0,1) uniform, then you need
> lower- and upper-bound constraints on item_diff's declaration.
> Also, the "guessing" parameter is unconstrained, so you'll get
> negative values unless you constrain it or put it through an
> (inverse) link function yourself (inv_logit) or constrain it
> to fall in (0,1).
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
> code_mm<-'data {
> int<lower=0> n_student; # n_student: the number of students

> }
>
> parameters {
> vector[n_student] theta; // ability theta for student

> vector[n_student] guessing;  // guessing factor for item
> }
>
>
> model {
> // assigning prior distribution for paramaters;
> // item_diff is the item difficulty on a uniform(0,1)
> item_diff ~ uniform(0 ,1); # a normal prior for the difficulty
> // theta is the latent ability with mean 0 and variance 3
> theta ~ normal(0,1.732); # a normal prior for the student ability
> // guessing follows a prior of uniform(0,1)
> // guessing ~ beta(5,23);

>
> // Likelihood:
>

>       }

> '

>

messages.body_plain:
Sorry --- thought I'd written back.

That was confusing how I wrote it.  The point is that
we're defining q(s | D), which isn't normalized, then just
normalizing it by dividing each entry by the sum;  see
the following formula on p. 127.

On the log scale, that amounts to subtracting log_sum_exp(lp)
from each entry.

I tracked down my original code and I just did the normalization
in R using my own function:

  log_softmax <- function(x) {
    z <- exp(x - max(x));
    return(log(z / sum(z)));
  }

And it's not even good R code --- that last line should
be log(z) - log(sum(z)) for arithmetic stability.

I should've added the code direclty within the Stan generated quantities
block (I may have done it in R).  I'll do that going forward.
See:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1709#issuecomment-172069425

- Bob

Dustin and Alp,  What is your opinion about manually setting the "tol_rel_obj" option?  ADVI works well for my model and data, though I find I receive sufficiently different results when setting tol_rel_obj = 0.001.  Does changing this setting make it more likely that the gradient optimization will bore more deeply into a local optimum (assume the optimum is local) or jump between local optima?

thank you for your advice,

Terrance

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] try ADVI with multiple inits; we hope that ADVI autotuning will improve at some point
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] try ADVI with multiple inits; we hope that ADVI autotuning will improve at some point
messages.body_plain:
The challenge is that to get convergence you need upwards of one million iterations.   The convergence diagnostic makes sense, but it assumes that the algorithm is making appropriate progress at each step (this sort of diagnostic is fine if your algorithm has quadratic convergence properties ie Newton's method).  The problem here is that the algorithm does not make sufficient improvements at each step.

As I noted, some sort of stochastic quasi Newton method may be needed.  Gradient ascent is a terrible method for many problems.  Convergence can be made arbitrarily bad simply by rescaling the problem (eg expand one axis by a factor of ten and convergence will be ~ ten times slower).  This is a very bad property for an algorithm to have.  Any sort of second derivative information, probably regularised, would almost certainly be helpful here (even if noisy).

On Friday, 15 January 2016 22:27:42 UTC+11, Dustin Tran wrote:
> Oops, just saw this—it was under a different thread than the previous message. Yes this makes sense, I interpret this as the adaptation of eta being bad. That is, one can either force the relative tolerance for convergence to be very small as you put, or one can force the step-size eta to be very small. In any case this is a tell-tale sign that black box variational inference (and stochastic optimization in general) needs a better convergence diagnostic.
>
> Dustin
>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] ADVI and Rats example - very different parameter estimates
messages.body_plain:
RStan currently does not allow a set of initial values to be fed to the ADVI module.  You can only set init_r, which controls the scale of random initialisation.

My experimentation suggests that it's the optimisation, because if you run the optimisation with the right parameters you (eventually) get to similar parameter values to MCMC.  Ideally, ADVI should be used to produce parameter estimates which can be fed to MCMC, not the other way around ;)

On Friday, 15 January 2016 22:21:10 UTC+11, Dustin Tran wrote:
> With the normal hierarchical model that Rats uses, it’d be surprising if ADVI’s posterior mean estimates are really that off. A quick diagnostic: can you try initializing ADVI with the posterior mean estimate from NUTS? ADVI should not move very much from that initialization. This would tell us whether the problem is the optimization or the limited expressiveness of the normal mean-field approximation.
>
> Dustin

> > It is not so much the complexity of the model but whether the posterior distribution in the unconstrained space is multivariate normal (and uncorrelated in the meanfield case) and whether the globally optimal multivariate normal distribution is found. I think the point's that it might take 1M iterations
to get convergence to within epsilon using SGD.  Often,
though, in my experience, you can get close enough for
stats with many many fewer iterations.  So you might
find SGD converging to within 1e-3 faster than
L-BFGS but converging more slowly to within 1e-6.

Alp & Dustin:  Is there really no rescaling of parameters
going on?  That's going to be a killer for a lot of models,
because it's hard to get users to give you a standardized model.

In NUTS, we tune a mass matrix which determines relative
parameter scale (and optionally rotation);  the big problem
is that it's a global estimate, that it has to be estimated
during warmup when we haven't gotten to where we want to go yet,
and many of the posteriors we care about have varying curvature.
So something like L-BFGS makes a lot of sense because it
estimates the curvature directly (rather than using draws to
estimate covariance).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
The inverse Hessian/Fisher information, used in the second-order optimization, would be most appropriate for rescaling parameters. The current first-order optimization we use with an adaptive learning rate tries to do this as well: you can interpret the adaptive learning rate as a diagonal approximation to the inverse Fisher information. In other words, the learning rate attempts to rescale parameters but it can only do so much as it compromises for a simpler per-iteration complexity.

Dustin

You shouldn't need those lower=1e-20 bounds.

Rather than writing a parameter B and a comment that
says it's "beta", just call it beta!  Also, why constrain
it to (0,1)?

Adding multiplicative invariances (B * mu)
is problematic in that it makes banana-shaped posteriors.
You can multiply B by 1/c and multiply mu by c and
you get the same product.

And you really want to vectorize, but that's just an
efficiency issue.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Saturday, January 16, 2016 at 1:02:38 PM UTC-5, Fukiko Takamatsu wrote:
> I am new to Stan and I am still learning the stan program. I have a problem with using stan for simulation study. I have a model that I am going to test, and I will call it for 1000 times in the simulation. So I am using the stan_model() function to compile the model once, and then try to call the model in stan() function. Here comes my question, how can I do that?
>
> my_model <- stan_model(*****)
>
> fit_my_model <- stan(*****)

Marco's answer is true, although it shouldn't matter. If you call stan() multiple times within the same R session (and assign the output to an object), it should not recompile the Stan program. Even across R sessions, this should work if you call rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE) as is suggested by the startup message. Another alternative is to pass the previous stanfit object to the fit argument of stan() rather than specifying a file or model_code.

Ben

true if you lower learning rate as you go --- you can stop
prematurely because learning rate goes to zero, not
because you converged.

Normally, I could direct these questions to my major professor (very adept in BUGS), but she will be on maternity leave the next few weeks. I am a biologist not a statistician, but I expect most problems in my career will require strong modeling abilities to properly answer the questions I explore. I hope all this personal information doesn't strike you as strange, I am just trying to give an explantation for my overuse of this group. Bob has been extremely patient, Gelman has written the best Bayesian modeling book I know of, Allen has opened up a world of modeling in Python for me, and I have thoroughly enjoyed Dr. Betancourt's YouTube lectures. I am very lucky to have advice from all of you, it just may take some time before I can actually understand and implement that advice. I think STAN's greatness is the result of all of your enthusiasm to share knowledge, not only your brilliance. I am amazed that you all can even take the time to help people. I just want to let you all know that I am grateful for your help.

In general, this means that you have tried to compile too many Stan programs within an R session. In your case, you should call Stan once outside your Analysis() function that you pass to replicate(). For this purpose, you can call it with

  fit_my_guessing_rasch <- stan(model_code = My_Rasch_guessing, chains = 0)

Suppose we were considering using Metropolis sampling (sorry this example is easier said considering this, rather than HMC), and you had two areas of high probability mass, separated by a large area of very low, yet still finite mass.

If I were to specify a very small width for the proposal/jumping distribution, then it will take a very long time for the sampler to explore the typical set; resulting in slow convergence to the true distribution. My question is this: would one say that the Markov Chain is (practically) non-ergodic here, since it would essentially take an infinity of time to converge?

If not, can you advise me on a continuous example that is truly non-ergodic? Thinking of discrete examples is easy, but am having a harder time thinking of continuous ones.

Best,

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Practical lack of ergodicity vs slow convergence
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Practical lack of ergodicity vs slow convergence
messages.body_plain:
tl;dr: Markov chains will almost always be ergodic.  What we care
about in practice isn’t ergodicity but rather the type of ergodicity.

Firstly, what you describe is not “Metropolis sampling”.  The Metropolis
algorithm, and its generalization Metropolis-Hastings, is a general
algorithm for constructing a Markov chain.  Indeed Hamiltonian Monte
Carlo can be considered a Metropolis algorithm.  To what you refer is
_Random Walk Metropolis_.

Now on to your question.  Ergodicity is simply the guarantee that the
Markov chain will coverage to the target distribution asymptotically.
More specifically, for any given subset of the target parameter space
and initial point there exists some finite number of iterations where
the Markov chain initialized as the initial point has explored that
entire subset.  Of course that number of iterations could be insanely
large and impractical, but still finite, so at no point are we talking about
infinite times.

There are various way to obstruct even this ergodicity, the two easiest
being reducibility and periodicity.  If the Markov chain is reducible then
the target parameter space can be partitioned into subsets, and the
Markov cannot escape the partition in which is starts.  A periodic chain
will get stuck in a loop that explores only a small number of states.

Luckily these conditions are easily remedied by adding small tweaks
to a Markov transition.  Ultimately it’s really, really hard for a Markov
chain to not be ergodic if the target distribution is well-behaved.

But ergodicity alone may not be sufficient in practice, as we only have
computational resources for a finite number of iterations.  What we really
want to ensure good finite-iteraiton behavior are strong ergodicity results,
such as geometric ergodicity, which ensure that the Markov chain converges
to the target distribution at a geometric rate.  Proving that a Markov chain and
a target distribution are geometrically ergodic is really, really, really hard.
Usually we instead try to identify features that obstruct geometric ergodicity
(such as heavy tails) and try to diagnose those features in practice.  Some
colleagues and I are actively working on this for Hamiltonian Monte Carlo.

Now, all of that said, even geometric ergodicity can be insufficient in practice.
For example, consider a multimodal distribution as you suggested.  All
geometric ergodicity says is that you can find the modes really quickly, but
it doesn’t guarantee that you can sample between the modes all that well
(i.e. the Markov chain converges at a geometric rate, but that rate is really,
really slow).

Ultimately, Markov chains are subtle objects and that subtlety matters a
lot more in practice than most people consider.  We’re trying to identify
what matters and turn the into automatic diagnostics to improve the
robustness of these algorithms, but it’s an ongoing process.

Hi don’t worry about conjugate prior, just do whatever makes sense in context of model.  Once you’ve fit your model, you can simulate fake data from the model (as discussed in chapter 6 of BDA) and check that the simulated data look like the real data.  This is called posterior predictive checking and it is an important part of building trust in whatever model you fit.

messages.subject: would basically need a global variable in the model block - any tricks around this?
messages.subject_clean: would basically need a global variable in the model block - any tricks around this?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stan users,

I am fairly new to Stan but already a big fan (very powerful for the first models I have tested!).

Now I encountered an interesting problem which I think others must have before too (though skimming through the list I could not find an answer yet):

Basically I have a latent variable, which requires both transformation and sampling (it's goodwill carried forward and requires another parameter to estimate the weight from the previous goodwill vs. the new observation).

For the first model I ran (which converged fine), I simply defined this latent variable in the model block. Unfortunately, this makes it a local variable that gets lost afterwards.

The issue here is that I would need this variable to include in my log-likelihood calculation (done in the generated quantities block - also to use the loo-package later on). But because it was a local variable (defined in model block), I lost it .

However, I seem not to be able to put the latent-variable transformation in the "transformed parameter block" (which defines global variables) as I am not allowed to do any sampling outside of the model block.

Simply defining/ creating the latent variable in the "transformed parameter block" and adding the calculation in the model block later does not work either (error msg: "wrong side of equation").

What would be the solution to this problem? And why are there no global variables possible in the model block (or are there)?

Thanks
John

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] speeding up zero inflation model through vectorization?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] speeding up zero inflation model through vectorization?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,
thanks for your feedback and help!

I am attaching 3 files:
1) HZAxNB2Regression.stan
is a hierarchical zero inflated negative binomial model
(hierachical only for the count part, not the the zero inflation part).

2) sim_nbinom_data.R
simulates zero inflated data and returns those
and design matrix and parameters used to
created these data

3) test_HZAxNB2Reg.R
used files 1) and 2) to do a parameter recovery
test and plot the results.

I think the estimated are close enough to the
generative parameters, expect that
I am not able to fully recover the zero alteration
(which is more a hurdle model ...).
I am also sometimes getting messages about a few
divergent iterations. But the other diagnostic parameters
(Rhat, neff, msce) look fine. I am not sure what the problem here is .

Best - Guido

PS:
The reason I am so interested in optimizing the model
is that my models already run 20 or more hours (40000+ cases
and 20+ variables), and because I use them in a
multiple imputation context,I need at least 10 chains per model.
So a 20% faster model is worth something.

On Tuesday, January 12, 2016 at 8:54:18 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > On Jan 12, 2016, at 2:45 AM, Guido Biele <guido...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > I am following up with 2 points:
> >
> >
> > 1) My belief that the reference manual describes
> >
> > and incorrect optimized hurdle model is strengthened
> >
> > 2) Code for a faster zero inflated negative binomial model.
> >
> >
> > ### 1) The reference manual describes an ###
> >
> > ###      incorrect optimized hurdle model ###
> >
> >
> > Following up on my last message:
> >
> > I checked and, as described in the manual,
> >
> > poissonCDF(0 | lambda) = log(1-exp(-lambda)).
> >
> > However, to calculate p(y[n] | lambda) for the hurdle model,
> >
> > one has to divide (or subtract on the log scale) by the
> >
> > complementary poisson CDF. poissonCCDF.
> >
> > Instead, the code on page 115 of the
> >
> > reference manual uses the poissonCDF.
> >
> >
> > So it should not be
> >
> > increment_log_prob(-log1m_exp(-lambda))
> >
> > but
> >
> > increment_log_prob(-log1m_exp(log1m_exp(-lambda))).
> >
> > [Alternatively, I am making a fool out of myself ...]
> >
> >
> > ### 2) Code for a faster zero inflated ###
> >
> > ###      negative binomial model. ###
> >
> >
> > Replacing the model section from page 114 in the
> >
> > stan reference the following makes gradient evaluation
> >
> > ca. 20% faster.
> >
> >
> > This code is for a hierarchical model involving multiple
> >
> > groups, using following variables:
> >
> > y: vector of length N with observed counts.
> >
> > phi: vector with over dispersion parameters for groups
> >
> > etas: vector of length N containing log(mu) for the negative binomial distribution
> >
> > thetas: logit of p(y == 0)
> >
> > sx: design matrix
> >
> > sx0: design matrix for zero inflation
> >
> > g_start: index of the first entry for a group in y, sx, or sx0
> >
> > g_nzstart: index of the first nonzero entry for a group in y, sx, or sx0
> >
> > g_end: index of the last entry for a group in y, sx, or sx0
> >
> > betas: matrix with regression weights to obtain log(mu), by group
> >
> > alphas: regressions weight for zero inflation part (same for all groups)
> >
> >
> >
> > ### begin model ###
> >
> > ...
> >
> > thetas <- to_vector(sx0 * to_matrix(alpha));
> >
> >
> > for (gr in 1:M) {
> >
> >     log_phi <- log(phi[gr]);
> >
> >      etas[g_start[gr]:g_end[gr]] <- sx[g_start[gr]:g_end[gr],1:K] * beta[gr,1:K]';
> >
> >
> >      // y > 0  cases
> >
> >      increment_log_prob(bernoulli_logit_log(0,thetas[g_nzstart[gr]:g_end[gr]])
> >
> >                                    + neg_binomial_2_log_log(y[g_nzstart[gr]:g_end[gr]],
> >
> >                                                                          etas[g_nzstart[gr]:g_end[gr]],
> >
> >                                                                          phi[gr]));
> >
> >      // y == 0 cases
> >
> >      for (k in g_start[gr]:(g_nzstart[gr]-1)) {
> >
> >        increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(bernoulli_logit_log(1,thetas[k]),
> >
> >                                                          bernoulli_logit_log(0,thetas[k])
> >
> >                                                          + neg_binomial_2_log_log(0,etas[k],phi[gr])));
> >
> >      }
> >
> >    }
> >
> >
> > ### end model ####
> >
> >
> >
> > Following additional modifications did make the model
> >
> >  slightly faster (around 5%), but appeared to be less stable
> >
> > (i.e. produced NaNs or infinite values where the above model did not):
> >
> >
> >
> > bernoulli_logit_log(1,thetas[k]) can be obtained from log_inv_logit(thetas[k])
>
> Even better, it can be vectorized as bernoulli_logit_log(1, theta) if you do
> it for all of the k values.  It's useful to spend the time to put themtogether
> that way if you want.
>
> I don't want to get too carried away optimizing the code, but would you mind
> sending a complete working model?  I can check it into our example-models
> repo and credit you with it after I validate that it works.
>
> - Bob
>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] would basically need a global variable in the model block - any tricks around this?
messages.body_plain:
Yes, this comes up regularly, but Google groups are impossible
to search (no page rank info).

What you need to do is either

1.  Declare *and* define the variable in transformed variables,
but make all the density contributions (sampling statements
or increment_log_prob) in the model block;  the variables will
be visible in both the model block and generated quantities block.

2.  write a function that provides the value and recompute it
in the generated quantities block.  This isn't as expensive
as it sounds because we don't need to compute derivatives.

- Bob

messages.subject: Dealing with multicollinearity in a hierachical regression
messages.subject_clean: Dealing with multicollinearity in a hierachical regression
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am estimating a hierarchical regression as specified in section 6.12
of the stan 2.9.0 manual.

I have difficulties estimating some parameters, reflected
in high Rhat values, that are (relatively) independent in most groups,
but show stronger linear dependence in a few groups.

stronger linear dependence here means either:
a) full linear dependence because a variable does not vary in a small group
(and the design matrix also includes an intercept)
b) increased linear dependence (e.g. the correlation between two variables
is typically around r = .3, but .8 in few groups.)

I initially thought that this should not be a problem in a hierarchical regression,
but that does not seem to be the case.

My question:
1) For the problem of group-specific full linear dependence:
is it OK to simply ignore Rhat and n_eff of a regression weight beta[v,g] if
variable v does not vary in group g?

2) For the problem of increased linear dependence
QR decomposition of the design-matrix could be used.
Would anybody recommend alternative approaches?

Thanks in advance for your comments/suggestions.

Guido

messages.body_plain:
I will have to check out that book. I really don't understand how Dr. Gelman finds the time. Your timing is great. I was just trying to make sense of the negative binomial prior thing, and the fact that you asked why would I constrain β to be [0,1]. Well my thoughts were that with NB(r,p), the probability p can't be higher than 1 right? That was what tripped me up on this. I didn't realize that Dr. Gelman had his own pmf of NB. So I started playing, and now I realize why you asked me that. This is what I did in Python to test it:

import numpy as np
from scipy.special import binom

def Gelman_NB(theta, alpha, beta):
    term1 = binom((theta + alpha - 1),(alpha - 1))
    term2 = (beta / (beta + 1)) ** alpha
    term3 = (1 / (beta + 1)) ** theta
    x = term1 * term2 * term3
    return x

theta = np.arange(0,11,1)
pmf = Gelman_NB(theta, 2.2, 1.1)
plt.bar(theta, pmf)
plt.show()

print(pmf.sum()) # should intergrate to one for theta = [0, inf]

And sure enough, I could have β be greater than 1, and the sum in this range was close to 1. So I guess this makes me one step closer to understanding the proper prior for the NB. Its very useful that α / β = the mean as well. This is my pmf plot. Hopefully, I made the function right.

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-WcPwy3-ye1Q/Vp6uMYaZxfI/AAAAAAAAAD4/YEMOZMZTfUM/s1600/figure_2.png>

Jason

messages.subject: weighting the likelihood function
messages.subject_clean: weighting the likelihood function
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan Users,

I am faced with the problem that my model of social influence in human decision-making is fitting only the majority type of trials (stay trials), but not the minority type of trials (switch trials). Details are below. x

One idea is to make the switch trials more important for the model by imposing a penalty term for the likelihood function. Admittedly, it’s only a band-aid, but maybe it will generate new information to find out where the model is failing. Back in my old MLE days, this would be straightforward because the solver (fmincon in Matlab) would use the model likelihood as a cost function.

Can something similar be done in Stan, e.g. can I increment_log_prob() for this?

E.g.

if (isSwitch[t]) {
increment_log_prob( bernoulli_logit_log( chswtch[t], valfun2 ) + switchPenalty )
} else {
increment_log_prob( bernoulli_logit_log( chswtch[t], valfun ) )
}

where chswtch are the choice data ("switch" or "stay"), vafun2 is a value function (see below), and switchPenalty is a constant that is computed from the number of switch trials vs. the number of stay trials.

Does this look correct to you? And do I have to increase or decrease the log probability, i.e. in which direction is the gradient going?

Thanks for your insights,
Jan

Here are the details of the task and model.

Decision-making task:
Subjects make a choice in a probabilistic decision-making task (probabilistic reversal learning). Then, they see the choices of 4 other players and - endowed with this information - can make a second decision to "stay" with their first choice or to "switch" to the other option. Finally, the probabilistic reward is displayed.

Model:
We compute different value function for the two choices in each experimental trial. The value function for the first choice (valfun1) is composed of an updated expected value based on my reward experiences in the trial (myValue) and a composite value derived from the other players (otherValue). While still using softmax for action selection (the most commonly used approach in the field), we expanded it to a logistic regression with several predictors (t indexes trial number, choice1 is coded as 1 or 2, hence the use of categorical_logit):

valfun1 <- beta[1] * myValue[t] + beta[2] * otherValue[t];
choice1[t] ~ categorical_logit( valfun1 );

Similarly, the value function for the second choice (valfun2, choice are coded as 0=stay, 1=switch, hence bernoulli_logit) is also composed of several predictors:
a. the overal bias to switch or stay
b. the value difference in the first choice (chosen minus non-chosen)
c. the weighted count of the other players with the my first choice
d. the weighted count of the other players against my first choice

valdiff    <- myValue[t,choice1[t]] - myValue[t,3-choice1[t]];
valfun2   <- beta[3] + beta[4] * valdiff + beta[5] * wgtWith[t] + beta[6] * wgtAgainst[t];
chswtch[t] <- bernoulli_logit( valfun2 );

In order to implement a penalty term for the likelihood function, I would replace the last sampling statement, with the if-statement from above.

The full (unmodified) Stan code is attached (relevant lines are 94-100).

Hi all,

It looks like the main problem was the lack of constraint on the non-decision time (like you mentioned, Guido). I think too many initial proposals exceeded the total RTs for a few trials. I've made the non-decision time parameters non-hierarchical (one for each subject) and set the upper bound for each to the minimum RT for that subject. It seems to be working now, even without log transforming the threshold, and keeping the absolute value on the Q difference. Thanks very much for your help.

On Wed, Jan 13, 2016 at 7:42 AM, Guido Biele <guido...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Bob:
>
> q1 and q2 are not parameters.
> they are reward expectations learned in an experiment
> where  subjects learn from feedback how valuable two
> choice alternatives are.
>
> in this context, abs(q[1]-q[2]) serves as an indicator of
> decision difficulty, i.e. choices are more difficult when
> abs(q[1]-q[2]) is small.
>
> It is a common assumption that people take more time
> to make choices when they are difficult (commonly
> referred to as speed accuracy trade-off). When modelling
> choices with the the wiener distribution (which should be
> renamed to wiener first passage tome distribution ...) this
> can be achieved by making the boundary separation
> parameter of the wiener fpt distribution dependent on
> ab(q[2]-q[1])
