messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] weighting the likelihood function
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] weighting the likelihood function
messages.body_plain:
For optimization, Stan uses the complete log density
as the "cost function" that it maximizes.  So you can
work out your own polarity.

So yes, you can use increment_log_prob().  It just
adds its argument to the overall target log density.

It's hard to say more about a model without seeing
more of it and understanding your intent.  For example,
if isSwitch is not data, it's going to be a problem --- we
only have continuous variables, but if it's not data,
then what you've coded may work, but be inefficient
computationally.

- Bob

> On Jan 20, 2016, at 9:38 AM, glae...@gmail.com wrote:
>
> Dear Stan Users,
>
> I am faced with the problem that my model of social influence in human decision-making is fitting only the majority type of trials (stay trials), but not the minority type of trials (switch trials). Details are below. x
>
> One idea is to make the switch trials more important for the model by imposing a penalty term for the likelihood function. Admittedly, it’s only a band-aid, but maybe it will generate new information to find out where the model is failing. Back in my old MLE days, this would be straightforward because the solver (fmincon in Matlab) would use the model likelihood as a cost function.
>
> Can something similar be done in Stan, e.g. can I increment_log_prob() for this?
>
> E.g.
>
> if (isSwitch[t]) {
> increment_log_prob( bernoulli_logit_log( chswtch[t], valfun2 ) + switchPenalty )
> } else {
> increment_log_prob( bernoulli_logit_log( chswtch[t], valfun ) )
> }
>
> where chswtch are the choice data ("switch" or "stay"), vafun2 is a value function (see below), and switchPenalty is a constant that is computed from the number of switch trials vs. the number of stay trials.
>
> Does this look correct to you? And do I have to increase or decrease the log probability, i.e. in which direction is the gradient going?
>
> Thanks for your insights,
> Jan
>
>
>
> Here are the details of the task and model.
>
> Decision-making task:
> Subjects make a choice in a probabilistic decision-making task (probabilistic reversal learning). Then, they see the choices of 4 other players and - endowed with this information - can make a second decision to "stay" with their first choice or to "switch" to the other option. Finally, the probabilistic reward is displayed.
>
> Model:
> We compute different value function for the two choices in each experimental trial. The value function for the first choice (valfun1) is composed of an updated expected value based on my reward experiences in the trial (myValue) and a composite value derived from the other players (otherValue). While still using softmax for action selection (the most commonly used approach in the field), we expanded it to a logistic regression with several predictors (t indexes trial number, choice1 is coded as 1 or 2, hence the use of categorical_logit):
>
> valfun1 <- beta[1] * myValue[t] + beta[2] * otherValue[t];
> choice1[t] ~ categorical_logit( valfun1 );
>
> Similarly, the value function for the second choice (valfun2, choice are coded as 0=stay, 1=switch, hence bernoulli_logit) is also composed of several predictors:
> a. the overal bias to switch or stay
> b. the value difference in the first choice (chosen minus non-chosen)
> c. the weighted count of the other players with the my first choice
> d. the weighted count of the other players against my first choice
>
> valdiff    <- myValue[t,choice1[t]] - myValue[t,3-choice1[t]];
> valfun2   <- beta[3] + beta[4] * valdiff + beta[5] * wgtWith[t] + beta[6] * wgtAgainst[t];
> chswtch[t] <- bernoulli_logit( valfun2 );
>
> In order to implement a penalty term for the likelihood function, I would replace the last sampling statement, with the if-statement from above.
>
> The full (unmodified) Stan code is attached (relevant lines are 94-100).
>
>

messages.body_plain:
The centering technically refers to (mu, log sigma), so the
only "centered" normal is normal(0, 1).  Then if you want to
do normal(0, 5), you draw normal(0, 1) and multiply by 5.

Much less of an issue if 5 is a constant rather than a parameter,
where the funnel arises.

- Bob

> On Jan 20, 2016, at 2:22 AM, Guido Biele <guido...@gmail.com> wrote:

>
> I was under the impression that using the formulation
> of multivariate priors for hierarchical models as described in
> section 6.12 of the manual already implements non-centered
> parameterization. Is this incorrect?
>
> I am attaching the full stan program.
> This is basically the model on page 75 of the stan manual,
> that is modified to a zero inflated negative binomial model
> that uses more vectorization by looping over groups instead
> of over single cases/rows.
>
> here is the relevant portion of the program:
>
> parameters {
>   matrix[K,M] z;
>   cholesky_factor_corr[K] L_Omega;
>   vector<lower=0>[K] tau;
>   matrix[L,K] gamma;
>
>
>   // parameters for regression model for p(score = 0) (zero alteration)
>   // no hierarchical estimation here because some groups have only a few zeros
>   vector[K0] alpha;
>
>   // excess variance of negative binomial
>   real<lower=0> phi[M];
> }
>
>
> transformed parameters {
>   matrix[M,K] beta;
>   beta <- gx * gamma + (diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega) * z)';
> }
>
>
> model {
>   vector[N] thetas;
>   vector[N] etas;
>   real log_phi;
>
>   // sample parameters
>   tau ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
>   to_vector(z) ~ normal(0,1);
>   L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2);
>   to_vector(gamma) ~ normal(0,5);
>   phi ~ cauchy(0,2);
>   alpha ~ normal(0,5);
>
>   thetas <- to_vector(sx0 * to_matrix(alpha));
>
>   // loop through groups
>   for (gr in 1:M) {
>     log_phi <- log(phi[gr]);
>      etas[g_start[gr]:g_end[gr]] <- sx[g_start[gr]:g_end[gr],1:K] * beta[gr,1:K]';
>
>

>                                                  etas[g_nzstart[gr]:g_end[gr]],
>                                                  phi[gr]));
>      // y == 0 cases
>      for (k in g_start[gr]:(g_nzstart[gr]-1)) {
>        increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log_inv_logit(thetas[k]),// bernoulli_logit_log(1,thetas[k]), //
>                                       log1m_inv_logit(thetas[k]) // bernoulli_logit_log(0,thetas[k]),  //
>                                       + neg_binomial_2_log_log(0,etas[k],phi[gr])));
>
>      }
>    }
> }
>
>
> Guido
>

We strongly recommend using Cholesky factors to parameterize
covariance.  But we don't have the Wishart for that, only
the LKJ prior for correlation matrices, which we then scale.

The only advantage of Wisharts is that they're conjugate, which
doesn't matter for Stan.  Speaking of which, can the following
block be simplified given that m and B and W are data and W is a unit
matrix.

>   mu ~ multi_normal(m, B);
>   Sigma ~ inv_wishart(2, W);
>   theta ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma);

There's a discussion of multivariate reparameterizations
starting on p. 218 of the Stan 2.9.0 manual.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
And no, it's not 3x the cost of a function call.  All those
people at the DoE talk who told you otherwise had never
profiled anything.

And it depends on the function.  See, for example, this neat arXiv paper,
which has lots of graphs (though you won't like the tick
marks, the grey backgrounds, the legends not labeling the lines,
etc. etc. etc.):

  Bob Carpenter, Matthew D. Hoffman, Marcus Brubaker, Daniel Lee, Peter Li, Michael Betancourt.
  2015.
  The Stan Math Library: Reverse-Mode Automatic Differentiation in C++.
  http://arxiv.org/abs/1509.07164

You can see (p. 68) that sum is a factor of 16 and product a factor of 4, but
they're worse for smaller expressions.  Our vectorized sum is a lot faster.

- Bob

P.S.  Here are those plots, all relative to Stan, including the double value
      that just evaluates the function itself.

messages.body_plain:
Although that's not an array of vectors, either, we're
sympathetic to that problem.  We need functions that will
start at index N in an array and peel off any given Stan
data type.  We have all that in C++ as part of our I/O,
but not exposed as functions in Stan.  But it's on our to-do list.

For now, you can use the new slicing functions, though it
looks like there are still some include issues that's blocking
the full functionality there.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] quick tips on improving execution speed
messages.body_plain:
The real issue is that you probably don't want to expand
the Kronecker product as you do in the function, but rather
create a function out of whatever the inputs are currently
to kron(), plus whatever gets operated on by it.  For
instance, this is going to be a killer:

>  Sig_beta                  <- kron(Lambda,inverse(Q),P,T);
>   Lbeta                     <- cholesky_decompose( Sig_beta );

You're trying to Cholesky decompose the whole thing.  Hopefully
others who are better at linear algebra than me can jump in with
the right thing to do here.

The doc is so heavy that it makes the code hard to read here.
I'd recommend pulling math explanations into a big header doc
and then only documenting in code the things that are unusual in
the language.  And maybe what all the variables are in the declarations.

- Bob

> On Jan 19, 2016, at 6:53 PM, terrance savitsky <tds...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Hi experts,  I recently had some nice success using vb() on a mixture model for multivariate data where the mixture is imposed on a set of observation-indexed random effects.   A really nice attribute of stan is that the stan script I write for one estimation algorithm - in this case vb() - may be used for another.  So I'd like to perform exact Bayes NUTS and it is taking excessively long to complete a run.  My data are sized N = 1000 observations and T = 12 time points per observation.   Anyway, I know you're all super busy, so perhaps you might just have a quick look at the modeling block, ignoring everything else, to see if there are any quick tips you might offer on how I might change the sampler geometry.
>
> I wonder whether the observation-indexed random effects, u[i] (each of dimension T x 1), are the culprit since I recall Bob recently mentioning that computing the mass matrix is o(M^3), where M denotes the number of parameters in the model.   Alternatively, while the sampling statement for each u[i] is vectorized, I still loop over the N observations.  Could that be slowing me down, a lot? Lastly, I don't monitor the u[i], but that appears to make little difference on the speed.  I impose a dirichlet distribution on a vector mixing probabilities and I know the manual speaks of an approach for achieving it from a the sum of standard normals, but my intuition tells me that my plain use of the dirichlet() sampling statement isn't the issue.
>
> /*
>   y[i] ~ N_{T}(B'x[i] + u[i], sigma_y),  where sigma_y are known
>   B    ~ 0 + N_{PxT}(Lambda,Q^{-1})
>   Q    = (D - rb*Omega) - a proper CAR construction without precision param for identifiability
>   rb   ~ U(0,1)
>   Lambda = diag(lam_tau) * corr_Lambda * diag(lam_tau), of dimension P x P
>   lam_tau ~ cauchy(0,5)
>   corr_Lambda ~ lkj(4)
>   u[i] ~ prod_{k=1}^{K} theta[k] * N_{T}(0,mu[k],invSigma[k]^{-1}),
>   invSigma[k]  = tau[k] * (D - rho[k]*Omega)
>   mu[k,j] ~ N(0,5)
>   tau[k]  ~ Gamma(1,1)
>   rho[k]  ~ U(0,1)
>   theta   ~ Dirichlet(alpha/K), which limits to a DP mixture
>
> */
>
> functions{
>     // sum a matrix, by rows
>     vector row_sums(matrix X)
>     {
>       vector[rows(X)] s ;
>       s <- X * rep_vector(1, cols(X)) ;
>       return s;
>     }
>
>     // V \kron U
>     matrix kron(matrix U, matrix V, int P, int T)
>     {
>       // U is P x P and V is T x T
>       // result VU = V \kron U
>       // so P is fast and T is slow
>       matrix[P*T,P*T] VU;
>       for(ti in 1:T)
>         for(tj in 1:T)
>           for(ni in 1:P)
>             for(nj in 1:P)
>               VU[P*(ti-1)+ni, P*(tj-1)+nj] <- V[ti,tj] * U[ni,nj];
>       return VU;
>     }
>
>     // Convert an NT x 1 vector to an N x T matrix, by column
>     matrix vec_to_mat(vector v, int N, int T)
>     {
>       // Fill, by column, so N is fast and T is slow
>       matrix[N,T] V;
>       for( j in 1:T ) /* fill by column */
>       {
>         for( i in 1:N )
>         {
>           V[i,j] <- v[(N*(j-1)+i)];
>         }
>       }
>       return V;
>     }
>
> } /* end user functions{} block */
>
>
> data{
>   int<lower=1> N; // number of domains
>   int<lower=1> K; // *maximum* - truncated number of clusters
>   int<lower=1> T; // number of times points - months
>   int<lower=1> P; // number of predictors
>   row_vector[T] y[N]; // Set of N, T x 1 multivariate observations
>   row_vector<lower=0>[T] sigma_y[N]; // known area standard deviations
>   matrix[N,P] x; // matrix of predictors
>   matrix<lower=0>[T,T] Omega; // T x T CAR adjacency matrix for prior on cluster centers
> } /* end data block */
>
>
> transformed data{
>   vector<lower=0>[K] ones_K;
>   vector<lower=0>[T] d;
>   matrix[T,T] D;
>   ones_K <- rep_vector(1,K); /* dirichlet prior on alpha has equal shapes */
>   d <- row_sums(Omega); /* diagonal entries of precision matrix */
>   D <- diag_matrix(d);
> } /* end transformed data block */
>
> parameters{
>   row_vector[T] u[N]; /* latent random effects receiving Gaussian mixture prior */
>   simplex[K] theta; /* mixture probabilities after marginalizing over inclusions*/
>   row_vector[T] mu[K]; /* cluster centers */
>   real<lower=0> tau[K]; /* cluster precision parameters for T x T Rw(1) CAR precision matrix */
>   real<lower=0,upper=1> rho[K]; /* cluster strength of correlation parameters */
>   real alpha; /* DP concentration parameter */
>   //real<lower=0> tb; /* precision parameter for T x T, Q, precision matrix for rows of Beta */
>   real<lower=0,upper=1> rb; /* strength of correlation parameter */
>   /* parameters to form P x P covariance matrix, Lambda, of B ~ 0 + N_{PxT}(Lambda,Q) */
>   cholesky_factor_corr[P] corr_L; /* cholesky of correlation matrix for cols of Beta */
>   vector<lower=0>[P] lam_tau; /* vector of sd parameters for P x P, Lambda */
>   /* PT x 1, z ~ N(0,1), Lbeta <- chol(kron(Lambda,inv(Q)), beta_long <- Lbeta * z */
>   /* equivalent to B ~ 0 + N_{PxT}(Lambda,Q) */
>   vector[P*T] z;
> } /* end parameters block */
>
> transformed parameters{
>   vector[P*T] beta_long; /* P is the fast index, T is the slow index */
>   matrix[P,T] Beta;
>   cov_matrix[P] Lambda;
>   cov_matrix[T] Q;
>   cov_matrix[P*T] Sig_beta; /* Sig_beta <- kron(Lambda,inv(Q)) = Q \kron Lambda */
>   //cholesky_factor_cov[P*T] Lbeta;
>   matrix[P*T,P*T] Lbeta;
>   cov_matrix[T] invSigma[K]; /* invSigma[k] <- tau[k] * (D-rho[k]*Omega) */
>   row_vector[T] fitted_values[N]; /* fitted values for MSE computation */
>   /* P x P covariance matrix, Lambda for cols of Beta */
>   /* formed from correlation matrix, corr_Lambda, and std deviations, lam_tau */
>   Lambda                    <- quad_form_diag( multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(corr_L),
>                                                 lam_tau );
>   /* T x T precision matrix, Q, for rows of T x 1 rows of Beta */
>   //Q                         <- tb * (D - rb * Omega);
>   Q                         <- (D - rb * Omega);
>   /* Implement a Beta ~ 0 + N_{PxT}(Lambda,Q^{-1}) by using  */
>   /* beta_long ~ N_{PT}(0,Sig_beta), where Sig_beta = inverse(Q) \kron Lambda */
>   /* Accomplish by generating PT x 1, z ~ N(0,1) */
>   /* and forming beta_long <- Lbeta * z */
>   /* where Lbeta = chol(Sig_beta) */
>   Sig_beta                  <- kron(Lambda,inverse(Q),P,T);
>   Lbeta                     <- cholesky_decompose( Sig_beta );
>   /* P x T fixed effects, Beta, formed by re-shaping PT x 1, beta_long */
>   beta_long                 <- Lbeta * z; // Beta ~ 0+ N_{PxT}(Lambda,Q)
>   Beta                      <- vec_to_mat(beta_long,P,T); /* P is fast, T is slow */
>   /* Construct set of K (cluster-indexed) T x T CAR precision matrices, invSigma */
>   /* for mixture distribution for N x T, u */
>   for( k in 1:K )
>   {
>     invSigma[k]               <- tau[k] * (D - rho[k] * Omega);
>   }
>
>   /* compute fitted values for MSE computation */
>   { /* block to declare local variables, xb */
>     matrix[N,T] xb;
>     xb    <- x * Beta; // N x P, x, times P x T, Beta
>     for( i in 1:N )
>     {
>         fitted_values[i] <- xb[i] + u[i];
>     } /* end loop i over domains */
>   } /* end local block to declare xb */
>
> } /* end transformed parameters block */
>
> model{
>   // priors for mean and covariance cluster locations
>   alpha ~ gamma( 1.0, 1.0 ); /* DP concentration parameter */
>   theta ~ dirichlet( alpha/K * ones_K ); // instantiate a truncated DP prior
>   { /* local variable block for invSigma[k] */
>     /* priors for invSigma[k] */
>     tau ~ gamma( 1.0, 1.0 ); /* K x 1 vector of cluster-indexed precision parameters */
>     rho ~ uniform( 0, 1 ); /* K x 1 vector of cluster-indexed strength of correlation */
>     for( k in 1:K )
>     {
>       mu[k]         ~ normal( 0.0, 5.0 ); /* T x 1 cluster centers */
>
>     } /* end loop k over clusters */
>   } /* end construction of local variables, invSigma */
>
>
>   // prior for latent response, u_{i} ~ prod_{k=1}^{K}theta_k *N(u_{i},mu_k,Sigma_k)
>   for( i in 1:N ) /* by row of N x T, u */
>   {
>     real ps[K];
>     for( k in 1:K )
>     {
>       ps[k] <- log(theta[k]) + multi_normal_prec_log(u[i], mu[k], invSigma[k]);
>     }
>     increment_log_prob( log_sum_exp(ps) );
>   }

>   // prior for time-indexed fixed effects, P x T, Beta
>   // using separable covariance structure with PxP Lambda
>   // and TxT precision, Q (constructed as a CAR, RW(1))
>   /* sample parameters that compose PxP, Lambda and TxT Q */

>

messages.body_plain:
Nothing is platform dependent in Stan, but you have to give
us more context on what you're trying to do and what's going wrong.
It sounds like an installation problem or a problem with
how you're calling Stan.

And no, you don't ever want to create a diagonal matrix and

messages.body_plain:
You guys are funny. I like the enthusiasm.

I guess I'll add profiling to the PyStan feature request then, as I'm not so keen to set up shop in R for that one task.

Bob - Thanks for the suggestions, I think the implementation below is about twice as fast, but I'm not sure I caught your drift with non-centering. Would you mind checking at the lines marked with ** below?

New Stan model definition (new data also attached):

data {
    int N;  // number of samples

    int K;  // number of intercepts

    int L;  // number of categorical predictors

    int C[L];  // position of last coefficient in each category
    int M;  // number of non-zero values in sparse design matrix for intercepts
    vector[M] c_w;   // design matrix in compressed row storage where c_w[i]
    int c_v[M];      // is a value from column c_v[i], row j values begin
    int c_u[N + 1];  // at position c_u[j] in c_w, and c_u[N + 1] = M.

    int P;  // number of covariates
    matrix[N, P] x;  // covariates

    int R_1;
    int R_2;
    int b_1[R_1];
    int b_1_idx[R_1];
    int b_2[R_2 + 1];
    int b_2_idx[R_2];

    int Q;  // number of non-zero values in sparse sample matrix
    vector[Q] y;    // response value, from sparse matrix,
    int y_i[Q];     // such that y[k] reports have more than
    vector[Q] y_j;  // y_j[k] animals from market:county y_i[k]
}
parameters {

    vector[C[1]] alpha_1;
    vector[C[2] - C[1]] alpha_2_raw;
    vector[C[3] - C[2]] alpha_3;

    vector[P] beta;
    real<lower=0> sigma;  // SD for market-level random effect
}

model {

    // Prior
    append_row(alpha_1, alpha_3) ~ normal(0, 100);
    alpha_2_raw ~ normal(0, 1); // **
    sigma ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
    beta ~ normal(0, 100);

    // Likelihood
    {
vector[K] alpha;
vector[N] a;
vector[R_1 + R_2] b;

alpha <- append_row(append_row(alpha_1, alpha_2_raw * sigma), alpha_3);     // **

a <- csr_matrix_times_vector(N, K, c_w, c_v, c_u, alpha) + x * beta;

a <- exp(a);
b[b_1_idx] <- a[b_1];
for (i in 1:R_2) {
   b[b_2_idx[i]] <- sum(a[b_2[i]:(b_2[i+1] - 1)]);

}
increment_log_prob(dot_product(log(b[y_i] + y_j), y));
    }
}

Apparently the problem was due a the parametrization of the correlation. Windows and Mac allow the model to estimate with

cholesky_factor_corr[2] Ly_C;
matrix[2,2] Ly;

Linux was more sensitive to the misspecification

> demonstrates Stan (python or julia) in economics we would be happy to
> post them.

If anyone out there in Stan user-land is interested in doing this, that would be great!

See you
A

messages.body_plain:
Hello Bob, Daniel,

it seems I am confused. I believe I understand
what non-centered parameterization is. Looking
at the formulation of the betas I used (based on
the manual):

beta <- u * gamma + (diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega) * z)';

this seems to me to implement non-centered
parameterization. We have the mu [u*gamma],
the scale [ (diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega)]
and the sampling from a unit normal [z].
The manual also described that this approach
"... parameterize[s] the model directly in terms
of Cholesky factors of correlation matrices using
the multivariate version of the noncentered
parameterization...".
This also suggests to me that the model already
implements non-centered parameterization.

So I am stuck here and don't really know how
I should use your last answer to help the model
to deal better with collinearity.

Could anaybody give me more specific hints
and/or point me to what it is I am not understanding
correctly?

Thanks, Guido

> only "centered" normal is normal(0, 1).  Then if you want to

> where the funnel arises.

> For optimization, Stan uses the complete log density

>> On Jan 20, 2016, at 9:38 AM, glae...@gmail.com wrote:
>>
>> Dear Stan Users,
>>
>> I am faced with the problem that my model of social influence in human decision-making is fitting only the majority type of trials (stay trials), but not the minority type of trials (switch trials). Details are below. x
>>
>> One idea is to make the switch trials more important for the model by imposing a penalty term for the likelihood function. Admittedly, it’s only a band-aid, but maybe it will generate new information to find out where the model is failing. Back in my old MLE days, this would be straightforward because the solver (fmincon in Matlab) would use the model likelihood as a cost function.
>>
>> Can something similar be done in Stan, e.g. can I increment_log_prob() for this?
>>
>> E.g.
>>
>> if (isSwitch[t]) {
>> increment_log_prob( bernoulli_logit_log( chswtch[t], valfun2 ) + switchPenalty )
>> } else {
>> increment_log_prob( bernoulli_logit_log( chswtch[t], valfun ) )
>> }
>>
>> where chswtch are the choice data ("switch" or "stay"), vafun2 is a value function (see below), and switchPenalty is a constant that is computed from the number of switch trials vs. the number of stay trials.
>>
>> Does this look correct to you? And do I have to increase or decrease the log probability, i.e. in which direction is the gradient going?
>>
>> Thanks for your insights,
>> Jan
>>
>>
>>
>> Here are the details of the task and model.
>>
>> Decision-making task:
>> Subjects make a choice in a probabilistic decision-making task (probabilistic reversal learning). Then, they see the choices of 4 other players and - endowed with this information - can make a second decision to "stay" with their first choice or to "switch" to the other option. Finally, the probabilistic reward is displayed.
>>
>> Model:
>> We compute different value function for the two choices in each experimental trial. The value function for the first choice (valfun1) is composed of an updated expected value based on my reward experiences in the trial (myValue) and a composite value derived from the other players (otherValue). While still using softmax for action selection (the most commonly used approach in the field), we expanded it to a logistic regression with several predictors (t indexes trial number, choice1 is coded as 1 or 2, hence the use of categorical_logit):
>>
>> valfun1 <- beta[1] * myValue[t] + beta[2] * otherValue[t];
>> choice1[t] ~ categorical_logit( valfun1 );
>>
>> Similarly, the value function for the second choice (valfun2, choice are coded as 0=stay, 1=switch, hence bernoulli_logit) is also composed of several predictors:
>> a. the overal bias to switch or stay

>> In order to implement a penalty term for the likelihood function, I would replace the last sampling statement, with the if-statement from above.

I examined the samples more closely in
shinystan (great tool!) and have a better idea
what might be going on.

As a reminder, here is the central line of the model/program:
beta <- u * gamma + (diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega) * z)';

I found that it were primarily the parameters gamma
that had a low number of effective samples.
The non-centered parameterization is, however,
only implemented for the betas,and not for these
gammas.

So it seems that it would make sense to use non-centered
parameterization also for the gammas.E.g something like
this when using simple univariate priors:

parameters {
  ..
  matrix[L,K] gamma_raw;
  matrix[L,K] gamma_mu;
  matrix[L,K] gamma_scale;
  ..
}

transformed parameters {
  ...
  matrix[L,K] gamma;
  ...
  for (v in 1:L) {
    for (w in 1:K) {
      gamma[v,w] <- gamma_mu[v,w] + gamma_raw[v,w] * gamma_scale[v,w];
    }
  }
  ...
}

model {
  ...
  to_vector(gamma_raw) ~ normal(0,1);
  to_vector(gamma_mu) ~ normal(0,5);
  to_vector(gamma_scale) ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
  ...
}

Does this make sense to you?

Guido

Hello Daniel,
and other readers,

yes, in the original model gamma is sampled from normal(0,5).

Still, when I look at the correlation of the gamma values,
some of them are quite high, as you can see in the attached plot.
It shows the pairwise correlation of two gamma values for 19
individual level predictors*. The attached zip file has all correlations.
I find that the gammas are strongly correlated for some individual
level predictors.

So my thought was to use the non-centered parameterization, which
in the original model was used only for the regression weights beta,
also for the regression weights gamma used to determine
(the means of) group-specific betas based on group level variables.

I guess the idea is clearest when in the following model fragment, which
model's gammas just as betas with multivariate priors and non-centered
parameterization:

parameters {
  // multivariate priors and non-centered parameterization
  // for regression of means of group level regression weights (betas)
  matrix[L,K] gamma_z;
  cholesky_factor_corr[L] gamma_L_Omega;
  vector<lower=0>[L] gamma_tau;
  matrix[L,K] gamma_mu;

  // multivariate priors and non-centered parameterization
  // for regression weights beta for individual level predictors

  matrix[K,M] z;
  cholesky_factor_corr[K] L_Omega;
  vector<lower=0>[K] tau;

  ...

}

transformed parameters {
  matrix[M,K] beta;

  matrix[L,K] gamma;
  // regression weights for modeling the mean of
  // group level betas (gx*gamma) as depending on
  // gx is a matrix of group level variables

  gamma <- gamma_mu + (diag_pre_multiply(gamma_tau,gamma_L_Omega) * gamma_z);

  // group level regression weights

  beta <- gx * gamma + (diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega) * z)';
}

model {
  ...
  tau ~ cauchy(0,2.5); # orig scale = 2.5

  to_vector(z) ~ normal(0,1);
  L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2);

  gamma_tau ~ cauchy(0,2.5); # orig scale = 2.5
  to_vector(gamma_z) ~ normal(0,1);
  gamma_L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2);
  to_vector(gamma_mu) ~ normal(0,5);
  ...
}

so in essence I just applied the idea to model regression weights
as "location + norm(0,1) * scale" to a different set of regressors**.

Does this approach make now more sense?

Guido

* I have K=19 individual level predictors, 22 groups, and thus
19*22 regression weights beta. The mean of each beta depends
on group level variables in the matrix gx and regression weights gamma.
As gx has L=5 columns, this makes 5 *19 gamma values. The mean
of each beta depends gx and on the values of the 5 associated gamma
values. For the plot I choose a pairwise correlation between gamma values
and show it for all 19 individual level predictors.
Hence the plot shows if/how the the gammas associated if one predictor
are correlated for a particular individual level predictor.
... man, this is hard to explain ...
**just as was done for beta, which also could be samples as to_vector(beta) <- norm(0,5),
but instead is modeled with multivariate priors and non-centered

messages.body_plain:
That's very tricky to measure.  You need to first make
sure both models are really recovering the right values.
Then you need to measure time divided by effective sample size.
And for ESS, you want to compute it with our methods, which
are more conservative in dealing with long-period autocorrelation
and with non-convergence cross-chains;  this latter often leads
to a huge difference in results between RStan's n_eff and
the ones from Coda (it can be on the order of 50 vs. 10,0000 when
there are very long-period autocorrelations Coda doesn't catch).

- Bob

> On Jan 21, 2016, at 4:53 AM, Jan Gläscher <glae...@gmail.com> wrote:

We have run the previous model in Stan before and the simulation time was very good, e.g. compared to JAGS about a 40% reduction in simulation time.

> Jan

>> On 20 Jan 2016, at 23:15, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>
>> For optimization, Stan uses the complete log density
>> as the "cost function" that it maximizes.  So you can
>> work out your own polarity.
>>
>> So yes, you can use increment_log_prob().  It just
>> adds its argument to the overall target log density.
>>
>> It's hard to say more about a model without seeing
>> more of it and understanding your intent.  For example,
>> if isSwitch is not data, it's going to be a problem --- we
>> only have continuous variables, but if it's not data,
>> then what you've coded may work, but be inefficient

>>

>>
>>> On Jan 20, 2016, at 9:38 AM, glae...@gmail.com wrote:
>>>
>>> Dear Stan Users,
>>>
>>> I am faced with the problem that my model of social influence in human decision-making is fitting only the majority type of trials (stay trials), but not the minority type of trials (switch trials). Details are below. x
>>>
>>> One idea is to make the switch trials more important for the model by imposing a penalty term for the likelihood function. Admittedly, it’s only a band-aid, but maybe it will generate new information to find out where the model is failing. Back in my old MLE days, this would be straightforward because the solver (fmincon in Matlab) would use the model likelihood as a cost function.
>>>
>>> Can something similar be done in Stan, e.g. can I increment_log_prob() for this?
>>>
>>> E.g.
>>>
>>> if (isSwitch[t]) {
>>> increment_log_prob( bernoulli_logit_log( chswtch[t], valfun2 ) + switchPenalty )
>>> } else {
>>> increment_log_prob( bernoulli_logit_log( chswtch[t], valfun ) )
>>> }
>>>
>>> where chswtch are the choice data ("switch" or "stay"), vafun2 is a value function (see below), and switchPenalty is a constant that is computed from the number of switch trials vs. the number of stay trials.
>>>
>>> Does this look correct to you? And do I have to increase or decrease the log probability, i.e. in which direction is the gradient going?
>>>
>>> Thanks for your insights,
>>> Jan
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>> Here are the details of the task and model.
>>>
>>> Decision-making task:
>>> Subjects make a choice in a probabilistic decision-making task (probabilistic reversal learning). Then, they see the choices of 4 other players and - endowed with this information - can make a second decision to "stay" with their first choice or to "switch" to the other option. Finally, the probabilistic reward is displayed.
>>>
>>> Model:
>>> We compute different value function for the two choices in each experimental trial. The value function for the first choice (valfun1) is composed of an updated expected value based on my reward experiences in the trial (myValue) and a composite value derived from the other players (otherValue). While still using softmax for action selection (the most commonly used approach in the field), we expanded it to a logistic regression with several predictors (t indexes trial number, choice1 is coded as 1 or 2, hence the use of categorical_logit):
>>>
>>> valfun1 <- beta[1] * myValue[t] + beta[2] * otherValue[t];
>>> choice1[t] ~ categorical_logit( valfun1 );
>>>
>>> Similarly, the value function for the second choice (valfun2, choice are coded as 0=stay, 1=switch, hence bernoulli_logit) is also composed of several predictors:
>>> a. the overal bias to switch or stay
>>> b. the value difference in the first choice (chosen minus non-chosen)
>>> c. the weighted count of the other players with the my first choice
>>> d. the weighted count of the other players against my first choice
>>>
>>> valdiff    <- myValue[t,choice1[t]] - myValue[t,3-choice1[t]];
>>> valfun2   <- beta[3] + beta[4] * valdiff + beta[5] * wgtWith[t] + beta[6] * wgtAgainst[t];
>>> chswtch[t] <- bernoulli_logit( valfun2 );
>>>
>>> In order to implement a penalty term for the likelihood function, I would replace the last sampling statement, with the if-statement from above.
>>>
>>> The full (unmodified) Stan code is attached (relevant lines are 94-100).
>>>

On Thursday, January 21, 2016 at 8:29:11 PM UTC-5, Jason Tilley wrote:
>
> So if I'm following correctly, higher eta would be similar to having a higher multiplier for a diagonal matrix of ones (or any symmetric matrix for that matter)? And I suppose the diagonal would have a higher multiplier than away from the diagonal?

Well, we are talking about a (decomposition of a) correlation matrix, so the diagonal elements are all 1 and can't be multiplied without it ceasing to be a correlation matrix. But as eta gets larger, the correlation matrices near the identity matrix become increasingly likely.

Ben

messages.subject: Homebrew cmdstan install available (and cmdstan build/install structure)
messages.subject_clean: Homebrew cmdstan install available (and cmdstan build/install structure)
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have updated the Homebrew formula for installing cmdstan and had it accepted by the Homebrew maintainers. This means that Mac OS X users with homebrew can now install cmdstan simply by running:

brew install cmdstan

on a command line.

When creating the homebrew formula I had to rewrite the cmdstan make files in order to build files into the directory structure that Homebrew enforces. I'm not sure of the reasons for why cmdstan build object files into the bin dir (and related issues, see link to formula below) but I suggest long-term this might be changed to use a more standard build/directory structure. Please see this formula file for the 3 rewrite steps I had to introduce to build into "lib" rather than the "bin" dir (for non-binary files):

https://github.com/Homebrew/homebrew-science/blob/master/cmdstan.rb

A more detailed account of the steps I went through to get this past Homebrew maintainers can be found here:
https://github.com/Homebrew/homebrew-science/pull/3215

Best regards,

Robert Feldt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Estimating Parameters for ODE
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Estimating Parameters for ODE
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for this. I wrote up my notes here
https://idontgetoutmuch.wordpress.com/2016/01/15/inferring-parameters-for-odes-using-stan/
in the hope they might be of use to other Stan users.

On 11/01/2016 02:11, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Stan does use a symplectic integrator for the Hamiltonian simulation.
> We're using a 5th-order Runge-Kutta from Boost for Stan's language and
> we're about to add a stiff solver from CVODE (can't recall the algorithm
> it uses).
>
> If you're working in RStan, I believe the pairs plot will point
> out where things go wrong.  You can also inspect the divergences
> directly --- they'll be 1 or 0, depending on whether there was
> or wasn't an arithmetic issue.  There's some fiddling to get them
> out of the fit object.  You can also look at the traceplots,
> where a chain getting stuck for a long time will show up as a straight
> line.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
>> On Jan 9, 2016, at 6:46 AM, Dominic Steinitz <dom...@steinitz.org> wrote:
>>
>> Thanks very much for your response.
>>
>> My R code implemented Euler's method to solve the ODE (actually a version with "white noise" but the noise is very small in my example). I solved the same equation in Stan and got reasonably similar results. I assume Stan uses RK4? Although maybe it should use a symplectic integrator ;-)
>>
>> The initial value is the initial value for the simulation.
>>
>> I can't explain it but the inference is now working both for simulations generated by Stan and for simulations generated by my R code. It's possibly because I am not very used to imperative languages and assume when I calculate something then all the dependencies get re-calculated. Of course I thought I had selected the whole region (in emacs) and recalculated but maybe I was missing something.
>>
>> Yes I noticed n_eff=2 wasn't good but thanks for pointing it out.
>>
>> For future reference, how would one inspect how a chain is getting stuck?
>>
>> For info, I was using Stan to confirm that my Sequential Monte Carlo inference was giving sensible answers; it seems that it does.
>>
>> Thanks once more to everyone who responded. I hope to write up the example so it might be of some use to other Stan users.
>>
>> Dominic.
>>
>> On 08/01/2016 20:51, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>> Why doesn't the simulation code involve an ODE simulator?  Or
>>> does it implicitly somehow?  You might want to try verifying
>>> that the simulation is making sense somehow.
>>>
>>> Also, it looks like a different ODE, so it's a rather different
>>> simulation.
>>>
>>> I also wasn't sure what you mean for initial value --- is that
>>> where you start simulating or an initialization given to Stan?
>>>
>>> Also, what David Manheim said is important --- if you are
>>> only getting n_eff=2, your chains aren't converging.  So you
>>> might want to inspect how they're getting stuck.
>>>
>>> - Bob
>>>
>>>> On Jan 7, 2016, at 2:24 PM, idontgetoutmuch <idontge...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>
>>>>
>>>> I've modified the example in Stan Manual Figure 19.3 to have one unknown parameter, theta, but so that the observations are a noisy non-linear function of the state. The equations describe a pendulum with only noisy observations of the horizontal displacement available. I simulate data with a value for theta with the value 9.81 but the inferred value below is nowhere near this. I assume I have made a mistake in the model somehow. Perhaps someone can help me out?
>>>>
>>>>                mean se_mean       sd      2.5%       25%       50%       75%
>>>> theta[1]     -2.27    2.80     3.97     -8.84     -3.44     -0.97      0.20
>>>> lp__     -25397.21 9324.91 13194.01 -33838.87 -33044.87 -32592.90 -24948.26
>>>>              97.5% n_eff     Rhat
>>>> theta[1]     1.70     2   560.20
>>>> lp__     -2567.77     2 20217.25
>>>>   Here's the Stan
>>>>
>>>> functions {
>>>>    real[] pendulum(real t,
>>>>                    real[] y,
>>>>                    real[] theta,
>>>>                    real[] x_r,
>>>>                    int[] x_i) {
>>>>      real dydt[2];
>>>>      dydt[1] <- y[2];
>>>>      dydt[2] <- - theta[1] * sin(y[1]);
>>>>      return dydt;
>>>>    }
>>>> }
>>>> data {
>>>>    int<lower=1> T;
>>>>    real z[T];
>>>>    vector<lower=0>[1] sigma;
>>>>    real y0[2];
>>>>    real t0;
>>>>    real ts[T];
>>>> }
>>>> transformed data {
>>>>    real x_r[0];
>>>>    int x_i[0]; }
>>>> parameters {
>>>>    real theta[1];
>>>> }
>>>> model {
>>>>    real y_hat[T,2];
>>>>    real z_hat[T];
>>>>    theta ~ normal(0,1);
>>>>    y_hat <- integrate_ode(pendulum, y0, t0, ts, theta, x_r, x_i);
>>>>    for (t in 1:T) {
>>>>      z_hat[t] <- sin(y_hat[t,1]);
>>>>      z[t] ~ normal(z_hat[t], sigma);
>>>>    }
>>>> }
>>>>
>>>>
>>>> and here's how I am simulating the data
>>>>
>>>> library(rstan)
>>>> library(mvtnorm)
>>>>
>>>> qc1 = 0.01
>>>> deltaT = 0.01
>>>> nSamples = 500
>>>> m0 = c(1.6, 0)
>>>> g = 9.81
>>>>
>>>> bigQ = matrix(c(qc1 * deltaT^3 / 3, qc1 * deltaT^2 / 2,
>>>>                  qc1 * deltaT^2 / 2,       qc1 * deltaT
>>>>                  ),
>>>>                nrow = 2,
>>>>                ncol = 2,
>>>>                byrow = TRUE
>>>>                )
>>>>
>>>> bigR = matrix(c(0.1),
>>>>                nrow = 1,
>>>>                ncol = 1,
>>>>                byrow = TRUE)
>>>>
>>>> etas <- rmvnorm(n=nSamples,mean=c(0.0,0.0),sigma=bigQ)
>>>> epsilons <- rmvnorm(n=nSamples,mean=c(0.0),sigma=bigR)
>>>>
>>>> x <- matrix()
>>>> length(x) <- 2 * (nSamples + 1)
>>>> dim(x) <- c(nSamples + 1, 2)
>>>>
>>>> y <- vector()
>>>> length(y) <- 1 * nSamples
>>>> dim(y) <- c(nSamples)
>>>>
>>>> x[1,1] = m0[1]
>>>> x[1,2] = m0[2]
>>>>
>>>> for (i in 1:nSamples) {
>>>>      x[i+1,1] <- x[i,1] + x[i,2] * deltaT

>>>>      x[i+1,] <- x[i+1,] + etas[i,]

>>>>                  data = list (T  = nSamples,
>>>>                               z = y,

>>>>                               t0 = 0.0,

messages.body_snippet:
Hi everyone,

First, a big thanks too the Stan development team for putting out an amazing (group of) tools. I've been learning and working with Stan for about a year now, and am more and more amazed

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan/PyStan example from Economics/Finance/Investment: Investing in hydropower upgrades.
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Stan/PyStan example from Economics/Finance/Investment: Investing in hydropower upgrades.
messages.body_plain:
Thanks.  And good timing.  The good folks at QuantEcon were
just asking for PyStan examples in econometrics if you're
interested in putting the example into Jupyter and contributing
it:

  http://quantecon.org/notebooks.html

I suggested they make it clear that authors would maintain
copyright and I think they're going to do that.

The only thing I'd suggest for the code is vectorizing
the Cauchy sampling statements --- you don't need the loop.

  to_vector(mu_b) ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
  to_vector(re_b) ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

And I'd describe epsilon as an intercept in the GLM and use
a different letter for it.

You  might also want priors on all your parameters --- I
don't see any on sigma_bry, for instance.

- Bob

> On Jan 22, 2016, at 11:18 AM, Johannes Mauritzen <johannes....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi everyone,
>
> First, a big thanks too the Stan development team for putting out an amazing (group of) tools. I've been learning and working with Stan for about a year now, and am more and more amazed by what it can do and how helpful and user-oriented the development team is.
>
> I thought I would try to contribute in however small way by posting the Stan code and data for a project I am currently working on. But a strong warning: I am a Stan amateur, and while the code runs and Stan converges (quickly), I make no claims to my code being written in an optimum way or the statistics being particularily well thought out (yet). But for a complete beginner, perhaps it will still be instructive. On the flip side, should anyone see obvious problems with my code or statistics, I would be happy to hear criticisms.
>
> Let me start by trying to explain what I am doing. The research topic is to try to analyse the investment decision of hydropower plant owners who decide to upgrade their plants by installing new generators or upgrading existing generators. The dependent variable is then a 0/1 variable of whether or not an investment happens in a given year (2012-2014) for a particular plant. In particular, the question we want to pursue is what relation this investment decision has to the amount of renewable wind/solar energy that already exist in the area and how this interacts with a policy variable, which is whether there exists a Renewable Portfolio Standards that requires a certain percentage of renewables in the energy mix in the state where a hydroplant exists.
>
> I guess you have to decide yourself if this is interesting, but the idea in my mind is that the relationship could go either way. Hydropower - especially with a reservoir - can do a good job of balancing out the intermittency of solar or wind - that is the fact that you can not control when it is sunny or when it is windy. So a lot of solar and wind could lead to increased investment in hydropower plants. On the other hand, if owners are just trying to fill a quota - of which hydro counts, then we could expect a substitute effect where new hydro is installed instead of solar/wind.
>
> a data file in "pickle" format is included with this post. Below I will copy the Stan code and the very short PyStan call.
>
> In the stan code below, I will have 4 levels in the model hierarchy: observation level which is a plant-year. Each plant-year is then grouped by plant (so every plant has three observations - 2012, 2013, 2014). In turn each plant belongs to a certain Transmission System Owner (TSO) - the entity that owns the power lines connecting the different power plants and the rest of the grid. We can expect a lot of variation here - some TSOs are vertically integrated utilities that also own the plants, other times power plant owners are seperate and private. Finally, I group the TSOs into two groups - those that operate in states with renewable portfolio standards and those that don't.
>
> Starting at the model section of the stan code, I model the investment decision as a bernoulli model with logit link function. Going up a level to the transformed parameter section, the fitted values, y_hat are modelled as a random effect for each plant b_obs, a random effect for the report year, bry, and an error term epsilon, which is meant to capture over dispersion - that is an excess of zeros over what would be expected.
>
> Going up a level in the transformed parameters sections, I model each plant-level random effect b_obs as an additive function of an intercept plus the effects of 5 plant-level variables: whether the plant has a reservoir, whether it uses pumped storage (can pump up water to a higher level at low demand times, in order to generate electricity at high demand) whether the power plant is a vertically integrated utility or an Independent Power Producer, the nameplate capacity of the plant and the year the plant started operation.
>
> Again, moving up in the transformed parameters section, The coefficients on the plant level variables are modelled as an additive function of a coefficient on the percent of intermittents, mu_b of (wind and solar) in a TSO and a random effect. The mu_b variables are in turn modeled as having seperate distributions between RPS and non-RPS states. The posterior distributions of the mu_b coefficients are then what I am most interested in - comparing those in RPS and non-RPS states.
>
> Stan Code:
>
> data{
> int<lower = 0> N; // number of observations
> int<lower = 0> Y; //number or reporting years 2012-2014

>>>> On Jan 20, 2016, at 9:38 AM, glae...@gmail.com wrote:
>>>>
>>>> Dear Stan Users,
>>>>
>>>> I am faced with the problem that my model of social influence in human decision-making is fitting only the majority type of trials (stay trials), but not the minority type of trials (switch trials). Details are below. x
>>>>
>>>> One idea is to make the switch trials more important for the model by imposing a penalty term for the likelihood function. Admittedly, it’s only a band-aid, but maybe it will generate new information to find out where the model is failing. Back in my old MLE days, this would be straightforward because the solver (fmincon in Matlab) would use the model likelihood as a cost function.
>>>>
>>>> Can something similar be done in Stan, e.g. can I increment_log_prob() for this?
>>>>
>>>> E.g.
>>>>
>>>> if (isSwitch[t]) {
>>>> increment_log_prob( bernoulli_logit_log( chswtch[t], valfun2 ) + switchPenalty )
>>>> } else {
>>>> increment_log_prob( bernoulli_logit_log( chswtch[t], valfun ) )
>>>> }
>>>>
>>>> where chswtch are the choice data ("switch" or "stay"), vafun2 is a value function (see below), and switchPenalty is a constant that is computed from the number of switch trials vs. the number of stay trials.
>>>>
>>>> Does this look correct to you? And do I have to increase or decrease the log probability, i.e. in which direction is the gradient going?
>>>>
>>>> Thanks for your insights,
>>>> Jan
>>>>
>>>>
>>>>
>>>> Here are the details of the task and model.
>>>>
>>>> Decision-making task:
>>>> Subjects make a choice in a probabilistic decision-making task (probabilistic reversal learning). Then, they see the choices of 4 other players and - endowed with this information - can make a second decision to "stay" with their first choice or to "switch" to the other option. Finally, the probabilistic reward is displayed.
>>>>
>>>> Model:
>>>> We compute different value function for the two choices in each experimental trial. The value function for the first choice (valfun1) is composed of an updated expected value based on my reward experiences in the trial (myValue) and a composite value derived from the other players (otherValue). While still using softmax for action selection (the most commonly used approach in the field), we expanded it to a logistic regression with several predictors (t indexes trial number, choice1 is coded as 1 or 2, hence the use of categorical_logit):
>>>>
>>>> valfun1 <- beta[1] * myValue[t] + beta[2] * otherValue[t];
>>>> choice1[t] ~ categorical_logit( valfun1 );
>>>>
>>>> Similarly, the value function for the second choice (valfun2, choice are coded as 0=stay, 1=switch, hence bernoulli_logit) is also composed of several predictors:
>>>> a. the overal bias to switch or stay
>>>> b. the value difference in the first choice (chosen minus non-chosen)
>>>> c. the weighted count of the other players with the my first choice
>>>> d. the weighted count of the other players against my first choice
>>>>
>>>> valdiff    <- myValue[t,choice1[t]] - myValue[t,3-choice1[t]];
>>>> valfun2   <- beta[3] + beta[4] * valdiff + beta[5] * wgtWith[t] + beta[6] * wgtAgainst[t];
>>>> chswtch[t] <- bernoulli_logit( valfun2 );
>>>>
>>>> In order to implement a penalty term for the likelihood function, I would replace the last sampling statement, with the if-statement from above.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Gene,

Sorry for the delay, but I've finally got this sorted out. The problem is that your y_rep doesn't have the right dimensions but ShinyStan was just waiting for an object with the correct dimensions instead of issuing a warning. I'm going to fix that so the warning appears. You can get the PPcheck page to work for your model if you make a slight tweak to your Stan code. The problem is that you have y declared as a real array with Nobs elements but y_rep is only declared as a scalar real. y_rep should have the same dimensions as y, so you can just change your generated quantities block to

generated quantities{
  real y_rep[Nobs];
  for (n in 1:Nobs)
    y_rep[n] <- gamma_rng(alpha,beta);
}

and then you'll be getting the right posterior predictive distribution and ShinyStan's PPcheck should work for you.

Jonah

On Friday, January 22, 2016 at 7:35:47 PM UTC-5, Jason Tilley wrote:
> I am also having this issue for some of my parameters in PyStan. Rhat = nan, but n_eff=iterations.

For a Cholesky factor, L, the L[i,j] elements for j > i are fixed at 0. Moreover, for a Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix, the top left element is fixed at 1. Therefore, no function of their "distributions" --- including Rhat --- is well-defined.

messages.subject: stan_lmer getting stuck
messages.subject_clean: stan_lmer getting stuck
messages.body_plain:
I have a fairly large data set (190k observations) with multiple parameters / interactions and 3 crossed, unbalanced groups, each with 100 to 1000 members.

I'm used to working with this data set (and those like it) in lme4, but I would prefer to predict over a distribution rather than just means / modes.  The outputs are actually a series of categories, but each has a defined value in the currency of interest, so I am using those values to model the output as continuous and the relationship of the predictors to it as Gaussian.

The model resolves swiftly in lme4: about 3 minutes.  This is no surprise: lme4 is fast.  The predictions from the lmer model make good sense: except that confidence intervals are tricky without bootstrapping.  If I am going to do lots of bootstrapping, I'd rather do MCMC and get better answers along with decent intervals.

The model also works in MCMCglmm.  It takes an hour and a half to take 13000 samples (3000 of which are burnin), but the package models it fairly well.  MCMCglmm does use a method of Gibbs sampling that may be well suited for this application.  (Its predict function is also a memory hog, but that's another issue).

Stan_lmer, on the other hand, seems befuddled when asked to model the same data, and set to "sampling." The code seems to compile correctly, and warmup begins, but the chains quickly freeze or hang at 25 instances, once in a while getting to 50 and sometimes never getting off 0. The sampling has to be killed manually, which in turn requires terminating the R session, and there are no apparent diagnostics left behind when I reboot the session.

I've tried switching among the built-in priors, without success. Past posts have emphasized that Stan can handle large numbers of parameters, provided the priors are good.  But rstan_arm discourages switching the default priors. Another option might be to use the findings of the lmer model to set up priors and starting values for stan_lmer, but it feels like the problem here may be more fundamental that that.  Meanfield VI does converge, although the predictions are, as I would expect, not very good.

The coefficients, intercepts, and outputs are all close to zero. Scaling the continuous coefficients (using R's built-in function anyway) has not helped.

I am attaching a script containing dummy data (with scaled continuous variables) that replicates the problem, along with scripts for lme4, MCMCglmm, and stan_lmer that show what I am talking about. I'd appreciate any insight.

All this said, rstan_arm is terrific and I thank you all for the package.

Jonathan

messages.body_plain:
On Friday, January 22, 2016 at 8:57:03 PM UTC-5, Jonathan Judge wrote:
> I've tried switching among the built-in priors, without success. Past posts have emphasized that Stan can handle large numbers of parameters, provided the priors are good.  But rstan_arm discourages switching the default priors. Another option might be to use the findings of the lmer model to set up priors and starting values for stan_lmer, but it feels like the problem here may be more fundamental that that.  Meanfield VI does converge, although the predictions are, as I would expect, not very good.

This is a misinterpretation that I think stems from the startup message

- Do not expect the default priors to remain the same in future rstanarm versions.
Thus, R scripts should specify priors explicitly, even if they are just the defaults.

That doesn't mean that you should use the default priors; it means if you are going to use the default priors you should specify them explicitly rather than omitting them from the stan_lmer() call. That way, your scripts should still work the way you expect them to in a future version of rstanarm which may change the default arguments for the priors. Or maybe it is because specifying the priors on the group-specific parameters is a bit difficult, although it is not too hard when your model only has group-specific intercepts. I would say that if you are not going to specify informative coefficients on the common coefficients, then you should call stan_lmer() with QR = TRUE, which should help you sample efficiently if you are doing MCMC and may be essential for the variational approximation to the posterior to be reasonable if you are doing meanfield.

Also, we don't recommend scaling predictors by the sample standard deviation because that makes it hard to get the posterior predictions right. Scaling by constants is okay, but shouldn't really be necessary if QR = TRUE is specified.

All that said, it is going to take a while for a model with 190,000 observations and thousands of parameters.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
They're not margins in the sense that they're deterministic.
I just figured it'd be easier to scan that way, but it's
definitely wasteful.

Right now, the problem in printing is that there are two
ways things can have the same value in every draw.  One is
to be a discrete generated quantity that never changes.  This
can happen in event probability calculations if the probability
is very close to 0 or 1 or the chains aren't run for many
iterations (you need many more iterations to estimate tail
probabilities well).

So I don't know if there's a good way to tell the ones that
are constant by design (diagonal of a correlation matrix) and
ones that are random quantities, but constant in a chain
because every draw has produced the same value.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I've seen things like this before that basically boil down to the fact that the rstan being loaded is not 2.9.0 even though it claims to be. One way that this can happen is if there is a .RData file sitting in the working directory, which gets autoloaded when R is started, that contains a stanfit object created by an old version of rstan. Another way is that the installation of 2.9.0 did not remove / overwrite the libs/ directory of a previous rstan installation for some reason. In that case, do a remove.packages("rstan"). If that doesn't get rid of everything, then in a shell just do a rm -rf rstan/ from whatever directory you install packages into. Then reinstall rstan.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] K-fold cross-validation/Future predictions for hierarchical models
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] K-fold cross-validation/Future predictions for hierarchical models
messages.body_plain:
This gets to a subtlety in predictive comparisons in hierarchical models.  There are
two interpretations of prediction — either you can sample new data conditioned on the
same groups, or you can sample new groups from the hierarchical population distribution
and then new data from those groups.  Ultimately this is related to whether the random
effects are considered part of the prior (in which case predictions use set the random
effects to their inferred values) or part of the likelihood as missing data (in which case
predictions sample new random effects and then data conditioned on those).

If your random effects are individual specific then you’ll have to sample new random
effects from the hierarchical population distribution and then new data from those
random effects.  This will give you a predictive distribution that you can compare to
any new data.

Right --- you have to define variables in the transformed
parameters block before using them.  The only two kinds of

Thanks very much. The reason I had it in the transformed block was so that I could see the parameter values of alpha in the table output. I will work on incorporating your suggestions. Knowing that alpha is close to one for my data, I tested the fit of the model anyway (with alpha hard-coded to 1), and I am quite surprised by the goodness the fit. One thing I notice in that the output NB_beta parameters don't seem to vary between the 2 prey types. So there is still something wrong with the model structure it seems. Still I am happy with my progress so far. Anyway, if any of you are Python users, this is the code I used to view the negative binomial fits to my fake data. Blue represents the actual data, red represents the predictions (plotted as a line for simplicity in viewing).

# it might help to give you Gelman's negative binomial function!

from scipy.special import binom

def Gelman_NB(theta, alpha, beta):
    term1 = binom((theta + alpha - 1),(alpha - 1))
    term2 = (beta / (beta + 1)) ** alpha
    term3 = (1 / (beta + 1)) ** theta
    x = term1 * term2 * term3
    return x

prey = [prey_1, prey_2]

You need to *define* values before using them in Stan.

  real x;             // declared, but not defined
  x ~ normal(0, 1);   //  BAD, crashes with NaN

  real x;
  x <- alpha + beta * 3;
  x ~ normal(0, 1);   // OK, assuming alpha and beta are defined

The only time you don't need to define a variable is if it's
declared in the data or parameters block.

- Bob

>>>>>                 qc1 * deltaT^2 / 2,       qc1 * deltaT
>>>>>                 ),
>>>>>               nrow = 2,
>>>>>               ncol = 2,
>>>>>               byrow = TRUE
>>>>>               )
>>>>>
>>>>> bigR = matrix(c(0.1),
>>>>>               nrow = 1,
>>>>>               ncol = 1,

messages.subject: Re: How would one declare a covariance matrix with different bounds on different entries of the matrix?
messages.subject_clean: How would one declare a covariance matrix with different bounds on different entries of the matrix?
messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, January 26, 2016 at 11:32:38 PM UTC-5, Qian Zhang wrote:
> J is an integer read in as data.
>
> I'd like to use a J x J covariance matrix Sigma in the model block that has diagonal entries bounded between [0,1], but off-diagonal entries bounded in terms of diagonal entries like so:
>
> 0 < Sigma[i,j] < sqrt(Sigma[i,i] * Sigma[j,j])
>
> How would I pull that off in STAN?

I would do it by declaring a Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix

cholesky_factor_corr[J] L_corr;

and a vector of standard deviations that are bounded

vector<lower=0,upper=1>[J] sigma;

as parameters, and then

diag_pre_multiply(sigma, L_corr);

is a Cholesky factor of a covariance matrix whose diagonal elements would be between 0 and 1.

Ben

set.seed(12345)

K<-dim(X)[2] #number of regression params
betas<-runif(K,-2,2)  # betas
# true betas :
# [1]  0.17718465  0.78518356 -0.75241019  0.02661803

phi <- 5
#simulate gamma data
mus <- exp(X%*%betas)
y < -rgamma(100,shape=mus**2/phi,rate=mus/phi)

# and define it in the formula syntax
df <- data.frame(y=y_g, X[,-c(1,4)])
# rstanarm model
mm <- stan_glm(y~x1+x2+x1*x2, data=df, family = Gamma(link="log"), iter=5000)

#results
> print(mm, digits=2)
stan_glm(formula = y ~ x1 + x2 + x1 * x2, family = Gamma(link = "log"),
    data = df, iter = 5000)

(Intercept) -0.17   0.60
x1           3.03   1.06
x2          -2.86   0.94
x1:x2        3.37   1.94

When I fit this model in pure stan:

data {
int N; //the number of observations

}
}
"

m2 <- stan(model_code = model_string, data = list(N=N,K=K,X=X,y=y_g),pars=c("betas","phi","y_rep"),

betas[3]    -0.68    0.00 0.10  -0.87  -0.74  -0.68  -0.61  -0.48  1165    1
betas[4]    -0.45    0.01 0.18  -0.80  -0.57  -0.45  -0.33  -0.11  1249    1

What am I doing wrong?

Christoph

messages.body_plain:
Hi Christoph,

If I'm not mistaken I think when you're generating your y variable you want

y <- rgamma(100, shape=phi, rate=phi/mus)

(See here <http://seananderson.ca/2014/04/08/gamma-glms.html> for an example of simulating data for a gamma glm)

Then if you run R's regular glm and then stan_glm, both with family = Gamma(link = "log"), you should get similar point estimates. With only 100 data points you're probably not going to recover the true parameters very precisely but you should at least get the right signs and somewhat close to the right magnitude. But either way, stan_glm shouldn't be too far off from regular glm for this particular example, so you can use regular glm as a sanity check.

Hope that helps,

Jonah

I need to save summary results for each of a large number of replications to summarize results for conditions of a simulation study.

Best,

messages.body_plain:
It's not so much Windows vs. Mac as most likely differences
in machine bit size (is one 32 bit and the other 64 bit),
CPU (same CPUs?), and compiler (even the same compiler on different
optimization levels can give you different results).

There's a chapter on replication in the manual that's basically
a list of everything that can go wrong.  The only way to get
reliable replication is to lock down everything (hardware, OS
version, compiler version, compiler flags).

- Bob

Yes, that's the right way to do non-centering for alpha_2.

You could do the same for alpha_1 and beta (multiply a unit normal
by 100).  Generally, we recommend tighter priors.  So unless you
think 200 or -200 is a resaonable value for elements of alpha_1
or beta, that prior's too fat.

- Bob

> Bob - Thanks for the suggestions, I think the implementation below is about twice as fast, but I'm not sure I caught your drift with non-centering. Would you mind checking at the lines marked with ** below?
>
> New Stan model definition (new data also attached):
>
> data {
>     int N;  // number of samples
>
>     int K;  // number of intercepts
>     int L;  // number of categorical predictors
>     int C[L];  // position of last coefficient in each category
>     int M;  // number of non-zero values in sparse design matrix for intercepts
>     vector[M] c_w;   // design matrix in compressed row storage where c_w[i]
>     int c_v[M];      // is a value from column c_v[i], row j values begin
>     int c_u[N + 1];  // at position c_u[j] in c_w, and c_u[N + 1] = M.
>
>     int P;  // number of covariates
>     matrix[N, P] x;  // covariates
>
>     int R_1;
>     int R_2;
>     int b_1[R_1];
>     int b_1_idx[R_1];
>     int b_2[R_2 + 1];
>     int b_2_idx[R_2];
>
>     int Q;  // number of non-zero values in sparse sample matrix
>     vector[Q] y;    // response value, from sparse matrix,
>     int y_i[Q];     // such that y[k] reports have more than
>     vector[Q] y_j;  // y_j[k] animals from market:county y_i[k]
> }
> parameters {
>     vector[C[1]] alpha_1;
>     vector[C[2] - C[1]] alpha_2_raw;
>     vector[C[3] - C[2]] alpha_3;
>     vector[P] beta;
>     real<lower=0> sigma;  // SD for market-level random effect
> }
> model {
>
>     // Prior
>     append_row(alpha_1, alpha_3) ~ normal(0, 100);
>     alpha_2_raw ~ normal(0, 1); // **
>     sigma ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
>     beta ~ normal(0, 100);
>
>     // Likelihood
>     {
> vector[K] alpha;
> vector[N] a;
> vector[R_1 + R_2] b;
>
> alpha <- append_row(append_row(alpha_1, alpha_2_raw * sigma), alpha_3);     // **
> a <- csr_matrix_times_vector(N, K, c_w, c_v, c_u, alpha) + x * beta;
> a <- exp(a);
> b[b_1_idx] <- a[b_1];
> for (i in 1:R_2) {
>    b[b_2_idx[i]] <- sum(a[b_2[i]:(b_2[i+1] - 1)]);
> }
> increment_log_prob(dot_product(log(b[y_i] + y_j), y));
>     }
> }

messages.subject: Avoiding Segmentation Faults in rstan 2.0.9 / R 3.2.2 / Ubuntu 15.10
messages.subject_clean: Avoiding Segmentation Faults in rstan 2.0.9 / R 3.2.2 / Ubuntu 15.10
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I just installed rstan on a fresh Ubuntu 15.10 box and encountered
segmentation faults when running any models.

When you encounter the same problem (as you would, I think, setting up
system with the current versions mentioned in the subject line, and
following the usual instructions):

* Use remove.packages('rstan') to remove any already installed package
* remove.packages('Rcpp')
* Then, install.packages("Rcpp", type = "source")
* And install.packages("rstan", type = "source")

(I saw this solution somewhere before for some older versions, probably
on this list).

Best regards,
Jan

messages.body_plain: I agree with Andrew about not using the constrained uniform, but even if it were a good prior to use you would need to tweak your Stan code a bit to use it correctly. Right now you have the parameters declared with <lower=0>, but uniform(0.01, 100) means that the constraints need to be <lower=0.01,upper=100>. That said, it'd be better to leave the <lower=0> and use a prior that imposes a "soft" constraint by decaying quickly enough to put very little probability mass at extreme values. So maybe a half-normal or half-cauchy with a moderate scale parameter, or something like that. The nice thing is that you don't need to use a special half-normal or half-cauchy function: if you use normal or cauchy (or whatever) for a parameter declared with <lower=0> then Stan knows it needs to be the half-normal, etc.

messages.body_plain:
I am getting this warning at every step.

On Wednesday, January 27, 2016 at 6:29:08 PM UTC-7, Jonah Gabry wrote:
> Also, are those warning messages you're getting occurring during warmup or sampling? Like the message says, if the warning only happens occasionally (especially during warmup) then you're fine. If you're getting a lot of those during sampling then that's a problem.
>
> On Wednesday, January 27, 2016 at 8:06:52 PM UTC-5, Jonah Gabry wrote:
> > I agree with Andrew about not using the constrained uniform, but even if it were a good prior to use you would need to tweak your Stan code a bit to use it correctly. Right now you have the parameters declared with <lower=0>, but uniform(0.01, 100) means that the constraints need to be <lower=0.01,upper=100>. That said, it'd be better to leave the <lower=0> and use a prior that imposes a "soft" constraint by decaying quickly enough to put very little probability mass at extreme values. So maybe a half-normal or half-cauchy with a moderate scale parameter, or something like that. The nice thing is that you don't need to use a special half-normal or half-cauchy function: if you use normal or cauchy (or whatever) for a parameter declared with <lower=0> then Stan knows it needs to be the half-normal, etc.

messages.body_plain:

Am Mittwoch, 27. Januar 2016 19:47:01 UTC+1 schrieb Jonah Gabry:
> Hi Christoph,
>
> If I'm not mistaken I think when you're generating your y variable you want
>
> y <- rgamma(100, shape=phi, rate=phi/mus)
>
> (See here <http://seananderson.ca/2014/04/08/gamma-glms.html> for an example of simulating data for a gamma glm)
>
> Then if you run R's regular glm and then stan_glm, both with family = Gamma(link = "log"), you should get similar point estimates. With only 100 data points you're probably not going to recover the true parameters very precisely but you should at least get the right signs and somewhat close to the right magnitude. But either way, stan_glm shouldn't be too far off from regular glm for this particular example, so you can use regular glm as a sanity check.
>
> Hope that helps,
>
> Jonah
>
>
> On Wednesday, January 27, 2016 at 3:45:37 AM UTC-5, Christoph wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > I'm comparing a Gamma regression model (log link) using pure rstan and rstanarm and I'm unsure if it's the same.
> >
> > Generate data:
> >
> > set.seed(12345)
> > N<-100 #sample size
> > dat <- data.frame(x1=runif(N,-1,1),x2=runif(N,-1,1))
> > # model matrix
> > X<-model.matrix(~x1*x2,dat)
> > K<-dim(X)[2] #number of regression params
> > betas<-runif(K,-2,2)  # betas
> > # true betas :
> > # [1]  0.17718465  0.78518356 -0.75241019  0.02661803
> >
> > phi <- 5
> > #simulate gamma data
> > mus <- exp(X%*%betas)
> > y < -rgamma(100,shape=mus**2/phi,rate=mus/phi)
> >
> > # the model matrix contains the intercept and the x1*x2 interaction, we remove these for rstanarm
> > # and define it in the formula syntax
> > df <- data.frame(y=y_g, X[,-c(1,4)])
> > # rstanarm model
> > mm <- stan_glm(y~x1+x2+x1*x2, data=df, family = Gamma(link="log"), iter=5000)
> >
> > #results
> > > print(mm, digits=2)
> > stan_glm(formula = y ~ x1 + x2 + x1 * x2, family = Gamma(link = "log"),
> >     data = df, iter = 5000)
> >
> > Estimates:
> >             Median MAD_SD
> > (Intercept) -0.17   0.60
> > x1           3.03   1.06
> > x2          -2.86   0.94
> > x1:x2        3.37   1.94
> > shape        0.05   0.00
> >
> > these estimates are quite far away from the truth.
> >
> > When I fit this model in pure stan:
> >
> > model_string <- "
> > data {
> > int N; //the number of observations
> > int K; //the number of columns in the model matrix
> > real y[N]; //the response
> > matrix[N,K] X; //the model matrix
> > }
> > parameters {
> > vector[K] betas; //the regression parameters
> > real<lower=0> phi; //the variance parameter
> > }
> > transformed parameters {
> > vector[N] mu; //the expected values (linear predictor)
> > vector[N] alpha; //shape parameter for the gamma distribution
> > vector[N] beta; //rate parameter for the gamma distribution
> >
> > mu <- exp(X*betas); //using the log link
> > alpha <- mu .* mu / phi;
> > beta <- mu / phi;
> > }
> > model {
> > betas[1] ~ cauchy(0,10); //prior for the intercept following Gelman 2008
> >
> > for(i in 2:K)
> > betas[i] ~ cauchy(0,2.5);//prior for the slopes following Gelman 2008
> >
> > y ~ gamma(alpha,beta);
> > }
> > generated quantities {
> > vector[N] y_rep;
> > for(n in 1:N){
> > y_rep[n] <- gamma_rng(alpha[n],beta[n]); //posterior draws to get posterior predictive checks
> > }
> > }
> > "
> >
> > m2 <- stan(model_code = model_string, data = list(N=N,K=K,X=X,y=y_g),pars=c("betas","phi","y_rep"),
> >           chains = 3, cores=3)
> >
> > here the estimates are better (except for the interaction term):
> >
> >              mean se_mean   sd   2.5%    25%    50%    75%  97.5% n_eff Rhat
> > betas[1]     0.06    0.01 0.16  -0.22  -0.05   0.06   0.17   0.39   931    1
> > betas[2]     0.82    0.00 0.10   0.63   0.75   0.82   0.89   1.03  1390    1
> > betas[3]    -0.68    0.00 0.10  -0.87  -0.74  -0.68  -0.61  -0.48  1165    1
> > betas[4]    -0.45    0.01 0.18  -0.80  -0.57  -0.45  -0.33  -0.11  1249    1
> >
> >
> > What am I doing wrong?
> >
> > Best,
> > Christoph
> >

Hi Shravan,

That seems reasonable and the more I think about it the more I'm open to the idea of including functionality like this that is intended solely for pedagogical use if it's accompanied by warnings. So far we've been thinking of rstanarm as a way to promote best practices, providing as few ways as possible to go astray, so to speak, but I do see the educational value of allowing some things to be done the "wrong way".

I'm curious what the other developers think about this, and feedback on this issue from you and other current and potential rstanarm users is very much appreciated.

Jonah

On Thursday, January 28, 2016 at 10:52:46 AM UTC-5, Jonah Gabry wrote:
> I'm curious what the other developers think about this, and feedback on this issue from you and other current and potential rstanarm users is very much appreciated.

I'm reluctant to put knowingly wrong things into rstanarm because most users will not have an instructional environment where they can learn why it is wrong. The perils of bounded uniform priors can sort of be demonstrated by doing prior = NULL, as.matrix(), and then deleting draws where the coefficients on the common parameters fall outside given bounds. But it can also be demonstrated in a simple Stan program that estimates a linear model that just has one predictor and no group-specific parameters. Finally, you can get the rethinking package to generate a Stan program that has uniform priors. I'm not sure about brms.

Ben

I agree — there’s no point in teaching bad priors in rstanarm if rstanarm doesn’t
allow them!  The utility of teaching about these pathologies arises when users
are building their own models, which means not using rstanarm but rather Rstan
proper.  If it’s this hard to do, you probably shouldn’t be doing it — I’m sure there’s
some corollary to the Folk Theorem that covers it.

models that you use (cleaned up to be more presentable and less optimized
for generality) and then discuss what happens when you try to tweak the
model away from our recommendations?  Having “bad” models in rstanarm
wouldn't be helpful, as you’d just be teaching what settings not to use.
