messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: How would one declare a covariance matrix with different bounds on different entries of the matrix?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: How would one declare a covariance matrix with different bounds on different entries of the matrix?
messages.body_plain:
> On Jan 28, 2016, at 1:12 PM, Qian Zhang <qian.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks Ben!
>
> So it turns out I have informative priors on entries of the Sigma matrix. The problem with using these sigma and Cholesky matrices you mention is I don't know how to derive priors on the sigma and Cholesky matrices from the priors on entries of Sigma, and it seems not-worth-it to go down that route.

It'll be worth it computationally, but the Jacobians
are painful.  They're spelled out in the manual.

> I tried 2 approaches:
>
> (1) Declare Sigma as a cov_matrix in the parameters block, put priors on its entries in the model block, and rely on rejection of proposed Sigma values that are out of bounds (Code Excerpt 1 below)

This is bad for Stan.  It causes its nice Hamiltonian flow to
devolved to a random walk.  And if rejection's bad, it'll just lock.

> (2) Define Sigma as a cov_matrix in the transformed parameters block, define it in terms of sigma and Cholesky matrices, put priors on Sigma entries but not on sigma or Cholesky matrices (Code Excerpt 2 below)

You need to define it as a cov_matrix in the parameters block and put
priors on it.  Otherwise, you'll have to deal with the Jacobian in
the prior on Sigma entries.

> Both approaches gave me draws. Approach 1 was a lot faster (~ a few minutes) than Approach 2 (~ 30 min), so I'm going with Approach 1.

You need to (a) measure convergence and time per effective sample size,
and you need to (b) make sure with simulated data you recover the right
results.  Fast is meaningless if it's wrong!

> (I guess you put bounds in Approach 2 to encourage movement to a new position in the parameter space at the next draw, while in Approach 1 you tend to stay put at the last parameter draw because you propose something out of bounds and then reject it, so the only difference is mixing time, both real human time and time in terms of number of draws.)
>
> Question 0: Both approaches work, i.e. I'm not coding up something totally non-sensical either way? They should both implement MCMC procedures to draw from the same posterior.

See above.

> Question 1: Since Sigma is a cov_matrix, in the model block I only need to put priors on the upper diagonal entries of Sigma, and the lower diagonal entries will automatically be filled in with the upper diagonal draws?

It depends what you want the priors to do!
You are putting priors on the covariance matrix at this point.
We've already done the Jacobian for you.

What's really going on is that the unconstrained parameters
are the Cholesky factor L_Sigma and then it gets multipled
to give you Sigma = L_Sigma * L_Sigma'.  So you need the
Jacobian if you're going to be putting priors on Sigma and
the declared parameter is L_Sigma.

>
> I got many warnings in Code Excerpt 1 of the following 3 types.
>
> Type 1:
>
>                                                                                                                                                                 count
> validate transformed params: thetaB is -0.00107406, but must be greater than or equal to 0                 4
>
>
> Type 2:
>
>
>
> Exception thrown at line 97: beta_log: Random variable is 1.00308, but must be less than or equal to  2

I find these truncated messages hard to read --- the constraint is that it must
be less than or equal to 1, and I believe the 2 means it showed up twice.

>
> Type 3:
>
> Warning messages:
> 1: There were 132367 divergent transitions after warmup. Increasing adapt_delta above 0.8 may help.
> 2: Examine the pairs() plot to diagnose sampling problems

This means it's not working!  You get numerical issues.

> Question 3: Is the following understanding correct? My understanding is Types 1 and 2 come from drawing Sigma entries that are out of bounds, or result in out-of-bounds thetaB, in which case such draws are rejected.

And 3.  Whenever you get a numerical exception.

> Also, I never need to worry about this divergent transitions warning message, as you say here: “There are almost always some divergent transitions during the warmup phase but we don't really worry about them.

You should still worry about them.  It means you'll bias
warmup.  Starting with lower stepsize can mitigate in
some cases, but won't here because the models are broken.

> It is trying to find a stepsize during the warmup phase that achieves the target acceptance probability without diverging and without hitting the max_treedepth.” (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/hjYWqJZfSgw) But then why do you have this warning message at all?

The message indicates that you're going to get biases in your
estimates.  We don't want to set our default parameters too far out
or it'll give the impression of hanging.  We'd rather hit max
depth and then diagnose.

- Bob

>
>
> Code Excerpt 1:
>
> parameters {
>
>   //  Covariance matrix. I don't define constraints on it and rely on rejection in the model block.
>   cov_matrix[J] Sigma;
>
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
>
>   real<lower=0,upper=1> thetaB;
>
>   thetaB <- 0;
>
>   for(j in 1:J){
>         for(jprime in 1:J){
>             if(j != jprime){
>                  thetaB <- thetaB + Sigma[j,jprime];
>             }
>         }
>   }
>
>   thetaB <- thetaB / (J^2 - J);
>
> }
>
> model{
>
>   // Try putting priors on the entries of Sigma
>
>   for(j in 1:J){
>       Sigma[j,j] ~ beta(1,3);
>   }
>
>   for(j in 1:J){
>       for(jprime in (j+1):J){
>
>             // CONTINUE HERE: Hope that I only need to specify one off-diagonal
>             // and that the other will get filled in by the fact that Sigma is a covariance matrix
>
>             Sigma[j, jprime] ~ uniform(0.0, sqrt(Sigma[j,j] * Sigma[jprime,jprime]));
>
>       }
>   }
> }
>
> Code Excerpt 2:
>
> parameters {
>
>   // Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix
>   cholesky_factor_corr[J] L_corr;
>
>   // Vector of standard deviations that are bounded
>   vector<lower=0,upper=1>[J] sigma;
>
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
>
>     cov_matrix[J] Sigma;
>
>    # p.74 STAN manual shows how to multiply matrices
>    Sigma <- diag_pre_multiply(sigma, L_corr) *  diag_pre_multiply(sigma, L_corr)';
>
> }
>
> model{
>
>   // Try putting priors on the entries of Sigma
>
>   for(j in 1:J){
>       Sigma[j,j] ~ beta(1,3);
>   }
>
>   for(j in 1:J){
>       for(jprime in (j+1):J){
>
>             // CONTINUE HERE: Hope that I only need to specify one off-diagonal
>             // and that the other will get filled in by the fact that Sigma is a covariance matrix
>
>             Sigma[j, jprime] ~ uniform(0.0, sqrt(Sigma[j,j] * Sigma[jprime,jprime]));
>
>       }
>   }
> }
>
>
>

> On Tuesday, January 26, 2016 at 9:23:52 PM UTC-8, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Tuesday, January 26, 2016 at 11:32:38 PM UTC-5, Qian Zhang wrote:
> J is an integer read in as data.
>
> I'd like to use a J x J covariance matrix Sigma in the model block that has diagonal entries bounded between [0,1], but off-diagonal entries bounded in terms of diagonal entries like so:
>
> 0 < Sigma[i,j] < sqrt(Sigma[i,i] * Sigma[j,j])
>
> How would I pull that off in STAN?
>

> I would do it by declaring a Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix
>
> cholesky_factor_corr[J] L_corr;
>
> and a vector of standard deviations that are bounded
>
> vector<lower=0,upper=1>[J] sigma;
>

> as parameters, and then
>
> diag_pre_multiply(sigma, L_corr);
>
> is a Cholesky factor of a covariance matrix whose diagonal elements would be between 0 and 1.
>
> Ben

messages.subject: Re: no uniform priors
messages.subject_clean: no uniform priors
messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, January 28, 2016 at 5:33:35 PM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Uniform is a default.  If you have a bounded parameter and you don’t specify a prior, uniform is what is being done. There is never a reason to use a uniform on a space different from the bounds of the parameter.

To clarify --- because Shravan was originally asking about rstanarm --- there is no option in rstanarm to put additional bounds on the parameters in its pre-compiled Stan programs. Either the parameters are unbounded on both sides in the case of coefficients, bounded only from below at zero in the case of standard deviations, etc. Consequently, we have not implemented and do not plan to implement proper uniform priors, although in most cases it is possible to utilize an improper uniform prior by specifying prior = NULL in the R function that calls it.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
I think it's more a matter of what tools are in your
toolbox.  But there's been a lot of geometric analysis of
stats, not just for MCMC.

There's a nice survey of (Euclidean) HMC by Radford Neal in the
Handbook of MCMC (it's a free sample chapter).

The original Riemannian HMC paper is Girolami and Calderhead (Royal
Stats Society B), but I prefer the way Michael presents
it here:

  http://arxiv.org/abs/1212.4693

and in a more general way, without the concrete smoothing proposal
for RHMC, here:

  http://arxiv.org/pdf/1410.5110.pdf

There's a citation to the original paper RHMC paper in these if
want to track it down.  Then there's the NUTS paper
for (Euclidean) HMC by Hoffman and Gelman (JMLR) and
Michael's generalization to RHMC (arXiv).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Stan doesn't support integer parameters.  And it looks
like clin[n] doesn't have an upper bound, so you won't be
able to marginalize it out by brute force.

And you have an undefined variable propClimZone.

But I don't see what this has to do with the structure of

If you can write out your models data and parameter variable
shapes and sizes and write down the density, we can help you code
in Stan.  It's hard to guess what you're trying to do from code
that doesn't work.

For instance, here's what I'd want for a simple regression:

   data:  y  an N-vector of scalar observations
          x  an N-vector of predictors

   parameters: alpha  scalar slope
               beta   scalar intercept
               sigma  noise scale (must be positive)

   density:  p(y, alpha, beta, sigma | x) =
                 normal(y | x * alpha + beta, sigma)
                 * normal(alpha | 0, 1)
                 * normal(beta | 0, 1)
                 * cauchy(sigma | 0, 2)

messages.body_plain:
Here's what a logistic regression model with two latent variables (uncertainty in the covariates) may look like. For each data point yn in N there are two latent variables z1n in {1,…C} and z2n in {1…R} with categorical distributions parameterized by the two matrices Q1 and Q2.  Q1 and Q2 are matrices, as the mixing proportions may vary for each data point. I included two latent covariates, as start towards a multiple regression problem.

 data:  y  an N-vector of binary observations
        Theta1  an N×C matrix of mixing proportions  (where theta1(n,c) ≥0 and rowsums = 1)

        Theta2  an N×R matrix of mixing proportions (where theta2(n,c) ≥0 and rowsums = 1)

 parameters: mu   scalar intercept
                     alpha1  vector of coefficients for each level in C

                     alpha2  vector of coefficients for each level in R

transformed parameters:

                        z1 latent variable in {1,…C}

                        z2 latent variable in {1,…R}

 density:  p(y | Theta1, Theta2, mu, alpha1, alpha2) =
                 Bernoulli(y | mu + alpha1[z1[n]] + alpha2[z2[n]] )
                 * categorical(z1 | Theta1)

                 * categorical(z2 | Theta2)
                 * normal(alpha1 | 0,  1)

                 * normal(alpha2 | 0,  1)
                 * normal(mu | 0,  1)

Mixture models seem to be the way to go but so far I have problems, some linked to use matrices of mixing proportions

Thanks for all help. Learning Stan is fun!

messages.body_plain:
The density you're defining is the joint over the latent
parameters

  p(y, Theta, mu, alpha, z)

not the data sampling distribution,

 p(y | Theta, mu, alpha)

And you need a product over the n in the Bernoulli, but now
I see what you're doing.

The big issue is that Stan doesn't support discrete parameters!
So you can define the model this way, but you can't code it this
way in Stan.  You have to treat it as a mixture model, as Andrew
saw right away.  This will work and actually be much more efficient
than sampling the unknown levels if there aren't too many level
combinations.

You need marginalize the z out as follows:

  p(y, Theta, mu, alpha)

  = p(Theta, mu, alpha)    // priors

    * PROD_{n in 1:N} p(y[n] | Theta, mu, alpha)

The key is this step:

  p(y[n] | Theta, mu, alpha)

  = SUM_z[n] p(z[n]) p(y[n] | z[n], mu, alpha)

And it's a double sum, because z is 2D;  and you need to use
log_sum_exp as explained in the chapter on mixtures and on
marginalizing out discrete parameters.

There'll still be a label switching non-identifiability (as
explained in the problematic posteriors chapter of the manual),
but that's to be expected with a 2D latent structure.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: Estimating errors in predictive accuracy using K-fold cross validation
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I've built a stan model used k-fold cross validation as done in Aki's paper. The only difference from the paper is that I've monitored the sum of the log likelihoods as opposed to the individual log likelihoods. I did this because of memory issues as I'm dealing with a large dataset.

In my case, the point of doing cross validation was to compare predictive accuracy between a suite of models and ultimately choose a single 'best' model. I was hoping to do this using the mean and credible intervals of the monitored log likelihoods pooled across kfolds.

Specifically I'd:
Pool the samples of the sum log likelihood across all K-fold fits and then estimate the mean and the lower and upper 95% quantiles. My thinking was that this would capture the full uncertainty associated with estimating the log likelihood of the heldout data and allow people to determine whether there was a significant difference between model predictive accuracy.

However, I'm beginning to think my approach isn't technically correct. Reading Aki's paper again I see that the standard error is estimated as: SQRT(N) x SD(log likelihoods).

Another approach I've seen people use is a point estimate approach whereby they extract the mean log likelihood for each kfold and then use these values to estimate the average log likelihood and confidence interval (i.e. across kfolds).

Does anyone have any guidance on how I should best approach this?

messages.body_plain:
I have made some progress on my multivariate multilevel negative binomial model. I thought I'd share what I have and see if there are any suggestions. I have attached an html of the iPython notebook if you'd rather look at that.
Multivariate Multilevel Negative Binomial Model

Here is what I have for my model so far. First make any imports and create a Python function for STAN's negative binomial formulation:
%matplotlib inline
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pystan
from scipy.special import binom

def stan_negbin(theta, alpha, beta):
    term1 = binom((theta + alpha - 1),(alpha - 1))
    term2 = (beta / (beta + 1)) ** alpha
    term3 = (1 / (beta + 1)) ** theta
    x = term1 * term2 * term3
    return x

Now let's create some fake data. EDIT: I have fixed a few mistakes and lowered the sample size compared to my earlier code.
# fake data
N = 60 # number per groups (must be factor of ten)
G = 3 # number of groups
# array of temperatures
base_temp = 25
# temperature for group 1
temp_1 = np.random.normal(base_temp - 4, 0.1, N)
# temperature for group 2
temp_2 = np.random.normal(base_temp, 0.1, N)
temp_3 = np.random.normal(base_temp + 4, 0.1, N)
temp = np.append(temp_1, temp_2)
temp = np.append(temp, temp_3)

# array of hours past sunrise (10 per day)
hours = np.tile(np.arange(0, 10), N * G / 10)

prob_param = temp * 0.1 + hours * 0.5

prey_1 = np.empty(N * G)
prey_2 = np.empty(N * G)

for i in range(0, N * G):
    # number of prey 1
    prey_1[i] = np.random.choice(100, 1, p=stan_negbin(np.arange(100),
                                                       prob_param[i],
                                                       2.2))
    # number of prey 2
    prey_2[i] = np.random.choice(100, 1, p=stan_negbin(np.arange(100),
                                                       prob_param[i] - 0.1,
                                                       2.2))

group = np.append(np.ones(N), np.ones(N) + 1).astype(int)
group = np.append(group, np.ones(N) + 2).astype(int)

y = np.matrix([list(prey_1), list(prey_2)]).T
x = np.matrix([list(temp), list(hours)]).T

Now let's look at the distibution of prey item 1 for each temperature group.
ax1 = plt.subplot(311)
ax1.hist(prey_1[group==1], np.arange(0,11,1))
ax1.annotate('temp=21', xy=(6,16))
ax1.set_ylim(0,25)

ax2 = plt.subplot(312)
ax2.hist(prey_1[group==2], np.arange(0,11,1))
ax2.annotate('temp=25', xy=(6,16))
ax2.set_ylim(0,25)

ax3 = plt.subplot(313)
ax3.hist(prey_1[group==3], np.arange(0,11,1))
ax3.annotate('temp=29', xy=(6,16))
ax3.set_ylim(0,25)

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-WJ2DZj-u7bg/Vq_KFwX6rlI/AAAAAAAAAHU/opwkX0qhE_M/s1600/Unknown.png>

Good. Feeding success is showing a slightly increasing trend with temperature. Now let's look at the distibution of prey item 1 (sums) over time.
num_prey = np.empty(len(np.unique(hours)))
for i in range(0,len(num_prey)):
    num_prey[i] = prey_1[hours==i].sum()

plt.bar(np.arange(10), num_prey)

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-au3h9hDGOag/Vq_KW6A3SjI/AAAAAAAAAHc/1pMz2AG_ETM/s1600/Unknown-1.png>

Once again, the data is behaving as intended. As the day progresses, prey items are accumulating in the predator's stomach. Now let's prepare the PyStan model for the data. This is done by creating a dictionary of variables to pass into the data block of the STAN code:
model_dat = ({'N':len(y),
             'X': np.shape(x)[1],
             'Y': np.shape(y)[1],
             'L': len(np.unique(group)),
             'y': y.astype(int),
             'x': x,
             'random': group,
             })

Now you can setup the STAN model code. This is beyond the scope of this thread. For more information see: https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/releases/download/v2.9.0/stan-reference-2.9.0.pdf.
model_code = """
    data {
      int<lower=0> N; //rows of data
      int<lower=1> X; // number of covariates
      int<lower=1> Y; // number of responses
      int<lower=1> L; // number of groups
      // vector[X] x[N] is an array with N elements, each of which is a vector of X elements,
      vector[X] x[N]; // design matrix (predictors)
      int<lower=0> y[N,Y]; // response (outcomes)
      int<lower=1, upper=L> random[N];
    }
    transformed data {
      vector[Y] zeros;
      vector[L] zeros_u;

      zeros <- rep_vector(0, Y);
      zeros_u <- rep_vector(0, L);
    }
    parameters {
      vector[Y] intercept; // Population intercept
      matrix[Y,X] beta; // Population slope parameters
      cholesky_factor_corr[Y] omega;
      cholesky_factor_corr[L] omega_u;
      vector<lower=0>[Y] sigma; // population standard deviation
      matrix[L,Y] u; // random effects
      vector<lower=0>[L] sigma_u; // random effects SD
    }
    transformed parameters {
      // mu has N rows and Y columns
      matrix[Y,N] mu;

      // should be random effects for each y at each station
      matrix[L,Y] beta_0j; // random intercepts

      // negative binomial beta parameter for each group and response
      matrix<lower=0>[L,Y] NB_beta;
      // negative binomial alpha parameter for each group and response
      matrix<lower=0>[L,Y] alpha;

      //Varying intercepts definition
      for (i in 1:Y) {
          for (l in 1:L) {
            beta_0j[l,i] <- intercept[i] + u[l,i];
          }
      }

      // each response may have different slopes and intercepts
      for (i in 1:Y) { // for each response
        for (n in 1:N) { // for each individual
          mu[,n] <- beta * x[n] + beta_0j[random[n],i];
        }
      }

      // group-response - I have to do this manually at the moment
      NB_beta[1,1]<-exp(mean(mu[1,1:60])); // log link
      alpha[1,1] <- NB_beta[1,1] * mean(mu[1,1:60]);
      NB_beta[2,1]<-exp(mean(mu[1,61:120])); // log link
      alpha[2,1] <- NB_beta[2,1] * mean(mu[1,61:120]);
      NB_beta[3,1]<-exp(mean(mu[1,121:180])); // log link
      alpha[3,1] <- NB_beta[3,1] * mean(mu[1,121:180]);
      NB_beta[1,2]<-exp(mean(mu[2,1:60])); // log link
      alpha[1,2] <- NB_beta[1,2] * mean(mu[2,1:60]);
      NB_beta[2,2]<-exp(mean(mu[2,61:120])); // log link
      alpha[2,2] <- NB_beta[2,2] * mean(mu[2,61:120]);
      NB_beta[3,2]<-exp(mean(mu[2,121:180])); // log link
      alpha[3,2] <- NB_beta[3,2] * mean(mu[2,121:180]);
    }
    model {
      matrix[Y,Y] Sigma;
      matrix[L,L] Sigma_u;

      to_vector(beta) ~ normal(0, 2);

      Sigma <- diag_pre_multiply(sigma, omega);
      Sigma_u <- diag_pre_multiply(sigma_u, omega_u);

      // Priors
      for (i in 1:Y)
          u[,i] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(zeros_u, Sigma_u);

      intercept ~ multi_normal_cholesky(zeros, Sigma);
      omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(4);
      omega_u ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(4);
      sigma ~ normal(0,2);
      sigma_u ~ normal(0,2);
      for (i in 1:Y) { // for each response
        for (l in 1:L) { // for each group
          alpha[l,i] ~ gamma(1,1);
          NB_beta[l,i] ~ gamma(1,1);
        }
      }

      // Data Model
      for (i in 1:Y) // for each covariate
          y[,i] ~ neg_binomial(alpha[random,i], NB_beta[random,i]);
    }
    """

Now finally we can run the model.
fit = pystan.stan(model_code=model_code, data=model_dat,
                  iter=1000, chains=2,
                  model_name='diet_model',
                  sample_file='/Users/<username>/Desktop/sample')

Now lets look at the fit... I've omitted the mu values.

messages.subject: Value-added model coding question (based on Mariano, McCaffrey, and Lockwood 2010)
messages.subject_clean: Value-added model coding question (based on Mariano, McCaffrey, and Lockwood 2010)
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

My question is about the efficiency of my code. I am not sure if I am leveraging Stan properly to take advantage of all its speed to estimate a value-added model, especially in the presence of missing data in the dependent variable vector.

Here is a brief explanation of what I am doing:

I have a few research projects that are using Stan to perform value-added estimation using the generalized persistence model that was developed by Louis Mariano, Dan McCaffrey, and J.R. Lockwood. The model was originally coded in WinBUGS, but I have translated it into Stan code. As I understand, very few people have attempted to estimate their model because it was prohibitively slow using WinBUGS. I started out using WinBUGS, but I could not estimate the model with a large data set. I have since transitioned to Stan and have had success.

The model leverages the longitudinal nature of student test scores; however, in many cases, student test scores are missing. The model is layered so that one can account for the full history of teachers that a student has. Here is an example:

y_1stgrade = mu_1 + theta_11[grade1teacher] + error_1
y_2ndgrade = mu_2 + theta_12[grade1teacher] + theta_22[grade2teacher] + error_2
y_3rdgrade = mu_3 + theta_13[grade1teacher] + theta_23[grade2teacher] + theta33[grade3teacher] + error_3

In this model, y is the test score vector for a given student, mu is a vector of year fixed effects, and the theta variables are random effects or the effects that teachers had on student test scores. What is unique about this model is that we can obtain the effect of the teacher in the year he or she teachers as well as the effect that he or she has when the students is in a future grade.

Overall, the model above and my explanation is a gross simplification of everything the model can do; I just wanted to give a brief summary. The original paper can be found using the following doi: 10.3102/1076998609346967

Back to my question...

I would appreciate any general feedback about my code, but I think I found a reason why my model tends to run slowly; specially, I am not sure if I am handling missing test score data values efficiently. Specifically, I have been filling in missing test score data values with parameter values as necessary. Please see lines 153 to 167 for specific details. I borrowed some code from Ben Goodrich to do this, but I am not sure if there is a better way of handling missing values given that Stan has been updated regularly over the past year. I will also say that I am trying to estimate this model using a large, district data set.

Any feedback would be greatly appreciated.

Thanks,

Chris

P.S. I am also happy to share any other details that may be needed. FYI, I am using CmdStan given the complexity of the data.

messages.body_plain:
The missing data handling is OK.

The covariance matrices are very slow. Models are much faster (and more
robust arithmetically) using Cholesky factors.  We don't have the (inverse) Wishart
implemented for Cholesky factors because we use the LKJ prior on correlation
matrices and scale it.  I think you'll find that more flexible in terms of prior
(choose degree of concentration for correlation matrix around the unit vector and
flexible scale modeling).  It'll also be a whole lot faster.

You also want to vectorize the multi_normal calls.

  for(i in 2:Ntch[5]) {
        theta5[i] ~ multi_normal(rep_vector(0,ih_l[5]), Gamma5);
  }

is more efficient as

  theta5[2:Ntch[5]] ~ multi_normal(rep_vector(0,ih_l[5]), Gamma5);

because you only need to solve (invert and determinant) Gamma5 once.

I find using Gamma5 and Gamma05 as variables very confusing!

There are a lot of these --- it'll make a huge difference in speed.

Also vectorize this:

 for(i in 1:N) {
   ...
   y ~ multi_normal(u[i], Sigma);

Also things like rep_vector(0,ih_l[5]) can be declared as transformed
data --- it's a bit more efficient than creating and destroying it each
time it's used (but with just data, it's not too bad).

The loops like these can be made more efficient

 for (i in 1:N) {
   u[i,1] <- mu[1] + theta1[tchid[i,1],1];

as

  u[, 1] <- mu[1] + theta1[tchid[, 1], 1];

but that's not going to work until I fix the includes for our next release.
But you can do this:

  u[1:N, 1] <- mu[1] + theta1[tchid[1:N, 1], 1];

Or, you can transpose the represntation of u and tchid and just do

  u[1] <- mu[1] + theta1[tchid[1], 1];

- Bob

On Saturday, January 30, 2016 at 6:42:21 PM UTC-5, Christopher Candelaria wrote:
> Back to my question...
>
> I would appreciate any general feedback about my code, but I think I found a reason why my model tends to run slowly; specially, I am not sure if I am handling missing test score data values efficiently. Specifically, I have been filling in missing test score data values with parameter values as necessary. Please see lines 153 to 167 for specific details. I borrowed some code from Ben Goodrich to do this, but I am not sure if there is a better way of handling missing values given that Stan has been updated regularly over the past year. I will also say that I am trying to estimate this model using a large, district data set.

If you have multivariate normal priors on unknown parameters, I pretty much always do a multivariate Matt trick and it pretty much always seems to be fine. In other words, instead of having
theta ~ multi_normal(zeros, Gamma);
in the model block, put
theta <- L * z_theta;
in the transformed parameters block where L is a Cholesky factor such that L * L' = Gamma but you often don't need to form Gamma until the generated quantities block if at all and put
z_theta ~ normal(0,1); // implies theta ~ multi_normal_cholesky(zeros, L);
in the model block. Then you can compose L as the product of a diagonal matrix of standard deviations and the Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix that has an lkj_corr_cholesky() prior. You can do whatever you want for the prior on the standard deviations and it usually doesn't matter too much.

Ben
